It can be paid for over a fifty-year period, a long drawnout things so that we're adding pennies to the monthly water bill for people to pay for that.

passages.q: What is that actually going to cost?
passages.t: I don't remember the figure, and I'm not even sure there is a current figure on that. As a matter of fact, there never has been an agreement reached between the federal government and the city of Weston. So, I don't know whether they're going to ignore it and forget about it or what, but there is no agreement to that effect. It was a proposal made at one time. But the dam is being built at the height. The water's going to be there when the city of Weston, although it's not a city of water system. It's a private corporation and the water system begins with drawing water out of the river. Whether the government's going to say, you can't have it or not, doubtful to me. But, anyway, the whole point of the small watershed dam is that a really comprehensive system would've cost Lewis County people one way or another, many millions of dollars. I don't think people in Lewis County were about to stand, to pay millions of dollars for it, when the federal government was willing to do the other project, let's say solely at its own cost. To all intents and purposes, it really amounts to that. Although those facts were stated time, again, the people in the watershed area kept saying the smaller watersheds were a feasible alternative. Beyond that, there is very little money in the cell conservation services budget for small watershed projects today. We were told that it would be eight years in the planning alone. Eight years in the planning alone to come up with a plan for small watershed dams. I don't think they've even built any small watershed dams in West Virginia in recent years, because that particular budget is so very small. The only money they've had for years is planning. Now, this is information told to us by the soil conservation people themselves, who would have a vested interest in building small watershed dams. But they told us realistically it was a near hopeless alternative. So, we gave no credits to it, whatever. Got a little slightly sore throat. Excuse me. Go ahead.

passages.q: Tell me when you've talked enough. Bet the recreational aspect of it had a lot of appeal too.
passages.t: Well, not so much locally, I don't think. So, I say primarily we were concerned about getting flood stopped. Now it has a greater appeal as time goes on, because as a former businessman here, and I'm retired, but certainly the business community is concerned about, the economic future of Lewis County and does see a great potential benefit from the recreational development. But personally speaking, I don't have a boat, don't intend to buy a boat. I don't fish. [laughter] So, I'm not personally interested in that. I think people outside this county probably are much more interested when the plans that the department of Natural Resources had for the recreational development began to be made known. A great deal of interest began to be exercised in the project by people outside Lewis County. That is to say, people who were interested in fishing and in boating and what one can get off of a large impoundment of water. So, I think there's more interest in that outside of Lewis County in terms of numbers of people than it is, than there is actually in Lewis County.

passages.q: Are the dollars, though, generated going to stay here? Dollars generated from that recreational business? Do you predict the –
passages.t: You look at Grafton, you look at Sutton Dam, and it doesn't appear that the large numbers of dollars are generated by those projects or Summersville. But on the other hand, there are many people who come into those communities every summer and the weekends. Their populations are certainly swollen by a few thousand people. They do buy gasoline, and they do buy some food and some bring it with them, I suppose, depending on how long I'm going to be there. There's bound to be some benefit from it. I don't think it will be a major concern. On the other hand, I think that – let's say Sutton has not exploited, its Braxton County's two lakes, if you like. Or Gassaway or Burnsville, have exploited them as much as they might. There've been some new motels built in those communities, which I suppose in part their customers come from people who come in to enjoy the recreation. But the old saying, if you build a better mousetrap, the world will be the pathway to your door is not really true. You can build a better mousetrap, but you still got to exploit the fact you have. Now, I think there is a spirit within Lewis County in its business community to begin to exploit the recreational advantages of Stonewall Jackson Lake. I think we'll see more benefit here than I have noted, at least in other projects of this kind in West Virginia. The Chamber of Commerce is initiating a study to determine what's been done in most successfully in projects of this kind in other areas outside of the state of West Virginia. So, we can try to incorporate some of those kinds of plans and ideas in the thinking and the planning that goes on here. I'm very much interested in that. But that's only in the very earliest stages of study. I do believe that one can do an awful lot more than has been done so far by projects at this time. I think the figures that are often put out by the Corps of Engineers about the numbers of visitors that come into these projects is exaggerated. But on the other hand, I'm sure will benefit if we have the right push on the part of the local community wanting to see it happen.

passages.q: Has there been a projection of about how many new permanent businesses will locate here? / The label that you have in your shirt, maybe in your coat jacket.
passages.t: Not that I'm aware of, no. The opponents have said that the area is not conducive to industrial – bring them employed about 1,100 people, one's around six hundred people, one around 500. We have a silk label plant here in Weston. A lot of those are made here in the plant, employing around a hundred people. So, there is a small industry in Lewis County. There is no small industry in Lewis County that's dependent upon the water, because there never has been any adequate water supply here. We did have, by the way, we had the core of our plant consider Lewis County as a location, the one that's in Buchanan. You're familiar with that plant?

passages.q: Yeah.
passages.t: Showed them this site right here, which I owned at the time, which is now the golf course right beside our house. They were very much interested. It had everything they were looking for except water. They told the water company how much water they needed on a guaranteed basis, on a daily basis. The water company says, "We can't do it. We don't have it." So, that was an industry which perhaps we lost because of the lack of water. I'm not saying that they might not have made – if the water had been here, they still might have made a decision to locate Buchanan or somewhere else. But at least we know for certain that the basic reason they turned down that location was no water or not enough water. That plant – I wish I could remember the figures for you – seems to me is that they're in Upshur County. That one client is currently paying about $175,000 a year in property taxes. It employs roughly three hundred people. The payroll's about four million. It was a real plum and maybe plants of that kind can be attracted to Lewis County when there's plenty of water flowing down the river. I certainly hope that it will help us get some additional plants in here.

passages.q: But no one had got them located. / But there is a date by which it is proposed.
passages.t: No. Well, the dam is still under construction and things – Yeah. 1987, I believe. But, again, I don't know what industry would want to locate here until they see the water in the river. I mean, things happen. We could go to war and the construction could be held for years to come or something of that nature. So, the prudent businessman will wait, I think, to see that the water is there before he makes the move. But it does give us another leg up in the tracking industry. We've got the interstate. We've got a very favorable gas costs here in Lewis County, at least as favorable as anywhere else in the state of West Virginia. Our real handicap is land. This was a good site here, about fifty acres would've been more than enough for cohort's needs. But land will continue to be our big handicap in tracking anything like a fairly large plant. But a plant that needs only three or four acres, when we've got plenty of that kind of land for them.

passages.q: I guess one last question. What is your vision for Lewis County? What do you see it becoming someday and how do you see this project as being a link in that – / – development? / It is 3,400 acres. If that is the right size, stretched up and down all those little –
passages.t: Well – I think Lewis County has some potential as a recreational area. The dam will, I think, be the biggest lake – I believe the biggest lake in the state, manmade. The water quality should be quite good. If you looked at a map to see where that thing goes, it's quite incredible. Yeah. It makes an awful lot of shoreline, a great amount of good fishing area and so forth. I don't know how much more of a hunting mecca it will be than the average part of West Virginia is already. You see that fence back here behind my house, that's to keep the deer out of the garden in summertime. I don't think we'll have any more deer as a result of the lake. But the future of Lewis County lies in the recreational potential of Stonewall Jackson Lake. It lies in a small industry. I think it lies to a certain extent in developing what history there is here. I said earlier the great history of Lewis County – this is one of the most historic regions of the Hackers Creek area is, and early frontier settlement and early white man front and Indian warfare. Some of the most historic events of the Western Virginia frontier occurred right here in Lewis County on Hackers Creek, which is up in the northern part of the county, far from the dam area. So, there's a great potential there, I believe, in development. As a matter of fact, the Chamber of Commerce years ago, it was the Western Chamber of Commerce. About ten, twelve years ago, it became the Lewis County Chamber of Commerce. About two months ago, we changed the name to the Historic Lewis County Chamber of Commerce. Because it is a part of our plan to emphasize the past history of Lewis County two hundred years or so ago and the Stonewall Jackson in Jackson's Mill. So, there is I think, a considerable potential here for tourism income. Small industry tourism income from the historical background and Stonewall Jackson Lake.

passages.q: I guess one last question. What is your vision for Lewis County? What do you see it becoming someday and how do you see this project as being a link in that – / – development? / It is 3,400 acres. If that is the right size, stretched up and down all those little –
passages.t: Small industry tourism income from the historical background and Stonewall Jackson Lake. It's a pretty nice community now. It's west and the great shortcoming is the fact that it has flooded so often, and that's discouraged people from making any reasonable investment in their properties. They don't paint up, they don't fix up. Not knowing that next week, it will all be ruined. The river as it flows through Weston has been our greatest eyesore. Until we got the sewage plant going, a terrible stinking mess in the summertime. But it can be converted now that we will have water control, I think, into a lovely park right through the center of the community. That's one of the things we are also going to work toward. Have you ever been to San Antonio?

passages.q: No. / Good. Well, I certainly appreciate your time and it is nice to – / – nice to have. If I can put some of the material I am gathering together into a radio program, a documentary, is it all right to use your material for that? / Maybe I could get you to even – [end of transcript]
passages.t: San Antonio did a marvelous thing down there. They got a stream goes through that middle of that town, and they just converted it into a magnificent park. It's somewhat bigger than what we're talking about here. But there is that potential of converting what has been our greatest liability as far as Weston goes into our greatest asset by landscaping that river as it flows through town because we'll have control on the water. That's certainly something that we're very much interested in and I'm very much interested in. It's one of those projects we're going to have to have some governmental help on. We're going to be working with Washington and to the extent we can with Charleston to try to develop that, now that we're going to have some control. Weston can become one of the most attractive communities in West Virginia as long as I live and can spend some time working at it, I intend to. Very glad to give it to you. Sure.

passages.q: Today is the 29th of November, and we're sitting in the Sheraton Hotel trying to get some levels on this tape recorder. Testing one, two. Bob, you just drove up from – / Charleston for this gas and oil meeting tonight. I wanted to take the opportunity to ask you some of your feelings about the Stonewall Jackson Dam. Maybe just would start by telling me about your experience in trying to get the project defunded after you got to Congress.
passages.t: Charleston. I've been a longtime opponent of the dam. I was an opponent when I first started practicing law and actually was involved in a lawsuit in state Circuit Court challenging one aspect of the dam back in the mid to late, well, late [19]70s. Then when I was elected to the legislature in 1980, I voted for the resolution to pass to the state senate that what put the state senate on record as opposing the dam. When I went to Congress, there was a campaign issue bitterly fought out. I went to Congress and said that I would oppose the dam when the appropriations measure came up in Congress, and led a fight, and it bitterly divided the West Virginia delegation. The other members were for it. We prevailed, and our position prevailed in the House. The House voted to stop funding for the dam for that year. It went to the Senate. The Senate refused to go along with that. It went to conference, and the house conferees were appointed by the appropriations chairman all rolled over on me. So, the money was put back in. It was clear from that point that even if you could get the votes to pass the House, you weren't going to pass the Senate, and you weren't going to pass the conferees the political equation have to change. My position on the dam now – that's been two years – my position on the dam now is that the dam is being built. The actual physical construction has started on the structure itself. The dam is being built. I recognize that fact the political equation has not changed. Litigation was not successful. So, you accept the fact that the dam is being built, and you move on. I think that the dam, though, had some important lessons. First of all, I don't think that the Congress is as quick to rush into some of these projects as they were back in the [19]70s when this really began to gain momentum.

passages.q: Today is the 29th of November, and we're sitting in the Sheraton Hotel trying to get some levels on this tape recorder. Testing one, two. Bob, you just drove up from – / Charleston for this gas and oil meeting tonight. I wanted to take the opportunity to ask you some of your feelings about the Stonewall Jackson Dam. Maybe just would start by telling me about your experience in trying to get the project defunded after you got to Congress.
passages.t: First of all, I don't think that the Congress is as quick to rush into some of these projects as they were back in the [19]70s when this really began to gain momentum. I think that it's taught all of us a lesson, both in the state and outside the state, on the feasibility of these projects. The federal budget deficit is not going to permit building projects that have such questionable cost-benefit ratio as a dam. So, as I say, we learned a lot of lessons. Unfortunately, it made a point, the dam is going to be built. That's, I guess, the way it is.

passages.q: What was your opposition in the Senate? Could you go into a little more detail there?
passages.t: Well, the dam was staunchly defended and advocated by both West Virginia senators. They performed their role, which was to lobby very hard within the Senate. First of all, to restore the funding, or to make sure that the funding was not cut in the (companion?] of Senate Bill. They also made numerous telephone calls to House members in the assumption that the bill would be coming back to the house at some time for a vote. They just wanted to try and make sure that the House members were prepared and had their side of the story. It's pretty extensive telephoning going on, and a lot of House members contacted. But as I say, each of us was definitely waging this battle as hard as we could.

passages.q: Is this generally how they do business, our two senators?
passages.t: Well, I'm not sure. As I say, they both felt very, very strongly about the dam, as I did some of the members of the West Virginia delegation. Their position was that they'd worked very hard to get the dam over many years and dog gone it, they were going to keep it. As I said, they presented their point of view, did it very forcefully.

passages.q: In the process of this fight, did you learn anything about why this dam is so important to them?
passages.t: I think the dam is the last of an era. The dam, I think, was conceived at a time when there was much more of a flooding problem than there presently is now. The dam has its origins in the [19]30s and the [19]40s. At one time there was a scheme, a plan, to build a series of dams in this area of the country to control flooding. There was a dam to be built that was twice the size of this dam at Rohrsburg right on the Pennsylvania-West Virginia line. It was to be a companion dam to the Stonewall Dam. It was today in the Cheat River at the same time the Stonewall Dam was being constructed on the West Fork. Interestingly enough, Congress deauthorized The Rohrsburg Dam long before Stonewall ever got its first money. Why did it deauthorize it? Because Pennsylvania environmentalists and hunters and fishers were pretty upset about what was going to happen in their area. So, the larger the two dams, the one that would have really meant more flood control, if indeed, that's an argument for it to Pittsburgh was deauthorized, and yet you have the dam over the smaller river. The other interesting thing when I started putting maps up on for display was, of course, this dam is 100 miles from Pittsburgh, and yet it was portrayed as stopping torrents of water pouring through Pittsburgh and wiping the city out. I don't doubt the sincerity of people who advocated for the dam. It's a very bitter, divisive issue in my district. I lost the county that the dam is in when I ran in the election the first time. I don't doubt the sincerity of it, but it just doesn't add up. It's a case of a dam, I felt, in which you took the law, and the law says that there has to be a cost-benefit analysis. In other words, for every dollar you put into a dam, you have to get more than $1 benefits out.

passages.q: In the process of this fight, did you learn anything about why this dam is so important to them?
passages.t: In other words, for every dollar you put into a dam, you have to get more than $1 benefits out. Well, at first, they went and tried to do it on the basis of pollution control. Well, in the [19]50s and the [19]60s, having large amounts of water that you suddenly flushed down a river to diffuse or dilute the pollution was an acceptable means. But then we went to sewer systems, and that's why EPA and construction grants program was created in the [19]70s. So, this is now an unacceptable system of pollution control, but yet was grandfathered in when authorizations began. So, you were still permitted to use for the purpose of this dam a cost-benefit analysis for pollution. I think pollution control, as I recall, it's considered 15 percent of the dam's purpose. Then came recreation. No other dam in the country has 52 percent of its cost-benefit analysis attributed to recreation. It becomes even more interesting when you recognize that the dam is going to flood some of the best hunting land in the state and farming land. So, I tell people a little facetiously, I think we're trading deer for fish. Then, there's boating in the marina. The state of West Virginia has been enticed into signing a contract for the dam that they will reimburse the Corps for the construction of the recreation facilities. Possible estimated cost may go as high as $50 million. Well, here's the state of West Virginia that three times had to freeze pay, has not given its public employees a pay raise in three years, until this last year, which is in great financial straits right now, as many states are. Yet it's been committed to an open ended obligation for who knows how long this payback. The cost, for instance, the initial cost simply that the state was going to have to come up with the upfront cost has gone from over $300,000 which was the initial estimate to well over a million dollars.

passages.q: In the process of this fight, did you learn anything about why this dam is so important to them?
passages.t: The cost, for instance, the initial cost simply that the state was going to have to come up with the upfront cost has gone from over $300,000 which was the initial estimate to well over a million dollars. Now, the rest of the cost-benefit analysis, we had pollution control, we had recreation, and flood control. Well, as I say, I think we've already dealt with flood control because it was to stop flooding both in the city of Weston, which has had serious flooding from time to time, as well as Clarksburg as well as Pittsburgh. But the interesting thing is that if you total up – we ran this check – if you total up the total damage caused by flooding of this river, and from the year, I believe, before the 20th century from I think 1885 to 1980, it comes to something like $25 to $28 million.

passages.q: In both in both cities?
passages.t: In both cities. In which case then the dam – I mean, it would be much cheaper just paying everybody off every time. The other thing I always thought could be done and never was satisfactorily investigated, was a series of watersheds. Now, one watershed has been built already and it seems to have controlled some of the flooding off one of the creeks. The trouble becomes, though, when the Army Corps of Engineers takes over a project, they take it over and preempt everyone else, including the Soil Conservation Service. The other nice thing about the Soil Conservation Service is it requires a local share to be put up. In other words, if flooding is that much of a problem, then the localities will recognize that and they'll put up part of the money to pay for the cost of construction. It was a dam, the local unit does not have to put up any money, and that's what happened. Now, the interesting thing to me is that in the Public Works authorization bill that was considered in this last session of Congress that passed the House, in which 180 new projects were authorized, there is a cost sharing element to it. For projects such as Stonewall, I don't think Stonewall Dam would be built today, if it were coming up and being considered solely on its merits. But it got its authorization many years ago from Congress, and it bumped along for a while. Then, it got its first appropriation. When I got to Congress, it had already had four years of appropriations. $83 million had already been spent. By that time, the thing has a life definitely of its own, and it gets real hard to stop.

passages.q: You said it had been grandfathered in. Who grandfathered in? How did they do that?
passages.t: Of course, I wasn't in the Congress, and that was several years before. But in order to make the cost-benefit analysis work, you had to give it a certain percentage dedicated towards pollution control. Well, the pollution control method that the dam would provide is one that's not accepted now by EPA. So, at some point along the line, as I say, I wasn't there. So, I can't say who did what and when. The dam maintained the life of its own and got an exception to that provision.

passages.q: That was about 1970?
passages.t: As I recollect, it was in the early [19]70s. Because in [19]72 is when the Clean Water Act changed, or actually came into being, and construction grants program started. You went to sewer systems as opposed to more – you went to source point control. You went to sewer systems as opposed to systems such as just flooding areas from time to time to wash pollution down. As I say, I refer to it, perhaps unscientifically, as pollution dilution.

passages.q: Well, that really covers what I wanted to talk to you about. Do you have any other feelings about the project, or do you know of other areas where the Corps is going to be working in West Virginia in the near future?
passages.t: No, I think the Corps has learned from this one too. I mean, if part of the justification for this dam is that we need more recreation and that it's going to be an economic boom, it's pointed out by many that within 100 miles of this lake that will be created, Army Corps of Engineers created lakes, the Sutton Dam, the Burnsville Dam and the Summersville Dam, providing recreation, doing good job in some instances. Braxton County, next county down from Lewis County, has two of these three projects, the Sutton and Burnsville Dam, yet has some of the highest unemployment in the state. So, I don't know that it is that panacea. I guess the point there now, and particularly as a representative of the district, I fought the battle. A lot of people fought the battle. It wasn't me. I was kind of the tail end of it. I got there. But a lot of people fought the battle. We've lost. I think two important things, one is we've got to now make the best out of the stain that we can and the second thing is I hope that we all learn from it, that we learn not to rush into these projects prematurely. We learned how much momentum they can gain on their own, and we learned not to do it again. I guess one of the things that bothers me a little bit about the dam, well, I've accepted the fact that dam is being built and that that's going to continue. The thing that seems to me is important now is to make sure that one, it's built properly, and it provides some of those promises that a lot of its question – but we have to hope – come to fulfillment. One is employment. First step is employment on the construction of the dam. I'm greatly concerned because I see a joint venture between a West Virginia firm and a Virginia firm.

passages.q: Well, that really covers what I wanted to talk to you about. Do you have any other feelings about the project, or do you know of other areas where the Corps is going to be working in West Virginia in the near future?
passages.t: I'm greatly concerned because I see a joint venture between a West Virginia firm and a Virginia firm. Every time I hold mobile office hours in Lewis county, I have people complaining that local people aren't working there in the numbers that they should. Then, of course, there's the employment we hope to come from whatever tourism is attracted. The economic incentives, hopefully, maybe it can be a water supply for industry locating here. So, I think that's important. Then there are other areas too. The vast amounts of land that are being taken by this dam; they won't be used for several years. It won't be flooded for several years. In many cases, they won't be used for many years after that. They won't be flooded. They'll just be acquired by the Corps, 20,000 acres has been acquired. I'd like to see a little better agricultural policy. We've seen some farmers land condemned, but at least, let's get the maximum use out of land that we can. So, I've spoken to the Corps of Engineers about the chance of an interim agricultural policy in which you permit haying to go on. You permit grazing to go on. That you permit more leasing of the land to go on than it's presently going on. Right now, only small trucks are being put out and people being permitted to use. It seems to me we've got the land there. It's not going to be used for much for a while. So, let's let the people use it, particularly giving first option to the people who once owned it. That only seems fair. So, it seems to me that the battle, to the extent, there's a battle, has moved now to okay, the dam is being built. But let's make sure it gets used properly, and let's make sure that it gets the maximum use that it can.

passages.q: I guess these feelings haven't been communicated yet to some of the farmers who are still there. Because the ones I've talked to have a lot of anxiety that they're going to be pushed off very soon.
passages.t: I think I can understand that that's a concern of mine, that there's not been good communication. Certainly, the (Hevner?) incident did not do anything to allay those fears. The farmers that I've talked to are having a lot of trouble trying to get some statement of whatever interim policy there could be. Some of them do not actually live in the take area. They may have a field there. They don't actually live in the take area, but they've worked there all their lives. The crops are there. The grazing is being done there. They hay there. It seems to me that there ought to be an easy-to-understand policy to permit them to continue doing so for as long as it's feasible. At this stage, I think the Corps could stand some good public relations over the dam. I think even some of the dam supporters have been a little shaken lately by the heavyhanded manner in which the (Hevners?) were taken off. I think some are genuinely feeling that, "Well, yeah, good. We support the dam, but we don't see any reason the land can't be utilized much more productively than it presently is being."

passages.q: Thank you very much. / Were you a part of that?
passages.t: Well, I worked in 1977. I've seen floods in West Virginia. I worked in [19]77 in the flood recovery of Williamson after it was washed out in that – Yes. I went in there as a legal aid lawyer, retainer to legal aid providing legal services, because I've been involved in the Buffalo Creek recovery also these several years after the Buffalo Creek flood. So, southern West Virginia, which has high mountains, steep terrain, not like this area of the country where the Stonewall Dam is being built. But southern West Virginia has real flooding problems, and you can't get a dam built there across the Tug Fork. Well, the cost-benefit ratio doesn't work out. So, what they're doing, they're dredging, and they're constructing higher flood walls. They're doing things like that, which hopefully will make Williamson in that area safe. But my question comes in why can't you do that elsewhere?

passages.q: For Weston? / Think of the cost of building a flood wall versus –
passages.t: Sure. Weston doesn't have a flood wall. I think it would be worth trying to see whether you can avoid the 250. But for a lot of people, one thing I was struck by is those people who were marginal on the dam, who weren't so sure it was needed. I mean, they didn't have a clear position. Remember that we're in a state with the highest unemployment in the country, and there's a lot of fear and a need for hope. What I think the main argument that I kept hearing for this dam is it's going to create jobs, both in the construction and in the afterlife. That, I think, was what finally motivated a lot of people and caused some to swing over that otherwise might have been opposed to it on strictly budget grounds. Yes. That's a tough argument when you're talking to somebody who's been out of work two years in the construction industry, and they're saying, "Bob, we need this dam, and we need the work. You go through all the rational arguments about why it's not going to do that much for you. It's very short term. I think I figured out at one point that based on the number of people they're projecting would work on the dam, versus the cost, each job was costing something like, $20,000 or something. It was some incredible figure. If you want to spend $250 million in the third congressional district of West Virginia, I've got a lot of places where we need roads, where we need flood control. The Kanawha River, for instance, the West Fork River, a lot of these. We need watersheds. There are a lot of infrastructure projects that you could build if you want to give me $250 million. I think what concerns me also is that when you put so much resources in one small area for such a questionable purpose, and then I think it's a lot harder to go back and get it when you really need it. But as I say, the dam is going to be built now that the key is we've got to try and make the most of it. I hope it lives up to its promise. I hope I'm wrong, but I don't regret making –

passages.q: Those promises were made at the Sutton, for the Sutton Dam too. If there's any place –
passages.t: What's interesting to me that the Sutton or the Braxton County Commission passed a resolution in the late [19]70s recommending to the Lewis County commission not to get involved with the dam. Pointing out that it was not the kind of economic panacea they had been promised. Right after I took office, I met with all the county commissions to find out what was on their mind and what we could work with them on. The Braxton County Commission, which was entirely new from entirely different from the one that had passed that earlier resolution, told me they'd do the same thing again. They'd put the dam? No. The county commission told me that they would make the same recommendation in 1983 that their predecessors had made in the late [19]70s, that it just was not an economically feasible or worthwhile enterprise. They really would urge him to be cautious about getting into it.

passages.q: When I asked Bill Adler about what industries he had lined up ready to take advantage of this wonderful source of water, he said that, of course, there weren't any. But he said the industries have a way of waiting to see the things completed before them.
passages.t: I hope he's right. I guess what I look at is the main area that I've seen develop in Weston, developed outside the dam area. Anyhow, it's a shopping area with new discount store, new grocery store, that has grown up in Weston. It grew up not because of the dam was coming. It grew up because of its proximity to the interstate. There's an industrial park, and we're trying to get a water and sewer line out to that industrial park, hopefully it will be filled. There were arguments made that this dam was necessary for the synthetic fuels plant that was to be built in Morgantown. The SRC II plant that was later canceled, but it would need a good water supply. But there was a letter from the under secretary of energy that we unearthed saying that that was not a consideration in the placement of that plant at all. They were looking elsewhere for their water supply. But I hope he's right. We've got to hope he's right.

passages.q: That something comes of all it.
passages.t: Sure. There has been so much divisiveness, bitterness, people have lost their homes. You've got 20,000 acres that's been acquired, 1,000 people that I know of, displaced, people out of work, desperately hoping something comes of it. After all these many years, I hope that something good comes to this dam. I mean, it's going to be built, and I hope that something comes out of it. But as I say, I'm not sure it's worth the price that's been paid for it, not only in dollars, but in terms of human problems.

passages.q: Yes. I've heard a lot of very sad stories. You might be looking into the thing about people who have died as a result of being moved out, older people mostly.
passages.t: As you all know, there's an incredible affinity for the land here in West Virginia. Particularly, that land which you've lived on, and that land which has been in your family for many years, generations. Particularly, in farming, poor West Virginia – except for the eastern end of the state – we don't have much farming. This is some of the best farmland in the state. That's why the State Agricultural Commissioner was always sort of a lone Indian out there fighting and resisting the dam at the state house because of the loss of the farming land.

passages.q: But people in Weston would argue the other way that the land wasn't very productive.
passages.t: Yes. They would argue that indeed, and that it can be put to more productive uses. Of course, they remember the flood in the late [19]60s that they had in which the water rose fairly high up on many of the homes, drove some of them out of their homes. It was a serious flood. The question is whether that flood could happen today because of the watersheds. Also, the question is whether flood walls and an adequate storm drainage system could handle the water. There are many other reasons. I held a public meeting right after I took office to give everyone a chance to tell me why the dam was necessary. There were some very dramatic presentations made. The ministry of the hospital told me about how when the water rises to a certain level, that you have to go take people and patients by four-wheel drive over a mountaintop to get them to the hospital. Owners of factories told me about how their employees couldn't get to work because of it and there was a lot of downtime. So, people, I guess just have to weigh that, though, how much was that economic loss compared to the cost of this dam? Also, those are situations that I think – and with the possible exception of the hospital – those are situations you run into in any normal locality. I got a road that has a chance of having water rise on it too and keeping me from driving across it at some point. So, once again, could there have been other flood control measures, watersheds, storm drainage systems, flood walls, and did we need to proceed with this dam? That question is not going to be answered. The dam is being built. As I say, I hope it fulfills all the purposes and more. It's got to because the price has been pretty stiff that's been paid for it. [end of transcript]

passages.q: Today is the 5th of February, 1985. I'm on my way to the Vandalia community to interview Jack Linger and maybe his son, Louis, and his daughter-in-law, Beth, I hope. It's a cloudy day. There've been lots of snow. I'm trying to interview and get home before it gets bad.
passages.t: But that whole strip developed around 33 is built on a swamp. When they were stripping out there, they'd haul the dirt off the coal job at night and evenings and weekends and fill the swamps. Now, you've got all the hecks and the high rise and Krogers, and just that whole damn thing down through there is all filled. The stone coal used to get up and run into the swamp. But now when it gets up, by God, it runs into West. There's no place for the water to go. No place for it to spread out. I can go out there right today and there's somebody dumping dirt in that stream channel filling the dent.

passages.q: That's because there's not enough – / – land around.
passages.t: Land. Yes. They'll go to Buckhannon or any of these little towns around here, and, hell, they've got room to expand around Weston. I mean, they've built on all their land. Of course, the buildings aren't much count. They've been flooded so many times. They weren't much to start with because they knew they were going to get flooded. So, they didn't put much into it and they haven't done much in the way of maintenance. The physical plan of Weston, West Virginia, it's gone. There's just nothing there. It's a shame. Any of those buildings downtown – main store buildings, the office buildings, hell, just stand back and look at them. Take a level with you. I mean, [laughter], some of those buildings are leaning. They're falling. Well, they're built on the swamp. There's not a real good foundation under there. So, they're falling in. Windows and doors don't open and shut. I mean, it's a joke to even spend a million dollars to save that town. They'd be ahead to just clean it off and plant the damn place some corn or something. That was the whole idea of the project when it first started though, wasn't it? To stop flooding. Yes. fifty years ago, we're saying. It's come this far, and now, they say that the only way the whole thing was justified was through recreation.

passages.q: Fifty-two percent.
passages.t: Yes. What do they say? Seventy or eighty percent of that – ninety percent of the planned recreation doesn't even require a body of water? [laughter] If they've got all the – they don't even need the dam. Let's just forget it and go ahead and have a park or whatever the hell they want to do. Well, what I know about this is what I found out mostly through lobbying up there in D.C. That the recreation is the only way they could justify it. They have to cost ratio benefit, whatever they call it. For every dollar they spend, they have to have a dollar in return or X amount of dollars. They couldn't do it with the dam. So, they added the recreation, forgetting the $80 million they'd already spent for the dam. They reevaluate the project now with this recreation. So, they didn't count that $80 million. Just so it happened, it turned out just right. They got that ratio they needed. According to this Corps own standards, if it doesn't meet that ratio, they drop the project. That's what I understand is how it got this far. Twelve thousand acres of recreation is what saved the dam. Well, what saved the dam is Jennings Randolph and Robert C. Byrd and (Robert Hahn?). I mean, that's what saved the damn Rockefeller. Then of course, the coal companies and gas companies and utilities, the people that support them. It's just Central West Virginia at its finest. It's the same game that they've [laughter] been playing here as long as I can remember. Well, I've always thought that if you can't get the people in the immediate town – the very first town below the dam with some kind of a decision of go or row on the project. But Weston itself had no influence on whether the project is going to be done or not. Nobody in West Virginia has any influence on it. Well, that's because – All the things are done by outside. Weston hadn't taken an interest in it.

passages.q: Fifty-two percent.
passages.t: Weston hadn't taken an interest in it. If they want a dam, that's what they should have. You don't know – nobody knows that for sure. There's never been a survey of who wants a dam and what they want it for or anything. That's just certain people in town, Bill Adler, and such, they have the influence and the opportunity to make it what it is. No one's dragging them back. They just keep going. No one's saying, "Well, what are we getting here? There's no guarantee of anything of what we're going to get. Once the project's built and all the recreation is built in West Virginia, the state taxpayers is responsible for the upkeep and maintenance of that recreation forever. Or until they push the big button or something. But when they're gone and the federal goes, it's all ours then. I don't know where the money's going to come from other than higher taxes, land taxes, and whatever.

passages.q: We're already a state that's leading the country in unemployment. / Can't even pay unemployment insurance. / How many are? Do you know anybody?
passages.t: Oh, yes. There's another good one too. He's working on that project around here. How many people around this town are working on that project? [laughter] I don't know anybody. The ones that have that I've heard of, they worked on a road job. Maybe they'd work eighty-nine days and then they'd get laid off. Which the way I've heard it is if they work ninety days, then they have to pay state taxes on them. If they drop at eighty-nine days, they don't have to pay state taxes – these companies that are building the roads; Virginia, Maryland, or wherever they're from. Pennsylvania. Pennsylvania. So, that's how they work them if they'd work them at all. I don't know of anybody working on the project at all. Matthew, do you know anybody? If Matthew doesn't know even then a couple truckers. Yes. The only time they're hauling for them is when they can't get a good job.

passages.q: Who's the rest of them working on it?
passages.t: Well, J.F. Allen built a lot of 81, North, South in Virginia. So, he kind of cut his teeth over there in that right-to-work state, and he found out how to do it. You simply bring these boys in from a poorer part of the country than what we have here, and they're willing to do it. Nobody knows who's in there. Nobody knows what's going on. I've talked to quite a few people that have tried to get on and couldn't. I've talked to a lot of people that were promised jobs and none of them are working. We have a lot of them up here at Walkersville, all the union boys. I mean, they were just red hot for it. By God, [laughter], not a single one of them working. You ask them about it and all, they'll hang their head and tell you it sure is a goddamn shame about people losing their home and all. But, "Well, we've got to work. Hell, I've got to have that $14, $15 an hour, work a couple months out of the year and then live on unemployment the rest. Well, hell, I get more unemployment than you make, you stupid bastard. You ought to do it too." Tell them about the – But none of them is working on it.

passages.q: [laughter]
passages.t: They're all sitting home. [inaudible] from Fairmont there to come down and saw us here last year or so. Oh, yes. The union. When the dam project went scab, then the union boys came to us. What are we going to do? Oh, what are we going to do? Just wringing their hands. See, they'd been promised. Washington promised them. Everybody promised them. Steel workers, same way. Steel workers and – nothing. Well, it's over. Those boys aren't going to work. They've been paying Joe Powell to go lobby against us for years. Now, they get nothing back. So, they're upset. I mean, it's kind of a private club.

passages.q: So, Weiss Brothers. / They're out now? / They built all these roads and –
passages.t: Weiss Brothers are just gone. I'm not sure if they managed to pay their state and local taxes yet or not. Last we heard, they owed them $27,000 to the county. $7,000 that they owed yet. Yes. Yes, they built one section. See, J.F. Allen is the big winner. I mean, J.F. Allen is – they'll call it the J.F. Allen Dam before it's over. He got the dam project and he's getting the rest of the roads. He'll have the bulk of them. I mean, that just takes you right back into this – Maxwell, Elkins banks. You heard about them loaning our money out, didn't you?

passages.q: No.
passages.t: The people down here that were condemned and couldn't get their money, well, they did a little investigating and here find out the government had deposited the money in the federal court. But Judge Maxwell had put the money in the Elkins banks in non-interest [laughter] bearing accounts. The Elkins banks had loaned [laughter] the money out [laughter]. So, they were making twenty percent on it, and, hell, the government didn't have it to give us. So, people here were – well, like Jim McLean was forced to go and borrow money to buy a house. I mean, you've got a zero vacancy rate in the county. So, when a house does come up, you just can't say, "Well, hold it for me." You've got to put your money down.

passages.q: What do you mean a zero vacancy rate? / Do you know anybody that's moved into places like that?
passages.t: There's no housing available other than low-income compartment or something, and there's not much of that. Trailers. Yes. There's a fellow right down the road here who would be a good man for you to talk to, Todd Harris. He's moved out of the big house, big barns, nice farm. He's now in a house trailer sitting, just [laughter] – they cut a little ditch back in the side of the hill – a little flat spot. That's where his trailer is. [laughter] He's just shaking his head. He can't believe it. The governments on him every day to get his cattle out and move off. Get out of here. They're not going to do anything with it. Let it grow up, they're supposed to do.

passages.q: What did this community used to be like years ago?
passages.t: Well, pretty much typical rural West Virginia community. Well, when I was growing up people still farmed with horses. A big crew would come around to make hay, maybe ten, fifteen, twenty men, for dinner. Sometimes, they'd have to eat in shifts. It's just gone from that to people importing hay now from out of state in order to feed what livestock's left. The government won't let us cut the meadows. You're supposed to stay off of them. Of course, now, the government sucks are going in there – people that are trading with them and cutting those same meadows for mulch. Or cutting the hay to sell. So, there's Aubrey West buying hay, John Radabaugh buying hay, Jim McLean buying hay. I mean, Jim has been a hay producer as long as I've known him. We were unloading hay this morning over there for Aubrey, and Jim stopped and wanted the [laughter] man's name and phone number. He needs hay. So, it's just been a complete reversal. I guess back in the fifties, there was more livestock within a fifty mile radius of West and West Virginia than anywhere else on the face of the earth. I mean, it was wall to wall. Yes, there's still some sizable herds, but nothing like there used to be. The Lingers, now they're one of the last big operators. They bought them another farm. There isn't enough room on their new place. If all their cattle would stand up all the time, there wouldn't be enough room for them to go in there and stand. [laughter] Yes, it's sad. I mean, this area was rich. People weren't flashy, but if they wanted a new truck, they paid cash for it. That kind of thing. But now, they're broke. Then you look across the fence and there's the gas company. New multimillion dollar facilities at government expense, and you wonder, what the gas company's doing that we weren't doing. Maybe we didn't make the right campaign [laughter] contributions or something's wrong there someplace. I mean, they're getting new roads, new wells, new pipelines, new compressor stations, everything, brand new. New microwave system. The boys that they have out in the field now tending the wells don't realize it, but they're helping to cut their own throats.

passages.q: How's that?
passages.t: Well, the microwave, they'll operate the whole storage field from Pittsburgh by computer. That's what they're doing. The government is paying to eliminate their workforce. So, all these fellows – it's been father to son for generations here, working this gas field. That's coming to a screech and halt. Of course, Congress knows this. They've discussed it. They asked the gas company about it. The gas company said, "Well, these people can either move or [laughter] go work someplace else or they can quit. It doesn't matter much to us what they do." That was the end of it. But it's just beginning to dawn on some of these boys that their head's on the chopping block now.

passages.q: Was this right here your grandfather's place? / What kind of people were they?
passages.t: Yes. Yes. He lived here and great granddad before him. I don't really know much about them. Granddad – [laughter] – tall and white beard, dark suit was about all. I was pretty small when he died. Well, actually he was my great-grandfather. My grandfather on my mother's side was already dead. He died out in Iowa someplace. I never knew him.

passages.q: But growing up here, you worked on a lot of horse-drawn farms? / What's become of the old people? / They don't transplant very well.
passages.t: Yes. All the tractors were coming on when I was growing up. Buried them. No. They get shipping fever or something. I'm not sure what it is they do. [laughter] Well, you've got people like (Vernon Tyre?), a perfect example of someone who just – when someone like that leaves, your heart goes right with him. I mean, Jesus, you have to know Vernon, of course, to really appreciate him.

passages.q: What was he like?
passages.t: He was a worker and had a good sense of humor and he just loved life. He and his wife both, they loved it out here. They lived right over there and married over there since – or lived over there since they were married anyway, I think. God, he lived to get out. He had a gristmill over there and the whole works. He was just what the country was all about – how it was made, I'd say. People like him stuck to it, took the hard times with the good times. Never took advantage of anybody other than some rough horse trade maybe. But [laughter] that'd be someone to go talk to maybe. Really good.

passages.q: What happened to him?
passages.t: Well, he got moved out into one of the little boxes they call trailers there. Overhead in his trailer [inaudible] now in that area somewhere. Over on Grass Run. But that's just a fine example of the kind of people they've moved out. I don't know. Like I said earlier, I've only been associated with this project and the people not too many years. There's been a lot of people gone that I don't know anything about other than just what I hear. I've met a lot of them those inside, many that aren't here now for either being thrown out or just up and died. Whether it was caused from natural causes or stress and worry that the whole thing brought on them. When you see a man crying because he is being thrown off his property, it'll get to you a little bit.

passages.q: Was he the guy at the festival who stood up? / Darrel Sennett. / He did?
passages.t: No, man, he isn't. No, no. That was (Darrel Sennett?). Darrel went right from the stage to the hospital. He damn near died. I mean, it just absolutely kills people. Just on blue. Several had heart attacks and strokes the same day that they received their condemnation notice. A man down here, Posey, federal marshals came and gave him the notice. He was sitting in his wheelchair and had his rifle across his lap. He told them. He said, "I got it." He said, "You might get me." But [laughter] he said, "You'll know it." He died that night.

passages.q: Who was that?
passages.t: Posey, a boy down here. Oh, he wasn't that old. He had a heart condition. Three or four kids. Who was it? Bill (Jewel?) had a stroke the same day he got his papers. I mean, it was really just unbelievable. But what they're facing, it's not like they can get another farm someplace. I mean, even the ones that have done well in condemnation barely get enough to buy them a tract house or a trailer and a lot, and that sort of thing. George and Teddy (Barn?) lived right down here at Roanoke. I think they had ten, fifteen acres of ground, milk cows. Raised heifers – registered jersey heifers. Of course, a big garden, cut their own hay, and just selfsufficient. Young people would jump in and help them if they needed a hand. But for the most part, they did for themselves. The government came in, evicted them. They moved, and in less than a year, they were both dead. They had nothing to do. All their livestock was gone. Their equipment was gone. They had a damn trailer and a porch and that was it. They just simply worried themselves to death.

passages.q: Why is this particular land so important to these particular people?
passages.t: I think they realize that this country needs it. That the world needs it. You can produce enough on this land to provide for yourself, your family, and a couple other families without any problem. I mean, here, we are looking at Ethiopia and Chad, and this country's not that far off. I mean, we're getting pictures that look like the thirties again out of the Dust Bowl. People that are plowing up the prairies, they do all right in a wet year, but that first dry year, she's all gone – all the soil. It'll never grow anything again.

passages.q: Is that what's happening to farmers in the Midwest now, do you think? / Just getting foreclosed on again.
passages.t: To a certain extent, yes. Yes. Well, they can't produce a crop. They were doing all right as long as their land prices were going up every year. But now, that's going the other direction. So, their hedge is gone and now they're being foreclosed on. So, those people go out of business and who's going to grow the food? I mean, we're sitting right here close to the eastern market. You could raise anything here. I mean, this is where the white people came when they came across the Allegheny's. They came right to this very spot. I mean, they had the choice. [laughter] They could have gone anywhere in the state, anywhere in the country, and this is where they chose to settle. Not that they didn't travel and look other country over, but this was it. This is where the Indians had their big corn fields.

passages.q: Bill Adler said there wasn't enough tax paid in this whole area to support a schoolteacher. About $17,000 a year, he said hardly enough to pay the salary of a schoolteacher. / But that's not the farmer's fault, right?
passages.t: I'd say he's probably right. Pretty close. No. You don't hear any farmers bitching about not having to pay taxes. Like I said, these people weren't flashy. I mean, you talk about underground economy. The government had no idea what was going on here. They never enforced the whiskey tax. [laughter] They just didn't have any idea. Of course, the county assessor, they're not going to do anything. Land prices were kept within reason. Just a few years ago, you could buy a good farm for eight or $10,000. People from D.C. hadn't even heard of Lewis County. They didn't want it. People traded. They sold land to the people that were going to farm it, maybe kept it in the family or in the community. Money just wasn't everything. Not to Bill Adler. I mean, Bill wants to see that money changing hands because he wants to get his little paws in there. That's what he wants. That's Bill's biggest gripe. The fact that they never cut him in on the game up here.

passages.q: They didn't? / Who never cut him in? / What kind of a cut did he want? / Was he in banking?
passages.t: No. The farmers. I mean, they need Bill Adler like they needed another hole in their head. I mean, some asshole like him, [laughter] you just ignore him. They just laughed at him. Well, I'd say he'd have taken the whole pie if he could have gotten it. Communication. What all was he in? Cable. TV cable. He married money, that sort of thing. Country club. Coal. He's big in coal. He's one of the front men for the coal company. I guess it's embarrassing to have these shitty cattle trucks coming through his town. There's a certain amount of mess made with them and fouls the air. Then you have these nasty smelling farmers. They go down there and come back through town. No one wanted them in the stores. Of course, they've changed that now. They even have specials on Tuesday when they run the stock sale. Those other things died out and maybe these farmers weren't so bad after all. But they've managed to kill the big farms. The major feed stores in town are all diversifying now, going into lawn and garden products and that sort of thing. The big feed mills, you don't see the trucks lined up waiting to buy several thousand dollars worth of feed every week. They've lost. Overall, the county is going to be much poorer. Now, the Bill Adlers, now, they'll do fine. They'll make their money. But the majority of the people are going to be much worse off. I mean, the lower income people worked for the glass plants and things here in the county. Well, even the gas company employees. I mean, everybody bought a beef. You didn't go to the store and buy your meat. You dealt with a local farmer and you bought a steer. You didn't pay near what you'd pay for it if you got a piece at a time. Well, that's pretty well gone. I mean, as you eliminate these farms – this whole thing, they're going more to, everything's got to be written down.

passages.q: They didn't? / Who never cut him in? / What kind of a cut did he want? / Was he in banking?
passages.t: I mean, as you eliminate these farms – this whole thing, they're going more to, everything's got to be written down. Everything has to be run through the bank and that sort of thing. Old people came to unload this hay this morning that had enough money in their pocket to pay for the load. Three or four men there could have pulled it out. I mean, it was fourteen, $1,500, but they have the money. You need a couple thousand dollars, all you have to do is go see them. The Bill Adlers don't want that. They want people my age. If I need $2,000, I've got to go to the bank and borrow it and wait for the approval and [laughter] all that sort of thing. There isn't just plunk your money down and go. As you drive through Weston, I want you to notice how cramped the town is.

passages.q: Yes.
passages.t: One rock can stop traffic every direction. There's no alternate route around town. They complain about the town being stopped when it floods. Yes, they're absolutely right. But they have never – I mean, if this problem is so bad and they've been here all these years, certainly, they could have built another road parallel in this thing. So, you could cut and go. When school was out and what state hospital that's out, there's a major traffic jam in Weston. It lasts twenty minutes, a half an hour, then the streets are empty again. Everybody has to go through the same path and just one set of doors down there. That's the way they want to keep it.

passages.q: So, the thing, it'll help the shopping, the economy in town or why is that? What would be the advantage in keeping it [inaudible 00:29:17]?
passages.t: I'd say that that would be a lot of it, funnel the traffic through. But they're a real paranoid town. Young people can't borrow money in that town and go into business. You work for someone else. Private enterprise does not exist. If you're an old country club type person, then, sure, you go into it, or if they sponsor you. But as far as a young person, starting out on his own and doing something, that's not going to happen. The ones that have borrowed money outside of Weston and come in and attempted to set up a business will just simply run out of business. They're hassled. The fire code man come, just, they are busy. They're kept busy with just petty bullshit until they finally quit. We go to town. They want a business, a franchise license. They want a Weston franchise license, on and on and on. Here comes the fire inspector, here comes – you can't get a thing done.

passages.q: What's been the history of resistance to the Corps of Engineers in this community?
passages.t: Pretty good. They played a waiting game and they waited until the men died. Then they came in and they picked on the women and the children and the wimps. That's just about the size of it. Divide and conquer. Notes called then the Corps contacts the local bank. They say, "Who's behind in their payments?" "Well, here, Michael Klein, he's missed three months now." "Now who else?" "Well, Ronnie Simmons. He's missed a couple payments." "Okay. Thank you." Then the Corps approaches Michael Klein first. "Mike, here's what we're going to do. We're going to give you enough to pay off all your debts.

passages.q: Was the Upper West Fork Watershed Association organized to combat the Corps? Was that the purpose of it?
passages.t: Stop the project. It wasn't so much anti-Corps. It was anti-dam. Yes, that was at first [laughter]. Of course, the watershed became radicalized, just like all organizations do over the years. It was pretty effective in a lot of ways until the Corps actually broke up the communities – destroyed the fabric of the communities. They toss you a hot potato. Then you have one shot, and there's one farm available and maybe you can make a go of it over there. If you sell early for what they're offering and you have enough for a down payment on that farm, they're going to give you fifteen or $20,000 relocation money. Maybe you can put this whole thing together and make a go of it. They picked through, and it's mostly economic pressure that they put on people. Some boys were hired who didn't have jobs. They were hired by the state road. They were hired by the gas company. Various people that trade with the Corps. Then once they were hired then the propaganda, career and retirement and health benefits and all this and that and that, sure, it was pretty good. Some boys that worked for me – excellent jobs. I mean, just fantastic jobs. I was glad to see them get it. But once they moved, [laughter] once they were out of here, then somehow their services were no longer required by their [laughter] new employers. No benefits, nothing. They were terminated. It was all just a –

passages.q: Mine drive.
passages.t: – yes, a little shell game. But there's a lot of different ways. I mean, this coal business, people going around telling them that there's no way that you're going to get paid for your coal unless you lease to a certain company. The company, I mean, hell, it was obvious that the company was in on this. They weren't fighting the project, and no way in hell they were fighting for it. Because then they turn around and sell this coal to the government. So, they get paid a hell of a lot more for the coal than if they'd have actually mined it and marketed it. They get their money all on paper. Of course, the more leases they have, the better they do. So, the coal people here in the community were working against us. Then the oil and gas, they did the same with them. For a long time, the Corps employees didn't show up. They came disguised as gas men. They rode in the gas company vehicles and wore gas company hats. They did that until the gas company started getting stopped. That kind of freaked the gas company. Because they realized then that there were a lot of people standing between them and their profits. They turned the wrong valve or happened to close the road or something like that at the wrong time of year, then you can cut Pittsburgh's gas right off. So, then they started to cool it. They started telling the Corps, "Hey, maybe [laughter] you drive your own vehicle and wear your own damn hat. We don't want to take you in anymore."

passages.q: The community put enough pressure on them, you mean?
passages.t: Yes. Yes. Well, they had an aerial survey. See, they still don't have a good picture of this area – a good map of it. I mean, they're bluffing. A lot of their plans are just smoke. They don't have any idea. The recreation plan, I think they said someplace in it that they'd know more about areas of local interest once they obtained access to the property, things like that. Well, some of this property they've owned for eight or ten years [laughter] and they still don't have access to it. But anyhow, they were trying to get this aerial survey done. They put big white crosses around in people's (matters?). They surveyed around and they laid off these crosses. Well, people just watched them. A few of them were taken up, but the majority of them stayed there. It finally dawned on people what they were doing. Then they watched the sky because you have to have pretty clear sky to take much of an aerial photograph, and you have to do it before the leaves come out in the spring. So, the buds are coming, everything's starting to green up. It's cloudy weather, and with cloudy weather, boy, here comes beautiful – I mean, beautiful blue skies. Here comes the airplane. He flew over this way and he looked, and he flew over that way, and he cocked his wings and he looked, and there wasn't one of those crosses left. Now, the night before, they were all over. For months after that [laughter], you'd see these old farmers, they'd flip their truck seat forward and there'd be a ball of that white plastic wrapped around survey stakes. Now, many people you'd – good church people, folks you never think would do anything like that. We followed a car down that had one of those hanging out of the trunk. A stream [laughter] was hanging out of the trunk. It was done at night and it was spontaneous. Yes. Miles and miles of road survey disappeared.

passages.q: The community put enough pressure on them, you mean?
passages.t: Miles and miles of road survey disappeared. It was there one day and the next day [laughter] it wasn't there. That brought the FBI in. I asked that little FBI agent, I said, "You must have really done something horrible. "What do you mean? I said, "Look, even if you get a bust down here, what's it going to look like on your record? You arrested some eighty-year-old woman for pulling up survey stakes in her yard. [laughter] I said, "That's really going to look good, isn't it? I said, "You're in a no-win situation. Well, anyway, it dawned on the boy maybe he wasn't, and he kind of backed off. He saw how stupid it was. But they came in here like gangbusters.

passages.q: The FBI did.
passages.t: Oh shit. I mean yes, it was a joke. The FBI's here. Here comes the FBI. I mean, hey, you've never seen the guy before and he was driving a government car. Tell him the first time with Aunt Alice in the cemetery. That was the first time the FBI was caught. Oh, they promised to leave. Well, originally, they were going to take all the cemeteries. Then they decided that since there was so much local hell raised over it, I don't know, people caught them in the cemeteries and took their maps from them and things like that. These three women looked over and these fellows were there in the cemetery. They went over to see what they were doing. Well, we're going to move this cemetery. This one guy was sitting on this lady's grandfather's tombstone, and she asked him to get off. Well, he wasn't getting up. He was pretty comfortable right there. So, she says, "Well, you can wait right there then. She says, "I'll be back. They said, "Where are you going? She said, "I'm going to the house to get my gun," and went to the house. By the time she got back [laughter], they'd all cleared out. It was just things like that. But undercover agents, I mean, state police in here, the damn FBI – who in the hell knows what all of them spooky bastards were up to. Hanging around the woods at night. That's how we ended up with these attack dogs and stuff. It got to the point where you'd hear the people out there on a nice quiet night in the brush. We'd go out to, of course, see what the hell they were up to. We divided them up one night. I've got that old ten gauge. When it goes off, it just lights up the sky. [laughter] Just throws a pound of lead in the air, and just forty-five minutes, there's still pellets falling. We just went right in on a nest up here, above the house watching us. When that gun cracked – of course, I shot it in the air. When that gun went off, they broke and run in every direction. We ran one right down the gully, just almost into the house.

passages.q: [laughter]
passages.t: Well, he was just like a turkey lost. The rest of the night, you'd hear him holler. [laughter] We'd answer him and slip up on him again, crack that old shotgun again. Boy, he'd holler and run [laughter]. But we finally just had to go to dogs. Then that was the end of that fun. We just turned the dogs loose and they'd put those boys to flight. But they'd be sitting on the ridge watching people and that sort of thing. Follow you. When your wife would go out to a meeting or something, they'd stop her and hassle her, and just small things. They had a (Cedar?) patrolman. I don't know. Do you know what Cedar workers are?

passages.q: The Cedar? Money?
passages.t: Yes, Cedar Money. The guy is not even supposed to be carrying a weapon. He's a little, old, white-haired fellow from down Lumberport. He's a ticket writing cop there – a Cedar cop. Well, he's in his pickup. He's got his deer rifle, a shotgun and a 357 Magnum. He's in his uniform and he keeps driving up the road – dead end road. I mean, we know no one lives up there and nothing he can be doing and turns around and drifts back down past the house. He does this for several evenings. One evening, I'm coming in from work and he's sitting down there at the intersection. I pull up, see what the hell he wants up. Comes that 357 and he's shaking. I thought I'd bought it that night. Well, somehow I left the truck in gear and I was clear down on the floor and [laughter] that truck, it took me right out of there. I felt pretty good. But the police came up and picked him up the next morning. Took a whole bunch of them in, and they were armed. Sheriff has a whole wall down there of weapons he has taking off these boys.

passages.q: So, who were they working for? / They sub out their protection?
passages.t: Ultimately, the Corps of Engineers. But it's broken down – Oh, yes. Yes. Oh, Christ, it's an outfit down Harrison County, Clarksburg. They go over to Glen Elk and get the street punks and give them a hundred bucks, a couple pistols, and a flashlight, and they're certified armed guards. These people started hassling folks. They started going around roughing people up and that kind of shit. We got old people and it just doesn't take a whole lot of that. So, then the old people, of course had shotguns and they pulled them out and dusted them off. Oh, it's just a miracle somebody hadn't been killed. It's just –

passages.q: Sounds like the old mine company and spread them in the system. / Sure.
passages.t: Yes. Now, the thing that really broke it up was Ralph Hall. That'd be a good man for you to talk to. But he's real shy of the press. He's been burnt a couple times and he just won't hardly talk. Yes. But he came up and pulled this Cedar cop and that whole crew in. It's funny that it snowed that night, and this Cedar cop – this guard had gone to an old neighbor's outbuilding. So, he'd moved the house and moved the neighbor out. But his outbuildings were still there and he still owned that part of his farm. This Cedar cop had gone into the buildings and had carried stuff back to his truck. The tracks were right there in the snow. So, a lot of burglaries. One old man lived over across the river – Pete Peterson. They tried him two or three times – tried to force his back door. Pete yanked the door open and stuck a .45 into this boy's chin, asked him if maybe he could help him with something. The kid louds how he was just getting [laughter] along pretty fine and [laughter], all he wanted to do is leave. They tried Pete in a whole month or two later. They drove a van right up to his bedroom window. Evidently, they were just going to knock the window out and load his stuff. If Pete had a lot of guns, they were going to load his collection and tag off. Of course, they'd have probably killed Pete. But he rolled out and he hollered at them, and the boys jumped back in the truck. Pete unloaded on him with his first gun. He took two pistols with him. He said he wasn't having much results, and he remembered they had bird shot. He was not real blood thirsty. I mean, he'd burn you, but he didn't want to kill you. He said, "I switched to the gun with solids in it. He said, "I started getting results then. [laughter] The police found the van. It was just shot all to hell. That's as far as that's ever gone. I mean, it's just almost like the state police and the FBI are encouraging this lawless element to come in here and hassle people.

passages.q: I interviewed a woman from Little Skin Creek, who told some of the worst horror stories I've ever heard about looters. / This was the source of it?
passages.t: Oh, it's unbelievable. Yes. You'll see the labor coming in for the road job. Clendenin, Point South, Charleston. There might be a half a dozen of them in a big old Buick or Oldsmobile. Maybe one or two of them go to work flagging or shoveling gravel or something. The rest of them just fan out in the community. They act like they're on the crusades or something. It's their duty to punish us for resisting the government and they're going to do it by taking, by God, whatever of value they can find. They'll come right in your house. They'll come right in your house, broad daylight, start carrying stuff off. If you say anything to them, "Well, it's government property. I'll take anything I want. We caught people stealing Christmas tree. Now, I've probably given more trees away than I've ever sold. This one fellow, he's worked a lot for some of my subcontractors. Of course, I knew him. He and his wife and another couple were down there on a Sunday. We just stopped by to pick up a tree for people. There they were. They said they wanted a tree. I said, "Fine. See if you can find what you want. Well, they looked the patch over and couldn't find anything that suited them. So, I asked them what they wanted. Well, they told me. I told them pretty much where that kind of tree was. Hell, no, there wasn't anything in there they wanted. In the meantime, the two women and this man went up to the old cellar loft, opened the door, and went in. The man stuck his head out. I was telling this boy who worked for the subs right at that moment about all these people that were stealing from us. This man sticks his head – he's a gas company employee, by the way. This man that stuck his head out has a pretty good paying job, benefits, and all. Sticks his head out the door and he says, "Hey, Mike. He says, "Come on up here.

passages.q: I interviewed a woman from Little Skin Creek, who told some of the worst horror stories I've ever heard about looters. / This was the source of it?
passages.t: He says, "Come on up here. Vicky's found some more goodies. Now, these people are from Weston, and that's what they do evenings and weekends. Come out, break locks, steal whatever the hell they can haul off. I suggested that maybe they leave. This boy was just embarrassed. There wasn't even anything he could say. He just left. Missy and I took the tree down we were delivering. On the way back out of town, we met him, and they had a tree. So, just for honoring this, I called the fellow that evening. I asked him if he found the tree he wanted. Well, they didn't get a tree. I told him, I said, "A thief's one thing. But a liar is maybe even a little worse. He said, "You better talk to my wife. Well, she started out by calling me a goddamn Jew. Claimed that I planted those trees down there and took care of them all those years, just making a trap for her. That people like me ought to be done away with. Oh, just unbelievable. I was, again, at fault. I should have never planted those damn trees. I surely shouldn't have sheared them and make them look like Christmas trees. I tempted them and they fell for it, but it was my fault. That's what you get. People that you know. Oh, that guy standing there and says, "Oh, it's union project. It's just horrible. Then you look around and see if there's anything in haul with him. They come up and cut your timber. They'll shoot your livestock. Or they'll cut the ear tag out so you know which one they got. Or maybe cut the head off of it.
