Sometimes, they just take the tenderloin, cut the stakes out of it, and leave the rest. Absolutely unbelievable. I've got a whole list of people that we've caught stealing. People that you just wouldn't think would live like that. Just for honoring us, when I run across them, I ask them about it, and you get some [laughter] really off-the-wall answers.

passages.q: Well, it's government property?
passages.t: Yes. You have no business in there. That's not yours anymore. Of course, once they get the project fleeced, then they just – well, there's no boundary out there. I mean, they can't tell where the thing ends. So, hell, they come up our road all the time. Come up, turn around, spot, and steal. If you want to get rid of stuff, all you have to do is put it out where they can see it, and, hell, it's gone. [laughter] You don't have to worry about getting rid of trash anymore. Just lay it out there and they'll tag it. These are good church people, taxpayers, good citizens. That lady, I told her. I said, "You're nothing but a thief." Oh, she just blew up. She was no thief. It was all my fault. I brought all that on myself. Well, you asked earlier what kind of community it was.

passages.q: Yes.
passages.t: I don't think there was a lock that worked in this end of Lewis County. If the lock did work, no one knew where the key was to it. If you needed something, you went and got it. It was just wide open. It's gone from that to, you see these poor old farmers, now they look like janitors. They might have a hundred keys on their damn belt. [laughter] They're forever losing the key to the lock and then have to cut these padlocks off. Most of them are going to go bankrupt just buying locks trying to protect the stuff that they have. It's a hassle. You leave a gate unlocked, next time you come back, maybe just a couple three hours later, someone's gone in, taken the batteries from all the farm equipment. Taken all the spare tires, the chains, the come alongs, axes, mattocks. I used to think people wouldn't steal anything to work with. I had a pair of pole loppers that I cut pine limbs with. They've hung down in the pine patch for fifteen years. You finish cutting, the end of the day, just hang it right there in the tree. Come back and get it the next day and go back to work. I'll be damned if somebody didn't steal it. I'm hoping they just took it and threw it in the river. But I'm afraid they might have actually carried it off the property. They'll tear the siding off of a barn. They'll go in and tear all the copper out of the house – all the plumbing. People living in the house. They'll take the windows out of it, take the doors off the hinges.

passages.q: Catch somebody gone.
passages.t: Yes. Well, it's just unbelievable. Like I say, these are the people with God on their side that are doing this. You got the praying hands and the whole damn nine yards. Bumper sticker is yours through Christ, and there they are, a bunch of thieves. Is (Joe Aldi?) still in business? No, not really. Give those to you. You can have those if you want. Those were a few of the businesses that are directly farm oriented that we asked, if this dam's built, how's it going to affect your business? There's $615,000 a year right there. One of those businesses says that they're going to lose a third. Two of them are out of business now. Two of those –

passages.q: Is Joe out of business now? / I wanted to ask you too about the history of the festival. Why you got that – / Yes. Tell me about the festival. / Didn't you tell me one time that through this festival, you were hoping also to show the strong cultural and historical –
passages.t: Yes. Joe Aldi's and Quarter Tractor. They're both out of business. I don't think Quarter's completely under. They're not doing much farm, but – Right, there's the brainchild of it. It was all his idea. [laughter] Well, just a chance to get people together, make as much money as we need to run on from year to year. Oh, yes.

passages.q: – aspects of the community?
passages.t: They call it an organizing tool. You get the exposure and people that have never really had much to do with outsiders, the press, that sort of thing. It was just a chance to get them together with the press plus our support people from Washington and Charleston – the young professionals. It just kind of answered a whole lot of needs there. We had people that wanted to come in. We wanted them to publicize, of course, what they were doing. Wanted to publicize what we had here, why we were willing to fight for it. I mean, right now, there's enough interest in the community that they want to see the festival go on come what may with the dam. They see it as, well, a good way to get their church windows fixed [laughter] and send the kids to camp. A lot of the different little groups, that's their sole money maker. Instead of having half a dozen bake sales and two or three dinners, they can do the festival one weekend out of the year and make all the money they need to run on. Yes, it spreads the message.

passages.q: There was some question about it being held this year, was there?
passages.t: Oh, there's been a question about it [laughter] being held every year. The first year was the worst. Well, yes, the first was the worst. People said, "Hell no. [laughter] No damn way." Rock and roll and drugs and – Woodstock. Yes. Those naked people in the creek, no way were they going to have a festival. Well, the first one, we scattered – well, you were down there. We scattered it out. That way when the riots started, it wouldn't be too hard to [laughter] corner the people. But now, it's gone from that to just about total community support. I mean, it's a nice way to get Bill Adler and Tom Feeney's money and use it against them. Because their families come out and support us. The men won't do it, but the women and their children know that – [laughter] Yes. Maybe it's just a way to rag the old man, I don't know. We really enjoy that. Bob Earl's kids and wife and – of course, we make everybody welcome. I mean, we're not saying they're not going to get a good cussing or something, but anyone can come. That's an open microphone. You can get up and say any damn thing you want to say. But it's giving the people some focus, I guess, to their life. Tell Mike about Marvin Marshall's kids and the square yard. Do you know Marvin Marshall? He was a real estate appraiser – contract appraiser for the Corps. One of his kids described him as being totally despicable, just no redeeming feature. The son of a bitch will do anything. They bought him a square yard of land. [laughter] So, he had to condemn himself in the end [laughter].

passages.q: How did that square land business get? / Tell me from the beginning about that whole strategy.
passages.t: It pretty much dog nodded the court there for several years. It just about caused internal hemorrhage. Well, just numbers. We were playing a numbers game with them. We figured as long as they were chewing on one the square yard at a time, it would take them a lot longer to get the rest of it. Of course, they said that they would condemn it with one fell swoop and that was it. But they didn't. They condemned it one square yard at a time. Some people divided their square yards, deeded their minerals [laughter] to someone else and maybe just broke it. I mean, the lawyers showed them no mercy. So, now, the scuttlebutt we got out of the federal court in Elkins, it just caused them a hell of a lot of work.

passages.q: Nobody ever condemned my square yard. I never heard about it. / It is?
passages.t: If they couldn't find the people, they just published it in the newspaper. Your money's sitting in the court in Elkins, Michael. They condemned it for less than what you paid for it. Eighty-five cents a square yard or something. Don't worry about that because a lot of people were condemned to less than what they'd paid for their property. [laughter] Yes. They didn't want you to feel any different. [laughter] Drove them nuts for a while and it made us a lot of money. Yes. It was a good money making trend, and again, spread the word. People owned a little square yard, they wanted to see it and plant flags on it and stuff. Or flowers. Yes, and they felt more part of the damn fight. They felt more that they were involved in what was happening to us. That was nice. Pope got some. President Carter, I think got three or four square yards. Pope got one square yard. Jennings Randolph and Bob Byrd, Jay Rockefeller, they all were square yard owners [laughter].

passages.q: Pretty interesting. / Well, Jack Linger told me with a real twinkle in his eye this morning that he didn't think that the water would ever rise over there. What do you suppose he was talking about? / You mean once they get the minerals out? / Who's they?
passages.t: I don't know how many we ultimately did sell. Sold a lot. Oh, I'd say once they get what they want, they'll lose interest in the dam. Yes. Well, the ownership of the minerals. Not necessarily getting them out, but just having the right to get them out. Powers that be. Don't know exactly who. They are a good name for them. They're the ones that ride in behind Byrd, Randolph, coal company, gas company. Hell, they might not even be in this country. J.F. Allen. Sure as hell aren't in this state [laughter], the Rockefeller people – the money people.

passages.q: Once they get the minerals in there, they may be content and just drop the whole thing. / What do you mean as a dry dam? / $250 million for a dry dam? / What?
passages.t: Yes or operate the dam as a dry dam. They just don't close it unless there's a hell of a flood. You got a lot of water coming down the creek, shut the gate, catch the water. We're trained not to let water out. I'd take it over a wetland, Michael. I'd take it over a wetland. [laughter] You could still use the land. Come down and look at the lake, and you're going to think, "$250 million for that fucking lake? Fat chance." I mean, it's a screw job no matter which way you go. The next time we have a good rain, come down and look at the river. That's the lake right there. Absolutely nothing. Oh, yes. A lot of shore. Hell, a lot of shoreline. That's just about the only thing. A fourth of the water that they have stored at Tygart. Same surface acreage, only it's broken up into a half dozen little fingers. So, you don't have a big expanse of water. Jack Lingers would be the biggest, and it's going to be so damn shallow. [audio gap] They're mining it, both sides of us. Rockefeller's into it. Metallurgical coal runs twelve to fourteen feet thick right through this area. It's gas. Then on top of that, you've got the gas.

passages.q: Rockefeller owns some of that coal?
passages.t: He'll end up owning all of it. Yes. Carter Oil Company, a subsidiary of Exxon, came through. I don't know if you heard about that coal scam or not. But they bought up leases all around the project area. This is when they didn't think the project was going to go. There was some chance of us killing it. Then as soon as the project started forward again, then they dropped those leases. But they came in and coal drilled. They've located the coal. They know exactly what it is and where and what it's worth. BTUs, ashcon, tanned ash, I mean, the whole – they've got our assay. They know what they have. Of course, you add in the strip coal, which there's quite a bit. Like over there at Aubrey West, the only thing on top of that strip coal is a little bit of clay. No brush grass there that they'd have to skin off. That's it. I mean, hell, send a damn loader in there, you can make some serious money. The Aspinall's farm, Jack's farm, that whole Skin Creek area, there's just nothing over the top of that coal. That's the Redstone Coal. They'll load it out. Of course, they build a road through it. They have to have a building site. That's the way they'll get that. The pond itself – the lake, it won't be any more than just a glorified sediment pond. That's really the only thing they're going to use it for. It's never going to amount to anything. The first time we ever went to court with him – the Corps's own attorney, our attorney asked him if there's going to be water skiing on the lake. The Corps's attorney laughed and said, "Well, it would require a certain amount of skill." You just about have to hold onto the back of the boat in order to water ski. You couldn't have over a couple feet of rope anyway. You can throw a rock across most sections of the lake.

passages.q: Like we were saying earlier this morning, the sediment from all this and the drainage from all this coal they're going to mine.
passages.t: Yes, and the expanded oil and gas development. The roads – I mean, the roads now are in the bottoms. The best spot to build a road is already occupied. Anything else is going to be less than a choice site. So, you've got a lot of erosion problems in the construction and in the maintenance. Now, equitable gas company is in the process of building roads all through what we always called the backwoodsy part. The part that had no roads in it is now going to be all developed. A dirt road – a mud road that you can run a tractor trailer on. Well, like the big roads in the federal forest. That's what we're looking at. They're dickering right now just how big and how many miles. The gas company writes and says, "Well, that's a nice road we have there. But, gee, if we had one halfway up the hill, then it'd be a lot easier to get the tractor trailers in. So, the Corps says, "Well, fine. The gas company said, "We have a local contractor working in the area and he's free to do the work now and has the equipment and the men. Save us all money if he goes ahead and does it. The Corps writes back and says, "Fine, you tell J.F. Allen to go ahead and build the road any way you want and send us the bill. Thank you very much. Then they write back a couple three weeks later and say, "Well, those two roads are sure nice. But if we had one right down the ridge, by God then that would really help. "Well, all right, go ahead. Build you one down the ridge. So, there goes the neighborhood. I don't know if you heard about the Horner Game Refuge or not – the big timber patch that they built the road through. You and I couldn't touch fingers around the oak trees that they cut. Virgin timber.

passages.q: Like we were saying earlier this morning, the sediment from all this and the drainage from all this coal they're going to mine.
passages.t: Virgin timber. Of course, they acted like they didn't know they were worth anything as they were loading them on the trucks, hauling them over to Mongold Lumber [laughter]. "What these logs? Hell, no. They aren't worth anything. That's the scam. They cut a big walnut tree back in that same hollow. I'd say it was close to a hundred feet to the first limb and it was a good four feet across the butt. They hauled it out and the gas company people took it out. These contractors, I mean, road builders, you see that yellow junk running every place back through the center of the project, and they're not on any kind of an authorized mission. They're doing nothing but stealing. No one owns it. It's the government. The government and these contractors are just in it hand in glove. Our little wildlife biologist, kind of a well-intentioned young fellow from over in the D.C. area, kind of idealistic. He called his corresponding member in the Corps of Engineers in Pittsburgh and called for a meeting. Brought him down here and took him in and showed him this virgin timber patch. Thought he'd get some help protecting it. The guy just immediately started [laughter] slobbering and rubbing his hands together, talking about what beautiful paneling that would make on his office back in Pittsburgh. Our little DNR man realized he might have made a hell of a mistake there. They're doing the same thing that they've done here since World War II, just pillage and rape. But it's now done at government expense and at a much accelerated rate. I mean, no one is there – they've got it behind gates. They won't let people in. If they catch you in there, they hassle the shit out of you and stick their dogs on you. They've pretty much managed to keep people out.

passages.q: So, who's profiting on all this? Is the Corps profiting?
passages.t: Kickbacks, yes. Corps employees are getting their share. The real estate men that came in here to buy these people out all started dabbling in real estate. Building, buying, remodeling, and got some real good deals and made some pretty good money. Of course, it was kind of playing the insider game. [laughter] They knew exactly what these landowners were going to be paid and they knew that there was no housing available for them. So, they started stuffing the market. You can just follow it right on through. The gas company, they're notorious. They've been robbing us since the turn of the century. Robbing billions and billions and billions out of this state and giving us damn little in return. Now, they'll come in the middle of winter when the road's soft and tear the hell out of it for you, stuff like that. They'll poison your livestock and cut your fence. But as far as sharing in the profits now, they don't do it. If you're lucky enough to have free gas in your deed, then they'll grudgingly let you have it. But that's just about it. If they could cut you off from that, they'd do it. For years, I kind of got the impression that they resented the landowners. Well, I guess they didn't mind driving their trucks through the meadows or through the corn fields to go in and play with their wells and change their charts. But, yes, I guess maybe it bothered them a little bit. Now, they're a lot more comfortable now that the landowners are gone and they can just drive their trucks any place they please. I think the gates probably did it. Having to open and close all those gates is – [laughter] – what finally got the gas company. But see, they opposed the project for years until they finally got it in writing that they got to do their own relocation work using their own men, their own contractors and subcontractors, and their own suppliers. The Corps said, "Oh, no, no, no. We're going to do it.

passages.q: So, who's profiting on all this? Is the Corps profiting?
passages.t: We're going to do it. Our contractors and our suppliers. The gas company said, "No, no, we won't trade. Some they held out. But see, these boys, I mean – well, it's something that since the turn of the century, they've learned how to fleece – every job is padded and you get your kickbacks. That's just the way things are done. That's the way you pay your politicians and that's the way you get your rates the way you want them. They're crooked as hell. These gas companies even steal gas and sell it back to each other, [laughter] that sort of thing. I mean, yes, it's just jam it incorporated. Only now, it's full blown. It's wide open. They don't have to open and shut any gates, just the big gate there at the project boundary. The rest of them, they can leave. That's one thing that there's few farm gates left. People have stolen them. They'll come in and take your gates right off your hinges. If they can't lift them off the hinges, then they'll take gate posts and all. They'll jack it out of the ground, throw it all on the truck. They've literally stolen thousands of gates. Just anything that you can pick up and run with.

passages.q: Anything that's not nailed down, and then they pry that loose.
passages.t: Yes, they'll pry that loose. If they can pull – How about a red maple tree? Oh my God. [laughter] A fellow over on Skin Creek had a specimen red maple tree in his yard. I don't know. It was about an eight, ten inch tree. What? Twenty, thirty feet tall? It was pretty. Absolutely – not a leaf out of place. These people that are helping the government, these crusaders – He was moved out by the dam. Yes, he was moved. These crusaders, well, they've got an appreciation for good looking stuff, and they spotted this tree. So, they spent, well, two or three weekends, just a couple different crews of people changing off, digging this tree out. They had, oh, eight, ten-foot hole, maybe fifteen feet across. Dug the root ball out and had it all wrapped in burlap, and I guess were going to bring a winch truck in to lift it out of the hole. Somebody finished up about midnight and they got back there, I guess about daylight Sunday morning to get the tree. Somebody had [laughter] gone in there and cut every limb off of it, except two little limbs [laughter] right in the top. All those people were just absolutely – they went wild. [laughter] Just danced up and down, hollered and cussed and carried on.

passages.q: Now, who would've done that?
passages.t: I don't know. I don't know. Some ornery person, but [laughter] that's just the way you get it. Metal detectors are another bet. People with their metal detectors all over the place on these old house sites. Cemeteries. Yes. Yes. A fellow took all the windows out of George Post's house down the road here. For some reason, he didn't put them in his truck. He carried them out and stacked them up against the maple tree, all in a row. He must have hauled something more valuable off that day and just didn't make it back to get the windows. When he came back, somebody had shot [laughter] right down through the whole row. [laughter] Every damn one of them was broken. Oh, I'll tell you, just not break your heart. Pilfering isn't what it once was.

passages.q: [laughter] What were the Weiss brothers like?
passages.t: Jewish mafia. [laughter] Gold rats. Tooth on a chain. He had his shirt unbuttoned down to his belly button, had an afro on his chest. White shiny teeth and all – a good looking fellow. Drove a Mercedes, had some kind of an extinct animal skin boots on [laughter]. True, Michael. They absolutely – [laughter] You'd loved him. They looked like Elliot Gould, that kind of work. I caught him up here in the hollow one day. I wanted to talk to him about the dusty conditions of the road. He was driving his brand new Lincoln. Well, I thought it was a mirage at first. I'd been working, and it was pretty hot and dry. Just coming into the hollow, his car was approaching me and had its turn signal on, like it was going to turn up Canoe Run. Then of course, they'd just torn hell out of Canoe Run. I mean, it took a pretty good vehicle to get up over it. I rubbed my eyes. Hell, I said, "That's not real. That's a mirage. Wheeled on in and that boy damn near hit me. He is cussing and hollering. So, I started up the road, noticed that I was throwing a good bit of dust in the air. He was right on my bumper. I thought, well, we don't want to get him dirty. So, I slowed down there, and he almost hit me again [laughter]. He got to talking to me, speaking in tongues and that sort of thing. So, I drove real slow there for a while. He kept honking his horn and raising hell. Gone on up the road here and I stopped at my mailbox. Well, here, they had a big crane. They got crossways in the road trying to drop a culvert in and torn the transmission out of it or something and had the road blocked. Around fifteen or twenty of his employees were up there. When I stopped at the mailbox, he suspected foul play. So, he waited way down the road.

passages.q: [laughter] What were the Weiss brothers like?
passages.t: So, he waited way down the road. I got my mail and I saw that I couldn't come on home. So, I said, "Well, what the hell? I'll go back and talk to him about this dust problem. Because we'd asked him maybe if they could put a little water on the road from time to time. Because it was kind of dangerous with school kids trying to walk in and all kinds of yukes and big pans and stuff running around. Hell, the damn dust was maybe fifteen, twenty inches deep. So, I thought I'd go back and talk to him. I turned the truck around and he broke and he tried to run. [laughter] He took off up a well road – access road and got up there [laughter] and realized he'd made a hell of a mistake because then I had him cornered. Round and round we went. Now, I didn't know one of those Lincolns would do that well, but now, he had the blue smoke rolling off those big old Michelin radios now [laughter]. Well, I finally got him high centered up there. [laughter] Then we did have a good conversation. I mean, these men, right? We've gone like maybe a half mile from this bunch of his employees and they're all running. They got wrenches and clubs and shit, going to come and save the big boss. [laughter] Of course, this dust is hard to run in. It's hot and they're tired anyway [laughter]. But we had a pretty good conversation. I'm telling him, "You know, calcium, you've got to put calcium on the – and you've got to put water. You've got to tank the tank truck and you've got to do this shit. He said, "Look at my car. Look at my car. Look what you did to my car. Of course, I spun a lot of rocks and shit up on his car. It just looked like hell [laughter]. I told him, I said, "We've got to do this every day. I said, "Look at my truck.

passages.q: [laughter] What were the Weiss brothers like?
passages.t: I said, "Look at my truck. I used to have a nice looking truck until you guys came in here. We had a lot of fun with them. Their chief engineer made a stab at me one day. Well, we have narrow roads and you have to watch ahead. If you see somebody coming and if they've come by the last stopping place, then you have to stop and let them come through. Well, these boys had God on their side and they were coming through and had court orders and all this stuff. If they met you, you had to back up. It didn't matter what you were doing. You had to back up and let them go through. A little bit of that went a long way. So, we decided two could play that game. I don't know. They used to call it chicken back in the fifties and early sixties before they got into drag racing [laughter]. But evidently, they were chicken because they found out how to get through barbed wire fences and up over banks and down into ditches. They tore up some equipment. This one engineer now, he'd made up his mind. He wasn't going to chicken anymore. Now, he was going get through with it. He'd talked to the local judge and they'd got the papers all fixed up. I mean, it was all set now. Just as soon as there was contact, they were going to arrest me and I was going to jail for a year for destruction of property. So, they built a four wheel drive vehicle, an old blazer, put a complete roll cage in it and just set it up like an off-road racer. They were going to hit me head on. The only problem was that I was coming back in the hollow just about the time that I should have been coming out. I mean, all you have to do is do something three times in a row, and that's your pattern. They'll sit there and watch for you forever more.

passages.q: [laughter] What were the Weiss brothers like?
passages.t: They'll sit there and watch for you forever more. You can change it five minutes and they'll never see you after that. So, yes, I was coming back in and he came up behind me. He realized that he was going to have to get his fresh paint on my front bumper or else it wouldn't hold up in court. Of course, he was so pumped up. He could have called the project off, but they had people up on the hill watching and radioing. It was like a big football play to him. So, he decided he'd go for it. But I don't know, he either ran out of guts or horsepower or something. He didn't get any further than just right behind my front wheel. But he proceeded to knock hell out of my old truck from there on back. I mean, it was awful. I couldn't really do much. I had my wife with me and she was seven months pregnant at the time. So, that kind of limited what I could do. He finally got enough of it and he broke and run. So, I left the vehicle right there and went to call the sheriff. Before the sheriff got there, here comes the state police, and they already had the warrant. It was already set up. It was just right in, and I was under arrest and going to jail. I said, "Wait a minute. It was the head of the state police detachment, Bob Castor. I said, "Come around here, Bob. "How by God? I said, "Well, I want to show you something. "Don't you try anything. I said, "Oh, I won't. Took him around and showed him my front bumper. There's ice and mud and snow on it. There's no paint. I showed him the side of my truck and the fresh paint – they'd just painted that blazer and there was paint all over it. All over the front of his truck, there was my paint. I said, "Now, you explain to me.

passages.q: [laughter] What were the Weiss brothers like?
passages.t: I said, "Now, you explain to me. I said, "I'm a little on the slow side, but I want you to tell me just how it was that I rammed the front of his vehicle with the side of mine. I said, "I'd just like to know that. He said, "All you sons of bitches [laughter] are coming into town. Well, in the meantime, these boys came back. But anyhow, we went to town. We finally got them to drop the charges, but it was only after a pretty good meeting down in their office trailer. It was my attorney and Francine and I and the Weiss brother and the chief engineer and all the people involved. But that fellow was so damn mad, he got up and walked [laughter] out of his own trailer. [laughter] He said, Mike – this is how bad they were. We were sitting and we were discussing the whole situation. He kept saying, "Matt had done this and Matt had done that. The telephone rings and he talk to this fellow on the phone. He said, "That was just one of my truck drivers who said that 3:00 p.m., Friday afternoon, you ran him off the road. We had our attorney sitting there. I looked at him and I said, "Bob, will you please tell this man where we were 3:00 p.m., Friday afternoon? He said, "Well, I'd have to check for sure, but I'm almost certain you were in my office. Now, we were in the lawyer's office at the time, but we had done all of this stuff. He said that Matt was the real nuisance. He was running his drivers off the road and he was doing this, and he was doing that. But they just set this whole thing up, and they swore up and down that I was not in the truck.

passages.q: But you were.
passages.t: Yes, I was in the truck. The school bus came by, and there I sat, waiting for Matt to come back after having called the sheriff. Nobody ever did investigate. There was no investigation of the accident. That's how set up that it already was. We got to the magistrate's office and I looked at him and I said, "Nobody in the world could believe that Matt tried to ram another vehicle with me in the truck." He said, "Are you sure you were in the truck? [laughter] I said, "How do you think I got here from up Canoe Run?" So, that's what engendered the first meeting with Mr. Weiss. That's also what broke the ice with the state police. I mean, they felt like fools. They really were made fools. I told them, I said, "Hey, boys, if I'm going to do anything, I'm going to do it right up front, and I'll tell you about it." I said, "There's none of this sneaky-peek bullshit with me." I said, "If I'm going to do it, it'll be high noon in front of everybody." I said, "Right now, you can see what the problem is."

passages.q: Did you ever get a new paint job out of the deal? / I thought he was gone.
passages.t: No. I got the pleasure of totaling their vehicle, and that was it. One of these days, Mr. Weiss and I are going to have a meeting. Mr. Weiss, as near as I can tell, still walks the same earth I do. One of these days, Mr. Weiss is going run into me, and then I'll get my paint job. [laughter] He told us, Michael – I said, "Look, we have to live there, and there are about fifty people that live up Canoe Run. We expect a certain amount of consideration. It's a one-lane road. Your big rigs don't need to be on the road the same time as the school buses." Just little considerations like that. I asked him, "Don't you feel any moral obligation whatsoever to the community in which you're working?" He said, "No." He was telling us a story about having armed guards on his other construction projects that shot a teenager for trying to steal from him. Shot and killed the teenager. Shot him in the head. They thought that was perfectly all right. All the kid was doing was like stealing batteries or something. He said, "I'm not afraid of you people." He said he had a lot of Italian mafia buddies up in Pittsburgh, and he'd bring them down to teach us a lesson. Said he'd take care of us. I asked him if he was threatening us [laughter]. Because he's always saying, "You're threatening us. You're threatening us." "Is that a threat, Mr. Weiss?" Our lawyer was there the whole time. Our attorney was there. He just couldn't believe this conversation [laughter] was actually going on. But I told him my maiden name was DeFranco, and I really didn't [laughter] think he could scare us very much.

passages.q: [laughter] / It went pretty good, though.
passages.t: But I mean, that was his general attitude. He was there to make a buck. He said to Matt, "Well, you're in business. He said, "Aren't you in business to make money? Matt said, "Not like that. He said, "I don't make money. Dealing in levels. So, on the surface, you have the little Bill Adlers, the local level. These people need flood control badly, and all that is a front. Then on the next level up, you have politicians who are supporting the project. But ultimately, the real level of it is the businesspeople – the people that make the real money. J.F. Allen is relatively small nationally, but he's a big contractor for West Virginia. We got the Dun and Bradstreet on him. I mean, he's a big growing concern for this state especially. Even beyond the contractors is you have people like Equitable Gas Company – these multimillion dollar companies. Equitable Gas Company makes or benefited – what is it? $26 million. More than that even. Something like an eighth of the project money is a direct benefit to Equitable Gas Company. I mean, relocating the utilities for the gas companies, the telephone companies, that's who's benefited the very most from this project. That's who really pushes these projects. Then you get way down here to little Bill Adler who's being used. The local people that think they want the project are just being used. They're promised all these development benefits. It's made to look so wonderful to them. They think, well, people like us are just standing in the way of progress. But in reality, it doesn't take too many of the looks at these projects across the country to see what happens. You can see that Bill Adler's being used, and he's too stupid to realize that the local people aren't going to benefit and don't ever benefit from these projects. But the big utility companies, they're the ones that benefit. As long as they control politicians, then how do you stop something like this?

passages.q: [laughter] / It went pretty good, though.
passages.t: As long as they control politicians, then how do you stop something like this? You can't get enough good, decent politicians like Bob Wise on your side. That's the problem. I think we could have stopped this dam if we could have organized – the way we organized now if we could have organized that way ten years ago or fifteen years ago. Because so many of our people are old now. There aren't enough young people that – we had the old people backing us, but there weren't enough of us young doers. There weren't enough strong feet and arms and heads left. I think that's what the Corps did. I think they really just bided their time until the Jack Lingers got old and tired. There just weren't enough of us to fill in the void because over the years, they'd all left. The area was so depressed to them. No future. There wasn't any future here. They were going to build the dam, and the Corps and the big utility companies, they can afford to do that. The big coal companies, they can afford to bide their time and wait. But if we would've had enough people, either our age now, or if we could have done what we did now ten or fifteen years ago when our people hadn't gotten so old and tired. I think we would've whipped them just on the sheer strength of just stubbornness. Just saying, "I refuse to leave. I think people would've done that. But by that time, you had husbands dying, wives dying. But I think you can do it. I think people can really beat something like this. But it takes heck of a lot of strength. It takes a real unity. I think you can just make it so nasty and so public and just beat out at the truth long enough that finally, the utilities will back off and the corporations will back off. Maybe not forever, but maybe you can buy enough time. We finally got the middle management people with the gas company to approach us. Said, "Leave us alone until we get what we want. [audio gap]

passages.q: These were local people your own age? / Local yuppies?
passages.t: Yes. Same with the union people. Yes, yuppies. Yes, and it was the same with the union people. The politicians promised the union people this big job. They were going to have this big contract. Three hundred thousand people. Yes. All these guys are going to go to work. For all these years. So, we didn't have labor support. Labor fought us tooth and toenail. Joe Powell fought us tooth and toenail. So, we didn't have that backing. But then when it comes to awarding the contracts, and contract after contract went to non-union, then we had the union people coming to us and saying, "What can we do? They promised us this work. Eighty percent of our guys are out of work and a non-union outfit gets the big dam – the big plum. We said, "Well, we'll do anything we can to help you, but we told you. They used you and they used your support and they used your power with the politicians." We told them all along that would happen, Michael. They were used just like Bill Adler and the local chamber of commerce was used. They found out that we were right, that there aren't any jobs. The local townspeople are beginning to find out, yes, there were no jobs for local people and there aren't going to be any development benefits.

passages.q: Did the association ever mount any strategy for trying to build a membership countywide or – / – in town? / Working with people in town?
passages.t: Oh, yes. Yes. Yes, the festival. The festival was part of it. We did series of newspaper ads, just trying to show – we do an ad, for example, that said, "The Corps has promised you industrial development will result from this dam. Then we put from the Corps own papers, their words saying, "There are no industrial development benefits connected with this project," and show them in black and white. It got to be to the level that Matt was talking about, where if you worked for the gas company, you didn't oppose the dam. You have a lot of gas company workers in this county. We had a fellow who worked for a coal company as a surveyor above ground. He came to a dinner that we were demonstrating at and went to talk to Jennings Randolph, and he saw his boss there. He was sent underground. Ultimately, he lost his job. Local. [laughter] Businesses that supported us would have to do it on the side, otherwise, they'd be in trouble with other businesses who were supporting the dam. So, we get anonymous contributions, but they didn't dare speak up and speak their mind. The project was so controversial that it's like the abortion issue. People were afraid to take a [laughter] stand publicly or say how they felt publicly. It was almost like their right to free speech was taken away when the government moved in. They were really fearful for their jobs. So, even though they knew the truth of it – and when they didn't – we went through this whole education project to make them see the truth of it – it didn't do any good. They couldn't do anything. It was frustrating [laughter]. It was the same with politicians. We went to Charleston to lobby and we talked to delegate after delegate, senator after senator. We'd say, "Do you know the states indebted for over $50 million for this? No, they didn't know that. "Well, we won't pay for it. "But the governor committed you to pay for it. You have to pay for this. Well, we won't pay for it. Let them go ahead and build it. We won't pay for it. So, even though you know the truth, you couldn't do anything with the truth. The truth wasn't enough. What more do you have but the truth? [laughter] What more do you have but the truth?

passages.q: Say that again about Bill Adler's father.
passages.t: Bill Adler's father was opposed to the dam. Paul Butcher, who has a local lumber company, his father was opposed to the dam. That whole generation was opposed to the dam. When their children got into power in town, that's when they changed. Then it was either greed on their part or ranked stupidity, or they were simply bought off in some way, shape, or form. Because up until then, everybody realized how bad the project was, and it wasn't going to benefit the county. I mean, they could look at Grafton and see it wasn't [laughter] going to benefit anybody. Then they went from that to – Bill Adler's people on the local level were able to use out and out lies. I mean, they would just out and out lie. Bill Adler has testified, time and time again, the Carhartt, which is a big industry in Buckhannon, wouldn't settle in Lewis County because they couldn't be guaranteed an assured water supply. So, I called Carhartts and I asked them, "Why did you settle in the Buckhannon area rather than Lewis County? The fellow said, "Well, one reason was because we had access to a lot more land. We had a bigger piece of land. We were given a tax break by the county. Because Carhartts is owned by Corning Industries, they always like to settle in a college town if possible. That's what decided them to settle there. But time after time, I can show you where Bill Adler testified that Lewis County lost that industry because they couldn't guarantee them an adequate water supply. So, Bill Adler would make a statement like that, even though it was a lie, and we were always in the position to have to respond. No matter how you do it, you're still responding. Whereas we never put out a statement that wasn't one hundred percent true. Maybe that was a mistake on our part. We should have used scare tactics [laughter]. We could have done all kinds of awful things. But we were so careful never to say anything that we couldn't demonstrate on paper. That's the way we always did it. Every statement we put out, we could visibly demonstrate that it was truthful. So, I don't know.

passages.q: So, if you had to do over, you might play by some of the same rules they were using? / Or selling dam insurance or something.
passages.t: Yes. Yes, I think so. I think we could have been a whole lot less cautious. I think we could have done maybe ads on the radio showing dams blowing up [laughter] or breaking away. Yes. Just any of the things. I think we probably did everything that we knew how to do. The fight just got beyond our ability. I mean, we had such a good shot at stopping this dam with Bob Wise behind us. We had the House on our side. It was just a matter of the Senate. Then in the meantime, Bob Byrd used his power to accelerate dam construction six months. When they did that, once they start the actual dam construction, to a lot of congressmen, that's the bottom line. We could say, "The dam is not under construction. The money that had already been spent on land acquisition can be recouped by the federal government by selling that land back either to the original landowner or putting it up for public auction. You can get this money back." But once Bob Byrd initiated dam construction, then that was it in the minds of a lot of congressmen. That was the bottom line to them. It was too late. So, I don't know. We were never able to get Bob Byrd. I mean, we were never able to convince him. The only thing I know, I mean, if the general accounting office can't convince him, if House Subcommittee Investigations can't convince him, if our congressman couldn't convince him. Our state senator, our state delegate, the local people here, if we couldn't convince him, then that tells me the only reason we couldn't convince him was because the corporations and the utilities and the coal companies were a lot more convincing than we were.

passages.q: That's pretty realistic [laughter]. / There's something I need you to do. I want to say a list of names to you. Each time I say a name, I want you to repeat the name and then say who it is, okay? Just say a sentence or two about them.
passages.t: It's pretty sad. It's pretty tragic. Most of the publicity on the project tends to make it rural versus town kind of a controversy. But in my mind, most of the people in the area in the county didn't view it that way. It wasn't a town versus farm situation. I think it was viewed that way by a few of the businesspeople who were in control of the Chamber of Commerce. I think it's viewed that way by a few of the farmers who are always suspicious. Because the town people tend to be elected county commissioner. The town people, the mayor, and those people tend to rule what's going on county wise. So, some of the farmers do. But the vast majority of people, I don't think ever viewed it that way, as one area being more valuable than another area. Or one lifestyle not being worthwhile. I think to the vast majority of people, for a long time, the question was flood control. A lot of people felt that Weston needed flood control. I think they just were fooled into believing that the dam was the only answer. Had the Soil Conservation Service maybe been allowed to have done a feasibility study to have demonstrated that there were alternatives – as it was, it was just our word against the Corps of Engineers' word. Because no other agency was ever allowed in to do any feasibility studies to demonstrate that there were alternative ways to provide flood control. So, the development versus rural aspect is really more in the minds of people like Bill Adler. Because rural is also development. I mean, just because it's rural doesn't mean that it's not economic or not economically viable. I think that Bill Adler and a few of the others were that powerful in convincing other people that that was the way to go. That the idea of industrial development was the way to go.

passages.q: That's pretty realistic [laughter]. / There's something I need you to do. I want to say a list of names to you. Each time I say a name, I want you to repeat the name and then say who it is, okay? Just say a sentence or two about them.
passages.t: That the idea of industrial development was the way to go. But as the dam fight progressed until close here towards the end, Bill Adler's rhetoric was toned down to the point where it was small, safe, nonpolluting industries, that kind of thing. Rather than the big, industrial development that they had envisioned in the beginning. So, I think he saw he was losing on that point. But I don't like to think of it, and I never really perceived it that way, except for a few on both sides. The overwhelming number of people in this county did not view it as rural versus town controversy. I really don't believe that. The nature of this county is rural. This is a rural county, period. I don't care who it is, they have a garden in their backyard [laughter], even Bill Adler. Even during the Stonewall Jackson Jubilee at Jackson's Mill, the Rotary Club, which Bill Adler's a big member of, put on straw hats and sold peaches as a money maker and called themselves farmer Bill or farmer Bob. So, maybe it's, you can't take the country out of the boy, I don't know. But it's a rural county. That was just the point that I wanted to make.

passages.q: So, in choosing a focus for the program, it shouldn't be painted that way, is what you're saying. / Well, that's how the big boys would like you to see.
passages.t: Yes. I think that's too simplistic. I think it's too easy for somebody to say the country people versus the town people because – Yes. Yes. I think that's exactly the way they want to see it. But see, I don't think it's true. There were too many businesses in town. Not just the agricultural businesses, but there were a lot of other businesspeople who opposed the dam. There were some farmers who supported the dam. Not many. There weren't many. But there were some people who viewed it as a chance to sell their farm and make some money, to the government. Who were ready to quit, and who would never quit if it wasn't that the government came in and forced them to do it. So, it's on both sides. But it's too simplistic to view it that way. I just really more look at it as the big corporations – those who are really in control in this country, seeing an area that was controlled by individual people. Rich in oil, rich in gas, rich in coal, rich in land, and saying, "Why not take it? We'll get the federal government to take it for us." Because as West Virginia as a whole, you never would've found an area more independent in West Virginia than Lewis County. It's like eighty-some percent of the land is privately owned – or was privately owned and rich in minerals. You don't find that anywhere else in West Virginia.

passages.q: So, you think that this is a pattern which could be repeated anywhere else? / And is being.
passages.t: Oh, yes. And is being repeated all over, yes. Being done to the Indians [laughter]. Being done to other West Virginians. I think the tragedy in West Virginia is there just wasn't very much of this left. Kentucky, Tennessee, I mean, you find very few areas with this much contiguous farmland that was still in the hands of the private people and had minerals too.

passages.q: Who is Ron Donnell? / Who is Mary Aspinall? / Who's Aubrey West?
passages.t: Ron Donnell is a federal marshal out of the Elkins District. Mary Aspinall and her husband, Bill, operate a large farming operation near Vandalia, which is within the take area of the Stonewall Jackson Dam. Aubrey West is a retired dairy farmer who is also within the take area of the Stonewall Dam, who is now facing condemnation and eviction.

passages.q: Who is Bill Adler? / Who is Bill Adler? / Who is John Radabaugh?
passages.t: Bill Adler used to own a cable television company based in Weston, who is an officer in the Lewis County Chamber of Commerce and has been a long time dam supporter. Bill Adler used to own a cable television station in Weston. He is an officer in the Lewis County Chamber of Commerce and a long time dam supporter. John Radabaugh and his sister, Regina, operate a dairy farm on Skin Creek, which is in the take area of the dam.

passages.q: Who is Edith Holden? / Who is Matthew Snyder? / Who is Bob Earl?
passages.t: Edith Holden lived on Skin Creek in the take area. She was moved out by the dam and relocated in Randolph County. [laughter] Matthew Snyder is a contractor and part-time farmer, who lives near the take area of the dam, whose family lost several farms because of the project. Bob Earl is the editor of the Weston Democrat and a longtime dam supporter. You've been listening to the Voices of Ron Donnell, Mary Aspinall, Francine Snyder, Bob Wise, Aubrey West, Matthew Snyder, Edith Holden, Bob Earl, Barbara, and Bobby Heavner. [end of transcript]

passages.q: This is Lewis County. It's March 17th. Doug Yarrow, Hugh Rogers, and I are on a little runabout with Francine Snyder and her little daughter, Lee. We've just stopped at the home of Barbara Heavner to get some photographs.
passages.t: Yes, assistant prosecuting attorney, [inaudible], said, "Mr. West, isn't it true that Mr. Snyder saw the Corps vehicle go by, and then he picked up a rock and threw it at the Corps?" Aubrey said, "I didn't see him." He said, "Then the car went on down the road and stopped. The men got out, and didn't Mr. Snyder make an obscene gesture with the third finger of his right hand? He said, 'Come on back, boys. Do you want to fight? Come on back.'" Aubrey looked at him for a minute. He looked at his hand, and he said, "Well, he did kind of motion them to come on back." Everything [inaudible] did, I mean, Aubrey just toned it down. He tried to get Aubrey to draw a picture of his place in relation to where all this happened, and Aubrey wouldn't do it. He said, "Now, Mr. West, I want you to draw a map." Aubrey says, "I won't do it." Finally, after about five minutes, he looked at him. He said, "Well, why won't you do it, Mr. West?" Aubrey says, "Because I haven't got my glasses on." He has glasses, and he couldn't see. He couldn't draw any map. It just went on and on and on like that. The jury was just in stitches over Aubrey. You know how he talks.

passages.q: Was the charge assault? / I don't know. Did he hit the car with it?
passages.t: It was destruction of property, I guess. Wouldn't it have been? Hell, yes. He hit the car with the pickup. But they went by and – but these fellows in the Corps, I mean, they're so stupid. The Corps is so stupid. Their witnesses had their testimony down so Pat, it just sounded like, you know, they made the whole thing up. So, they said they were – I'll show you when we're out here at Aspinall's. They came out of Aspinall's road there and were starting to turn right to come to Aubrey, you know, down past Aubrey's house, and they saw Matt in his truck. One of them said, "Isn't that Matt Snyder? This is their testimony. The other one said, "Yes, that's him. "Isn't that the fellow that's been causing all the trouble here? The other one said, "Yes, that's him. [laughter] You know, the way they talked. So, finally, they said they made the turn, and Matt picked – they saw Matt pick up this rock. They heard this huge crash. They thought they'd been shot. They went down the road. They tried to radio for help, but the radio was broken. So, they stopped at the bridge. They got out to look at it. That's when he made the obscene gesture, and he said something like, you know, "Come on, boys. I'm ready for you," or something like that. On the witness stand, then Martin got them – he asked each of them – of course, none could hear the other one's testimony. He asked them if there was a Corps insignia on the side of the Jeep. Because we kept telling Martin all these things to ask them. One said there was. One said there wasn't. All through the testimony, they kept saying that they had been in and out of the side of that Jeep all day. There was no damage done to it before that, right? One said there was a Corps insignia on it. The other one said there wasn't. So, finally, they bring the Jeep up.

passages.q: Was the charge assault? / I don't know. Did he hit the car with it?
passages.t: So, finally, they bring the Jeep up. Martin says, "Well, let's take a look at this, you know. They bring the Jeep up for everybody to go out – the jury to go out and see. The whole side of the Jeep had been scraped from one end to the other. They didn't even know what – it was a parking lot accident, they finally decided. They couldn't even see the dent that this rock of Matt supposedly had made, right? As soon as the jury saw that, they just started laughing. They just actually started laughing. Really wasn't funny. Could have gotten a year in jail for whatever they tried him for. I mean, the penalty was, you know, a fine and a year in jail. Although the magistrate never would have put him in jail for it. But Corps were – they just made fools out of themselves. Aubrey just – he was just funny. The jury just cracked up over him. But he said he was standing right next to Matt, and he didn't see him throwing a rock. Then you ask Aubrey about it, and he'll tell you, "I didn't see him. Not that he didn't know that he'd done it, but that he didn't actually witness him doing it. One of them said that Matt had nothing in his hand, and the other one said he thought he might have been holding something. He's holding a clipboard the whole time. On the back of clipboard said, "Stop – it's one of those big yellow bumper stickers. They didn't see it.

passages.q: What did it say?
passages.t: Said, "Stop Stonewall Jackson Dam," the bumper sticker did. But the Corps did not see that, him holding this clipboard. I mean, that's how great witnesses they were. Missed the maple tree – there's a huge maple tree in Aubrey's yard that had branches hanging down. There was no way in hell they could have seen Matt and Aubrey standing there. No way, for that tree. They said they saw him. They made this whole story up, you know, about, "Isn't that Matt Snyder. Yes. He's the one that's causing all the trouble." It was a great trial. We enjoyed it. I think the jury was out about thirty seconds maybe [laughter].

passages.q: Are those the two main entanglements he's had with the law? / [negative] / Tell that story.
passages.t: Yes, that – we arrested them once for trespassing. Matthew and I took their Jeep. I told you about that, didn't I? Matthew and I took their Jeep away from them. I didn't tell you that story? Matthew and I were – and Missy – were all home one day and looked out the window, and I saw the Corps go up the road, which is unusual, because they don't have any business past our place. Of course, as soon you see the Corps, it always makes you wonder what they're up to anyway. Darn if I didn't see them turn up the road there, across from our house, that well location road, they turned up that road and went on the hill. Well, that's private property. That's our property. I mean, if anybody else would have done it, that would have been something. But it was almost like it was a deliberate effort, you know, to upset us. So, Matthew been out groundhog hunting, and I hollered for him. We went up on the hill and waited for them to come down. There were No Trespassing signs there. We had all these No Trespassing Corps of Engineers signs we – everybody bought, had them posted. So, when they came down, we just stopped the Jeep. Matthew had a gun, and I had a gun. We told them that they were trespassing. They had to leave their vehicle and walk out. So, there was a fellow from the Corps – two fellows from the Corps, an appraiser, a gas well appraiser, who would come to appraise a gas well on the place, which wasn't even – the gas well wasn't even on our property, but that was easiest way to get to it. So, Matthew and I made those three fellows walk out of the holler then called the sheriff. Matt was over at Linger's at the time, called him. He said, "Call the police. So, we called the police, and they came over. Finally, we did let them come and get their Jeep and take it out.

passages.q: Are those the two main entanglements he's had with the law? / [negative] / Tell that story.
passages.t: Finally, we did let them come and get their Jeep and take it out. We had them arrested for trespassing. One of them decided to go ahead through magistrate's court, the appraiser, the gas well appraiser, had a trial through magistrate's court. They acquitted him. They had a hung jury and never retried it. The other two in federal court never did come up for trial. But the fellow that owned the gas wells, they said they had permission to be there. Well, he didn't have a right of way through us, and he knew that. He wasn't about to give them permission to go up there. So, they called the fellow in the gas well and tried to get him to write them a retroactive letter saying that they had permission to be on that road. Of course, the gas well fellow who has to work with the local people, he went about to do that, right, you know? So, anyway, Matthew was acquitted finally. But it was fun. (Monjar?) came up and begged to get his jeep back. Legally, we really didn't have any right to hold it, I guess. But the next time Matt went over to federal court was somebody who was involved in something and wanted Matt over there to witness something what was going on at the Corps. (Mac Lowe?) told me he was going to arrest Matthew and I for illegal weapons charges or something. I told him, go ahead. I'd like to see any jury in West Virginia convict you for having a shotgun on your own property. You know, I didn't point it at them. I said, "If we wanted to be nasty, we would have pointed it at them. I was holding the thing, and it scared them. Can't under understand why. But they knew better. I mean, the Corps had to have known. I mean, they knew where we lived. They know who we are. They know how hard we fought them. Yet they still do something that blatant. That's –

passages.q: Asking for it.
passages.t: That's asking for it. That's what I think they did. I think they just deliberately did it to provoke us. They weren't going to be intimidated. But they walked out of the holler, all three of them. It’s a long ways to a telephone too. I think they ended up going somewhere, finding one of the Weiss Brothers' people, and they radioed for help.

passages.q: Help [laughter]. / This is who's house?
passages.t: A bit of house that's still standing. This house was the McRae house where Ruth Post grew up. Down over the hill here is where Matt's family grew up. They were real ornery, all the kids in Matt's dad's family. They would always be down there playing in the river and whatnot. Ruth's dad and mom never let her go down and play in the river. She told me how she'd sit up there, and she'd watch the Snyder kids down there playing. It was just awful. But she used to walk down that hill, across the swinging bridge here, to get to school at Roanoke. Or she'd go on horseback to get to school down here at Roanoke. Then there was no – that was elementary school – there was no high school or junior high school. Matt's family, they took the train from here to Burnsville. The train went along the river there. The train would stop and pick them up and then take them on down to Burnsville. That's where they went to high school. Your other choice was to board in Weston, and Ruth boarded in Weston and went to high school in Weston. But Matt's – someone told Matt not long ago that Matt's great granddad had a still over there across the river. As the train went by, someone threw out a rock with a note on it that said, "The sheriff's on the train." Of course, the sheriff then had to go down here and get off at the station at Roanoke and then come back up through here and down to the river. Well, by that time, they had the still dismantled on a manure wagon and put all this manure on top of it when the sheriff got there. So, they never did get caught. I can't now remember who it was that told Matt the story, but it was like her grandfather or her father that had thrown the note out that warned the Snyders that the sheriff was coming.

passages.q: Is that swinging bridge still down there?
passages.t: Yes. There's a swinging bridge down there that – on that Matt's dad's place that goes across the West Fork River there. There never was a road down through there. Cemeteries are down there. See, there are two big cemeteries down there. One of the first fights we had with the Corps was that they planned to move all the cemeteries. This is the recreation area. They had a miniature golf course or something like that slated for one of those cemeteries. So, that was one of our success stories. The only cemetery that was moved was one that would be absolutely affected by water, and all the rest of the cemeteries stayed. Small but important to most people.

passages.q: Yes. Mary Aspinall said, "Yes, they'll let the dead people stay – the dead people and the gas well stay. The living people all get kicked out." / That's not the Snyder place that we're looking at there. / Now, who's not parts of that kind, do you suppose? Is that vandals, or is that Corps work?
passages.t: Yes, that sounds like Mary. Yes. That was there. Well, there was a barn standing there. I think his Uncle Tom tore it down or had it torn down. His uncle Tom, Matt's Uncle Tom, had this part of it, and across the river was his dad's farm. The two of them split the farm up, that one. Then his Aunt Alice lived over here in a trailer. Although Tom only was here in the summers. He's a doctor at Clarksburg. We see how it affected – you know, family-wise, you can get a whole group of people in one family affected. But Aunt Alice, Matt's Aunt Alice, ran the Corps out of the graveyard, threatened to go get her gun. Matt told you that story around the Corps and the graveyard. Did I tell you about the lady that lived – you can't see the house right now, but it was there where the – not this closest pine tree, but on down that, that's called Briar Point Road. She was 90 or 92 years old.

passages.q: [inaudible]
passages.t: Yes. There were three sisters that were all real old that lived there. They got along so well. I guess they had somebody live in with them, you know. But you can see nothing's yet ever been done to that property. I mean, she would have been dead now years if they had just let her stay. There wasn't any reason on earth to move her.

passages.q: What did you say?
passages.t: [inaudible] You're going to your elementary school. You you've been doing this now since kindergarten. You pass buildings deserted and boarded up, and other buildings all torn down. The rubble, just the rubble remains. There's road construction all around you. You're now totally isolated. Nothing else around you now. Makes for a real stable environment for these kids. These buildings that are here boarded up, this was the historic district of Roanoke.

passages.q: At what point was it decided that they would never be saved and that all they had to do was catalog them?
passages.t: Just recent. That was just recent, within the last year that the historic people and the Corps entered into a memorandum of agreement that that would be the case. You see, if this historic resource project had been done in the planning stages of the dam, then something might have been done. They could have changed the plans for the dam, or they might have decided not to go ahead with the project at all. Because so many historic sites would have been disturbed. But it wasn't done until construction was already underway. It wasn't then until they did what they should have done legally back in 1966. So, really, it's to the point now where the historic people felt the best they could do, you know, was simply to catalog these buildings and at least have a written record of them, except for Conrad Park back there. That'll be the only one moved.

passages.q: The old log house. / So, these buildings here will all be pushed out of the way? / You mean to tear it down?
passages.t: [affirmative] Basically, they'll be offered for sale to public auction, to any nonprofit group. If nobody buys them, they'll be destroyed. Right. If somebody buys them to move, they have to move them or tear them down and resurrect them again. There are a lot of people that still live there, and people still live on the other side of the interstate exchange there. All of them go to – all those kids go to school here at Roanoke. New school's out that road. It's – you can't see. This building's blocking your way. It's right there. Most of these, I don't remember all the details about them now. But it was a combination of their age and the kind of houses they were all grouped together that made the area one that the historic people felt should have been kept intact, as it was. At one time, we had a plot afoot to make the Corps relocate the entire town of Roanoke intact. They'd done that out in Washington for the Bonneville dam project. I mean, they relocated it, you know, phone pole for phone pole, home for home, just like it was. Oh, we didn't get very far with it. Would have been fun anyway. People really didn't want it, you know. If you're going to leave your area, they didn't want to, you know – back together that one.

passages.q: So, will the water actually be up here? / Right here. / It's hard for me to picture that.
passages.t: Yes. This will be about 8 feet of water. Right here. That's what horses. Yes, especially when you see the West Fork River. Now, the worst flooding that ever was here in Roanoke is just this road would get flooded some – a couple of times during the year, and it gets flooded pretty good. I mean, now, the water will get up really high. You remember I told you about Freida Fischer? She lived over there. She lost twin boys to a flood one year. They were crossing the swinging bridge here across the river. One boy fell in, and the other one went in after him to try to save him. She lost both sons that day. Really awful. So, it's not like our people don't understand about the water either. You know, it's not like we haven't suffered some from the water either. Now, we're suffering some again. (Doc Whalen?) lived there. I can't remember. There's a nice story about him. I think he was a bit of an alcohol – I shouldn't say this. Because I don't know this for a fact, Michael. You probably shouldn't publish anything like this. I think he was like an alcoholic. He ended up jumping off of that balcony or something, one of them. They were trying to sober him up or something.

passages.q: Did he have his office there in the house? / The river, and that's oil creek, all that big riprap. / Yes. I like the green sign that's still up, tell you where the roads used to go. Only it's up to its knees in riprap now.
passages.t: Yes. Pretty, isn't it? See, when they started construction, the State Road came in and put all these road signs up where there hadn't been road signs for years. Only trouble was we knew the roads by one name, and they were putting the roads in another name. So, we had to get on them and call them and made new signs, you know. Because they had all the roads called the wrong names. But they did that so the Corps could find their way around, see, as they were going to appraise people. It was a pretty place, all the holly trees.

passages.q: Holly tree kind of got overpowering. / I'm not building houses like this. There's slate roof on that. It survives very much in villages. Korea put in its first gosogdolo, which means freeway, high-speed highway. Just before we left Korea, we were coming home from the Peace Corps, we took a bus trip all the way from Seoul to Busan, which is on the south tip of the peninsula. This is what happens. You have these little villages with grass roofs and then this huge new road up on the hill above it. / Yes. / Yes. / Was the old road underwater up that high?
passages.t: Did you think about the waste, the monetary waste of these houses? Isn't it phenomenal? You see where the new road is now? All right. Can you see just down the hill a little ways? Can you see the line? See the old road there? Look how close the old road and the new road is. It couldn't have been underwater, because look, Michael, look where the new road is, just up above it. This is their main recreation area. I'm telling you. This is their big water area, and look where the road is.

passages.q: So, what are they going to have here?
passages.t: Boat docks, campgrounds, stables for horses, so you can go horseback riding. I think they are going to put in an amphitheater, no lodges or motels or, you know, stuff like that. In other words, everything that there already is right now. You know, people fish in the river. They go horseback riding. They camp. All the things that we do now, they're just paying $250 million to do it.

passages.q: This whole project is completely surrounded by other projects, just like it is, isn't it? / Developed. / Eastern United States [inaudible].
passages.t: Yes. The Burnsville dam and this dam connect by a trail that started out to be a footpath and turned out to be, you know, wide enough for a two-vehicle road now. [affirmative] Eventually, I think, what their plans are is to take everything from interstate exit to Burnsville exit, and then they'd have one big, massive federal area. Right.

passages.q: Everybody from Washington to New York to Boston. / Sure.
passages.t: Right. Do you want to take a short run up before we go over to Vandalia? I'll show you – it's not really far, but it's up the road here. Actually, we could take a loop. Do you want to do that? Won't take that awful long. But there's a magnificent view from the Jacksonville ridge I'd like you to see. It's going to be gone someday. But it's just a magnificent view. Then we'll end up in Walkersville and come back down 19 and cross over to Vandalia.

passages.q: There's some way you can really get a sense of the scale. Here you have this cute-scale little village, and there you have this monstrosity. It's –
passages.t: Progress. Bill Adler says that is progress, but there's no more traffic on that road now than there was before, when it was, you know, lower and small. Actually, they didn't upgrade the roads much. They didn't really change anything. You know, one point back in the fifties, the State Highway Department opposed this dam. One reason they opposed it was because they'd already put the roads on the best routes. That's why the roads were located there, and that the new road relocations would – there would be slips, and there would be all kinds of problems that would require so much more maintenance by the road department that they opposed the project back in 1950. So, you can see what a mess that's going to be.

passages.q: Six rooms?
passages.t: Well, yes, it's four rooms in the brick building and then the trailer and the pine trees in the back. They have a big playground. The road's safe. Here, behind the trailers, they're not as good as they used to be, but they're all these apple trees. Early on, in the school, kids used to go out, pick apples for the cooks, and the cooks would make applesauce.

passages.q: Did you say initially who taught at that school?
passages.t: Yes. Beth teaches at that school. I was talking to her about it. She wasn't really here when, you know, a lot of this went on. She said it would be probably better to talk to like Missy or Matthew about it. Yesterday or Wednesday, Missy had to go into town for school. She goes to those classes. She had a speech contest here Wednesday morning. So, she rode in with a woman, a speech therapist who was one of the judges in the speech contest. The woman said, "Well, I bet you're anxious to get to the new school." Missy said, "No." She said, "Well, just think, when the dam's finished, you'll be able to swim all around it." Missy said, "No. You can't swim in it." She said, "Well, I'm looking forward to it. I'm going to get a boat and find me a little place up here, have a nice place on the lake." I thought, how crass. You know, she asked Missy if Missy had to move because of the dam, and Missy told her no. But she thought that, you know, Missy would be real excited about having a place like this to come play in.

passages.q: Who was it? / Up here? / What are Missy's feelings about it?
passages.t: One of the teachers. No, not from here, from town. But I thought, how crass of that woman not to realize that the kids have feelings too. I think she's just experienced some feeling of isolation. It was awful having to – I mean, she started here in kindergarten, so she's really been here all through it – through the worst of it. She's probably more aware than most children are of what's going on, because of our involvement, you know. But she watched George and Ruth Post move away. That hurt her a lot. Because she used to go down there. She'd get off the school bus, and Ruth would always have cookies or something for them. Now there's nothing. There's nothing between the school and our house. There's not a single human being between the school and our house. Friends of hers moved away. She hated that. Wondering, she wondered for a long time if they were going to come and get us. That scared her for a long time. Because we lived close to the edge of the project, and she thought they were going to come and get us.

passages.q: What did she say about it? Just asked about it?
passages.t: Just asked. She was afraid. The dust and the dirt, you know, from here – from the school to our house, been under construction from us for years, and the dirt and the heavy equipment, you know. We wouldn't let her walk down to the mailbox or ride her bicycle because the place is full of construction workers. You don't let a little 10-year-old kid run around amongst construction workers, heavy equipment. So, she wasn't free to go down ride her bicycle or go down to the mailbox or anything like that. I don't know. It's not that any of them are anything major. It's just that, you know, you live in an area like this because it's a good place to raise your children. You put up with all the inconveniences for that reason. Then the government comes in and changes the whole complexion of the area. So, you're still living with all the inconveniences, but you've lost a lot of the other good reasons why you're living there.

passages.q: I guess most Americans would wonder why you don't just pick up and move.
passages.t: Yes, I suppose. We could probably sell our farm and just make an absolute fortune. I mean, it really is on the lake of this – on the edge of this wonderful lake project, you know. I suppose if we were concerned about, you know, the money end of it, we wouldn't have been fighting it. Matt's a contractor. He would have made a fortune working on this project close to home. But to quote one of the other fellows who lives around here, he said, "I'd never make – I wouldn't make my living on somebody else's misery." That's pretty much the way we feel about it. I don't know why. You know, the farm we live on has been in Matt's family now, six generations. Matthew's a seventh-generation there. Now, I think you owe them a debt. You owe the people that came before you. That's the debt you owe them to take care of it and pass it on to somebody else who cares. Not somebody who's going to take it and divide it up in lakeside campsites.

passages.q: Sort of a tenancy, kind of a thing.
passages.t: It is really. I mean, the ownership of it doesn't make any difference. That's one of the things that you owe your kids. Bring them up in a safe environment and the school – this is safe. It's safe for them. You feel comfortable with your children here. Then they're not out in traffic. They're not playing ball out on the street at recess like they do in Weston.

passages.q: Not too many drug dealers up in the pine here. / You give them the best.
passages.t: No, you don't have to worry about drugs. When they get older – you give them a stable environment when they're young. Then they get older, and they've got the foundation, go from there. Right. But that's all you can give them as a parent is a good foundation. All of this is all rubble. They did dozer all of this over, but you see the difference it makes now to the kids, rather than looking out your window and, you know, seeing all that mess. Maybe it's something the kids can't really verbalize. I mean, they don't say it's awful seeing all of that, necessarily. But it's the sense of impermanency, you know, if there's such a word. It's a sense that nothing's forever around you that they don't need when they're little. Those kinds of concepts come later on in life.

passages.q: [inaudible] / Yes. They made that judgment. / Corps engineers made that [inaudible].
passages.t: Well, they said that were no significant historic sites here. He said that in their environmental impact statement. Right.
