passages.q: That was a beautiful spot down here, wasn't it before the floods? / Right there on the banks of the river. / Roger, do you think you're all right now? / Because what you just told me would be enough to buckle the minds of a lot of people.
passages.t: Yes, it was. Yes. It was a beautiful place. But never know with that water though, just wipe things out. Yes, I'm getting along. I'm getting straightened up pretty good now. Well, yes, it hurt. Yes, I know it works on your mind. You just can't let it bother you. You've got to try to keep busy and keep your mind off of it. If you just sit down and start thinking about it or even start talking about it, it makes it worse.

passages.q: Do you think it's bad to talk about it? / But those things are in there, you know? / But those things are inside of you, and they have to come out.
passages.t: Yes, I think it is. I think it brings back old memories. It's best to try to forget if you can. Oh, yes, I know they're in there. But I try not to talk about it as much if I can help it. Oh, yes, you have to bring them out. Yes, that's true too. But I think really, it's once you said it, you shouldn't have to say it again. Everybody should know. You've told your story. I've told this story, I bet, twenty-five times.

passages.q: It may be good for you. / You're an awful good storyteller.
passages.t: Well, it might be, and again, it might not be. Yes, it's got to get out. But they were my good friends, and I don't like to talk about it really. But you've got to tell what you've got to tell. It's hard, but you just sit down and tell it. That's all you can do. [laughter] Well, I never did. I always was bashful. I never could talk very good.

passages.q: Oh, you talk fine. You're a good teller. I'd like to hear you tell some other things. / I bet you've got some good hunting stories. / Did you and John ever kill any bears? / He was a good hunter?
passages.t: [laughter] Well, that's about all I can tell you. Oh, yes, I've got a lot of good hunting stories. No, never killed any bear. We killed quite a few squirrels. Yes. He liked hunting, but he couldn't walk around very good. His legs hurt him off a bit. But he loved to hunt, loved to drink his whiskey. Me and him used to drink a lot of whiskey. Yes, I just finished his house, the one room he had down there. He wanted me to panel and drop the ceiling in. We got it all done. We did it on Thursday before this happened. I just finished it up all, and it was beautiful. We just got it done, and this thing happened Monday.

passages.q: So, you had been spending a whole lot of time with him?
passages.t: Oh, well, all around, yes. We'd go down and make hay. We'd help him make his hay. He came up here, and we sat down and talked. He came to my house. We'd visit quite a regular, didn't we, Peele? Yes. He was really nice. I liked him and Catherine both. Aunt Pearl, I didn't know her too well, not like I did Catherine and John. Catherine probably diapered my behind when I was a baby.

passages.q: Tell me again, you were related by blood to them? / Cut your chin?
passages.t: No, just good friends, neighbors. We've been neighbors all of our life. Aunt Pearl's diapered me many times. When I first came here, I was just a little fellow. My arms were only about that big around. I was about starved to death. My mother did that. Butcher knife. I was three years old. I got anything to eat really. I didn't get to eat with rest of the family, hardly any. I sat behind a chair. The chair was sitting in the corner like this, and I sat in the corner. I wanted anything to eat, I went out and waited until they left. Then I'd go out and go around the house and go up to my granddaddy's house. He lived about 50 feet from us. They'd give me cookies and milk. Then I'd go back to the house. Now, she was pretty rough on me.

passages.q: Why was she so hard on you? / But you found a wife to like you? / You found a wife who likes you. / Well, he's a wonderful man. / You've got anything else that I can add to that? I would like to use this material maybe in some radio work or – / – book or whatever. Is that all right?
passages.t: I don't know. I don't guess she liked me very good. I was the black sheep of the family. Huh? Oh, yes. My aunt likes me too. She's the one who raised me. I lived with them for nineteen years. Yes, my wife, well, she's pretty good when she wants to be. Sometimes she can be [inaudible]. I guess they all get that way. Yes. Go ahead. Yes. It's all right with me if it's all right with Aunt Peele. Go ahead. Why should I – [end of transcript]

passages.q: Can you tell me your full name? / Amy Renee. / Who are your parents? / Who are your dad's parents? / Your mother's? / Have both sides of your family lived in Tucker County for a long time? / How long? Do you know how many generations? / From Michigan to Hendricks? / How'd they happen to do that?
passages.t: Amy Renee Moore. [affirmative] Bob and Faith Moore. Charles and Helen Moore. Lowe and Louisa (Roy?), Lowe and Louise Roy. Yes. No, I don't. I know my dad's parents are from Thomas. My mom was born in Michigan, so her parents were there, and then they moved to Hendricks. [affirmative] I don't know. I don't know how they ended up in Hendricks.

passages.q: But that's where your parents met anyway. / What was the date of your birth? / Well, belated birthday greetings. So, you're just twenty? / Twenty-one. Right, this is [19]86. Do you have brothers and sisters? / You're by yourself? / Where were you raised? / On which street? / Had your parents bought a new home? / Build a new home in Holly Meadows?
passages.t: Yes. My mom and dad went to school, Parsons High together. January 5th, 1965. Twenty-one. No. Yes. In Parsons. First, we were above [inaudible] alley, and then we're on Quality Hill, and up on Spruce Street. Then we just moved down to Holly Meadows a year ago. It will be a year ago in May. Build a new home. Yes.

passages.q: Why did they choose to build there? / It's kind of pause. So, you had lived a, what would you say, a pretty normal life up through your high school years? / What was the most exciting thing that ever happened to you coming up through high school? / So, when did you start up there? / You didn't what you wanted to take? / From? / I bet you had some interesting courses then. / What do you remember about November 4th? Had it been raining all weekend?
passages.t: Mom liked the river before. Now she doesn't like it. [affirmative] I guess being able to get it every year. I was excited about that. In fall of [19]83. No. I changed my major three times. Journalism to business to nursery education. Yeah. It was tossup between journalism and nursery education. I didn't like business very well. Yes. It had been raining for a long time. But it just seemed like it wasn't going to be anything unusual. Because I'd been downtown from probably about 6:00 p.m. to 7:30 p.m., and we had left the house that night at 8:00 p.m. it just. Well, I didn't pay that much attention to the river either. I just figured it was going to be small flooding, like we usually had.

passages.q: So, when did you notice it was getting bad?
passages.t: After I got home. When I went down the road, there wasn't any water on the road, and all of our neighbors had left. So, dad thought maybe he should go out and look. He went and looked on the road that I just came down five minutes before, and there was water up to his ankles. So, he called (Allen Howe?). He's the one that owned the land. We bought it off from him. He said not to worry about it because all of Parsons would have to be washed away before we got flooded down there, and we didn't. Even when I was up here, I didn't know that it was that bad. So, then after he talked to him, he turned the lights on outback and the water was almost up to the back door. Mom had checked it at 6:30 p.m. and it wasn't up at all. That was something about 8:00 p.m. Then we left. By the time we got to the road where it was to his ankles, it was too much. It was too high for the jeep to go through. So, it flipped it over on its side and it washed it over across the street in the field and just sat there. We sat out on the side of it and yelled. Some of the neighbors that were higher up were still there and she was getting ready to leave. She saw us and she went and called the fire department. When they came, they couldn't get any ropes to us. So, they tried to pull down a little farther in the water, got a hold of their truck and washed it up. It wasn't very far away from us, maybe this far away.

passages.q: 30 inches.
passages.t: Yes. I didn't know how to say it [inaudible]. They said they'd throw us a rope to get us in the truck. But I guess when the water came up by them, it caused the water to pick the jeep up again. So, right when they got up to us, the jeep lifted up and started moving and it flipped again and we all fell off. Mom and dad got pushed towards the land. We didn't know how far we were from solid land, but I guess we weren't very far. And they got up to it. The first time I came up, I could hear them yelling, but I couldn't yell back because I couldn't breathe. So, they got out. Of course, I didn't know that they got out until they found me. They went to grandma's and dad went around and found some people to come and look for me, and they all came down. But when I went under three or four times, I got to a briar bush and I got ahold of it. It still kept pulling me under. So, I pushed my head up into the bush to try to get it stuck in it so that it would stay above water. But then the tree got washed out. So, I don't know how but somehow, I got a hold of a board. It was long and skinny, and I kept a hold of it. I got to a barbed wire fence. It turned out it was just on the other side of the (Moss Bridge?). But even when I got in the tree, I didn't know where I was at. So, I got to the fence and I could stand. The water wasn't swift there, and I could see lights up on a hill. So, I put the board over top of the fence and climbed over the fence. I was going to try to get to the house or wherever the lights were. The water picked up again and it knocked me down into the fence and I got caught in it.

passages.q: 30 inches.
passages.t: The water picked up again and it knocked me down into the fence and I got caught in it. I pulled out a bit and then I got caught. Something caught me just under my knees. I guess maybe it was a tree limb or something that grew in the ground, both sides or something. So, I held onto the fence post because the water was hitting me from the back. I was stuck there. Then the porch, it was a whole wooden deck and it came and it hit me in the back. I crawled up on it and laid on it until it floated into the tree. I climbed up in the tree, and then the porch floated away. So, I just sat there and waited. The water kept raising but none of the – that was the only big branch on it. All the rest of them were just skinny ones up higher. I sat in the branch and it probably got up to my hips, but it started going down again before they got to me. There was a trailer that crashed in the trees beside me. I wanted to try to get to it because the wind was blowing and it was cold. All I had on was a t-shirt and sweatpants. I could see, I guess, people. Some people told me they were trying to get home. So, I guess there were cars. I could see the cars pull down and then they'd back up and leave. I guess they couldn't go any farther. Then after a while, I saw three flashlights. I wasn't going to yell at them because I didn't think they'd be able to hear because the water was so loud. They moved down a little farther. So, I yelled at them and then all the lights popped up because they were looking in the water. Pretty soon, two ambulances came and a bunch of other cars. They were shining lights to see if they could see me, but dad said that they couldn't see me. They could see the outline of the trees and the outline of the trailer that was in the tree beside me, and that's all they could see. They sent a man out in a motorboat to get me. I got in the boat, and they took me out and took me to the hospital.

passages.q: Who was the man in the boat? / Had you known them before? / But you were glad to see them?
passages.t: (Donnie Goss?) and Dave Humphrey. [inaudible] Yes. Yes, kind of. I really didn't want to get in the boat near the water. I'd rather stay in the trailer because the water was going down. Because I just thought I was going to have to sit there until the water went down and then walk out. But I really didn't want to get in that boat because I couldn't. First thing, I didn't even think about it being a motorboat because I could see a light coming to me, and I figured it must be a boat. All I could think of was a rowboat. I couldn't think of a motorboat. I thought, I'm not going to get in that boat for nothing. But then when he got up there, he wanted me to climb out the branch, but there were branches. My back was up against the trunk of the tree. The branches grew out from between my legs all the way down the branch. So, they had trouble getting it backed up close enough where I could get on it. I put my foot on the motor and it slid off. I told him, "No." I said, "If you can't get it back any farther, then I can't get in." They got it to come back a little farther, and I got in.

passages.q: How old were you, Amy, when you learned how to swim? / You don't know how to swim? / So, we're talking about a miracle. / How long do you figure you were from the time you were washed off the jeep? How long do you figure it was till you got in the boat?
passages.t: I don't know how to swim. [negative] You couldn't have swim in it anyway, I don't think, because it was too swift. But I never did learn how to swim. [laughter] Yes. Dad thought he could see his watch when the fire truck came, and it was 9:30 p.m. or something until 10:00 p.m. When I got in the ambulance, they told me it was 5:00 a.m.

passages.q: Seven or eight hours. How long were you up in that tree? / What did you see while you were up in the tree?
passages.t: I have no idea how long it took me to get down there. I saw cars and refrigerators, and there was a little car. The first thing I thought was that it would be mine. Because I just got a car last May, and I thought it would be my car. I couldn't see cows, but I could hear them making noises and stuff. I knew they were in the water, but I didn't see any of them. There was a house – stories, and it was all together, windows in, doors shut and everything that floated right by. That's when I decided I had to stay awake because I was going to go to sleep. Not really go to sleep, but I laid my head on the branch that was in front of me. But then I was afraid that the next house that came would come to the tree I was sitting in.

passages.q: You were afraid it would crash into you?
passages.t: [affirmative] There wasn't any place I could have went. Because the trees, there was a whole line of them, but none of them were close enough that I could have went from one to the other. Because I wanted to try to move over into the tree beside me that was by the trailer to try to sit in it. Because I could see chairs and all kinds of stuff in it, I figured there must be something in there I could put on me, even if it was wet. But they weren't very close together. All the branches were a lot skinnier on top, and they wouldn't have held me.

passages.q: What did they say about you in the hospital? Had you pretty nearly frozen to death, do you think, or what?
passages.t: When she took my temperature, it was only down to ninety-seven. So, they said that wasn't very bad at all. When they put me in the ambulance, they put hot packs on me. When I got out of the water, there was a bunch of people, a lot of people out there. They passed me from one to the other and wrapped their coats and stuff around me. Then when I got to the hospital, they just put me in bed and put the hot water bottles around me. But I was cold [laughter]. Yes, my teeth didn't stop chattering until I'd been in the hospital, I think, for an hour. There wasn't anything else they could do. Doctor Pete wasn't there. So, they just put me in bed and gave me hot chocolate and stuff. I don't know how they got it because they didn't have any way to heat anything. I just stayed in there for about three hours just to get warm. Then my mom would come when I first got there. Dad went home and went to grandma's. She came down and stayed with me and then we walked up to grandma's.

passages.q: Your parents must have thought that you were lost.
passages.t: [affirmative] Grandma said that mom was hysterical and dad just didn't say anything. He didn't know what to do. They came to grandma's and changed clothes. Because mom was just in a bathrobe and a pair of sweatpants because she was getting ready to go to bed. After dad changed clothes, he decided he was going to go look. Mom told him there wasn't anything to look for because she was sure that I was gone. But he went and just got some guys off the street, and they went down. There were three of them. Mom ran out and told everybody that was driving down the road, she would stop them and tell them to go down. She saw (Donnie Goss?) after he'd been down St. George getting people out in his boat. She saw him and stopped him and told him to go down to Holly Meadows. He probably got there about ten or fifteen minutes after the ambulance did. So, probably about the time she was talking to him was when they heard me.

passages.q: What did you think about all that time? / Were you scared?
passages.t: I don't really know. I wasn't really that scared, I think, because there wasn't nothing I could do. I couldn't have gone anywhere else, and I couldn't have got out of it. But I thought a little bit about mom and dad because I didn't know what happened to them. But then I decided to quit thinking about it and just wait until it got daylight. But I didn't think it was that late when they came and got me, because I figured that I would sit there and it would go really slow just because I had to wait. So, I thought it was only about maybe 1:00 a.m. that late when they got me. She said it was 5:00 a.m. But I don't know what I thought about. I thought about our house. I was wondering if it was getting it really bad.

passages.q: What happened to the house?
passages.t: It's still standing. There are holes in it. We had to board them up, and everything inside was ruined. The walls were washed out. But mom thinks that maybe if the door wasn't facing the way it was, that we wouldn't have got it as bad. Because the house faced one way and the door went this way and the water came right up against the door and busted it down and went in. It broke the door and the sliding glass window and a few holes. But inside, everything was ruined. So, we just threw everything out and ripped up the carpet and the floor and the subfloor. Now they're putting the siding up on it and trying to get the garage fixed because there are three walls. The garage was knocked out by a tree. There was a tree laying in the garage. So, mom's car had to get out of somehow, and my car. My car ended up in the same place. Dad's jeep did. We were in the jeep and my car was left at the house. Mom's ended up on a hay wagon by the (Moss Bridge?).

passages.q: The water had tremendous power. / What have you thought about since the flood? / It's thirteen weeks, isn't it, today? / I think.
passages.t: [affirmative] It did. Going home. I'd like for us to get our house finished and go home. I wish that everything could be rebuilt in town. It's starting to look a little better now. We have [inaudible] novelty and drugstore. It seems a little better. Has it been that? I didn't even keep track of the days around that for about a month after flood. I think a lot of other people were like that too. If you asked somebody what day it was, nobody had any idea.

passages.q: These things all ran together in your mind, the days? / Do you dream about being in the river? / What happened on your dream? / You didn’t have any. / So, you haven't had any particular depression about it or fears or anxieties about it?
passages.t: Yes. Oh, I had one dream about it. I hope I don't. Mom says she has dreams about it. I don't know if dad does or not. I didn't have any, mom did. I haven’t had any. I was just depressed for a while because the town was gone and everything. But that was all just right after the flood.

passages.q: Now you feel like it's getting built back? / What are your plans? Do you think about making your home here in Tucker County? / Not as far as you think. / Did you have any questions, (John?)?
passages.t: Yes. I hope everything will get rebuilt and it will look normal. [affirmative] I always planned on staying here. I'd like to go back to school next fall if I can, and then come back here and open a nursery school. That's what I'd like to do, but that's a long ways off. Yes. I had a few things along the way and didn't want to interrupt [inaudible]. What have you been doing since the flooding? Right after, I helped at the school and the church for a while. Up at the elementary school? [affirmative] That's where I saw you. I came up there and sang some. Oh, did you? In the evenings. I was usually there in the afternoon helping them sort clothes and stuff. Then just before Christmas, I got a job out at CJ's Pizza. Then last, well, just Sunday, I went back to work. The [inaudible], because I already promised him when he rebuilt that I'd come back and work full time. So, I work there full time. When I get my schedule worked out, I work out at CJ's on the days that I'm off. Because I just got a car and I need all the money I can get. I guess you heard about that they brought in cars for flood victims from Maryland. I got one and I haven't got it ran in yet, but I just got the license plate just yesterday. What kind of car did you get? [19]78 Camaro. [laughter] Not bad. I know. I told (Ms. Gus?) she had pretty good taste because she picked it out for me. Not bad. Do you know the name of the people who gave it to you? Yes. I got his name from the title and I sent him a thank you card. I haven't heard anything from him. Well, that's great. So, you got wheels and – Yes. The snow would just go away, so I could bring it out. Today, by the way, is what? Is it the 29th? [affirmative] 29th of January 1986.

passages.q: Now you feel like it's getting built back? / What are your plans? Do you think about making your home here in Tucker County? / Not as far as you think. / Did you have any questions, (John?)?
passages.t: [affirmative] 29th of January 1986. One thing for sure about this recording, I'm going to give these tapes to the community probably for archiving the library. But I would also like to use these possibly in a radio broadcast or maybe even in a book, which is why we want to get pictures too. Is that okay with you to use the story that way? Yes. It's fine with me. What do you think? Would these stories be so great that everybody – Now I had people call me from Florida and interview me over the phone. I couldn't figure out how people in Florida even heard about – Is that right? -- the flood, let alone about me. They said that they got my number from Salvation Army, and they called me. One guy called me from Washington, D.C., and he said he was writing for a paper in Florida. Then another guy came to the house and he said he was a reporter for the Miami Herald. Well, that's interesting. Is there anything else you can think of that you'd like to add to this?

passages.q: You have any animals.
passages.t: A cat. I don't know. He was going pretty crazy when I went home that night. He ran in the house because he's a tomcat. He was throwing fits. We just thought he was scared a little bit. But we didn't know the water was up that high, and he probably had seen it. We put him back out and we left. We didn't see him. We heard that Bob (Getshaw?) had some extra cats down that barn after the flood. So, I sent my cousin down to look, and he said, "There's one dinner that looks like ours." But he couldn't tell because he wouldn't let him get near him. But I was afraid to go down because I didn't want him to see me and think that I came to get him. then I couldn't bring him up here. Yes. I don't think he'd like living up there anyway with all the dogs.

passages.q: Where are you living now? / With family or – / How's it been staying with her?
passages.t: On Spruce Street. My grandma, my dad's mom. I'd called her before we left and told her that we might be up because we thought we should leave. Then when we didn't come, she just thought that we changed our minds. She was going to go to bed until mom and dad came in. It's all right. I'm glad we have a place to stay, but it's kind of crowded. She has her own ways of doing things, and we have ours, and it's hard to mix them.

passages.q: Especially for months after month. / What kind of experience have your parents had working with some of the agencies, with FEMA, for example?
passages.t: Yes. Because she's used to living alone too. I don't think they had too much luck with FEMA. But I think just not too long ago, they had someone come down and reassess the house. I think we might get a little more help now. We've got clothing and food vouchers from Red Cross. Salvation Army gave me a box spring mattress. She's been talking to the people at (Tyre?) lately about helping us redo the house. But our problem is when they bring stuff in, we don't have any place to store it. Because grandma's house is full of stuff that we saved out of the house now. So, if they brought anything, we couldn't put it anywhere. The house was too cold and damp to put it in there. So, that's why we're trying to get the siding up and try to get it insulated and heated and everything, maybe we'll be able to get something stored in there.

passages.q: What does your dad work at? / So, he just can do this work on the house in his spare time? / Your mom, what does she do? / So, they're really busy. / Well, thank you. That's a really frightening story to me to hear that. Does it make you feel better to tell it, or would you rather not tell it? / Nothing seems to bother you a whole lot. [laughter]
passages.t: He works at (DMP?). Yes. That's why he's planning on doing the inside by himself. So, that'll probably be a while before we get into it. She's a nurse at Davis Memorial in Elkins. Yes. My dad just got back to work last week, so. I don't mind telling it. Doesn't bother me to tell it. [laughter] [end of transcript]

passages.q: How did that night start? / So, you are just holding on.
passages.t: At night I made it out there [laughter]. She was just about 10 feet ahead of me all the way [laughter]. Nicely. He did that. Both of those. This is Mr. Clemenson. I just went to feed the hogs and the horse and just came back to the house and started to eat supper. I heard a roar and then I ran out and the water was going over Cleta's car then. Just washing it right out of the driveway. Just washing it right out of the driveway.

passages.q: So, what time did you go out to feed the hogs?
passages.t: Oh, I'd say about 6:00 p.m. or 6:30 p.m. along there. It wasn't over fifteen minutes until the water went to pouring through there, and there wasn't any coming through whenever I left the barn. It just sounded like something roaring. It just came down all at once. All out on the porch and looked down and it just had her car covered. It was going over the top of it. I ran up there and cut the fence. I thought I would get my horse out, but I couldn't get into him. By the time I got back to the house, it was washing him down through the front of the house or down through the bottoms. That's the only time I shed tears for a long time since I came back from overseas [laughter].

passages.q: You could call to him but he couldn't come to you?
passages.t: He couldn't make it out. The water was too swift. It was just taking him down. Anyway, he got a rope and tried to tie the car and the truck fast to the pine trees so that they wouldn't wash away. By that time, it was coming up onto the front porch that quickly. So, I told him, I said, "If that starts coming through behind the house, we've got to get out of here." He said, "Oh, it isn't behind the house yet." But I told him he'd better go see. He took the light and went out to see and it was coming down through behind the house by this time too [laughter]. We just grabbed our coats on and a blanket and a package of cookies. That's all I could think of was something to keep us warm [laughter] and something to eat. All night long, I ran off without any chewing tobacco. All night long, she was cramming them over cigarettes in my mouth and chocolate cookies [laughter]. Every time he'd start shivering, I'd get him a chocolate cookie. I thought it might warm him up a little [laughter].

passages.q: Because what happened? You left the house with your cookies and then what?
passages.t: When we went off the back porch, the water was coming up on the back porch by then. Out through the garden, it was waist deep. We went over to a little calf barn and went in there after he loosened the dog. The dog was swimming right at the end of his chain [laughter]. So, we got in this calf barn, ran the calves out, and got in there. We were only in there like ten minutes until it was coming in there. So, we had to just head for the hills [laughter]. Of course, the calves were up against there so they didn't drown. The dogs followed us too. I left this dog, the small one, in the house. I figured she would die in the cold or I'd drop her somewhere [laughter] as she couldn't have walked. So, I just left her in the house and I guess she fared all right. She was upstairs the next day. But we came out around the hill then trying to get to Edith's house. When we got to Reservoir Hollow, which is normally a little stream that goes through a small culvert, it was really wide. I couldn't jump it, but Norman did. So, I had to step into it and thinking it was probably knee deep. But I knew it was swift, so I told him, "Hold on to me, because it might knock me down." But I had no idea. I went in almost up under my arms and it was just like a battering ram. It just knocked my legs right out from under me. She was heavy, all right, but she weighed 500 pounds in water [laughter]. [laughter] So, I was wet immediately up to my neck because I just went right down then. If he hadn't have had a hold of me, I'd have been in there drinking in about seconds flat because it was really swift. Just a little tiny string.

passages.q: You just bush whacked over the hill in the pouring rain and the pitch black to the point?
passages.t: Yes. Well, we had the flashlight and of course, he knows the way really well because we have a farm on out on the hill where he plants corn. We came out through there and all the way to this hollow over behind this house. It's called Rebel Run. But it's usually, oh, 2, 3 foot wide at the most. That night it was about 12 or 15 feet wide. So, we knew we couldn't get across that. The dog got in it and he's a big Airedale and he just went rolling down through them. We thought, oh, now he's drowned. But he got out of it. But we knew when he couldn't get across it, that we couldn't. So, well, Norman probably could have, but I couldn't [laughter]. So, we didn't know what to do. We were in sight to this house. We could see the barn and the lights over here and everything, but we couldn't get across that one little old creek. So, we turned around and went back out to the cornfield because there was no place else to shelter. He had left a couple shocks of fodder out there. He hadn't got it hauled in yet. So, I sat down on the side of the tree. By this time, we were both soaking wet; he from the rain and me from falling in and the rain. He put a pole up and then piled the fodder up around us. We sat there all night just listening to those horrible noises, houses tearing up over Hendricks. It was really bad. We prayed for daylight and everything else [laughter]. It was a terrible night. It wasn't too bad if she'd have had a little more Indian in her. But you see, my grandmother was Indian [laughter]. She didn't know how to make it through there.

passages.q: She did make it through it. / In a cave?
passages.t: I made it [laughter]. She could have stood it. I could have struck her with some good camp rocks back there where Mr. Simeon lived a long time. I know she couldn't make it up to that. That's a longway. I bet it's halfway up the top of the mountain. We moved in the mountain there. No, it's my camper rocks back there. It's like a ledge. It's just about like this room.

passages.q: A ledge. / Did you keep wood in?
passages.t: This is dry. Yes. I pile that full of – I burn out some, I cut some, put in. It was right back at the top of the mountain in there. All of us used that. We always did. That was probably because to a mile and half straight up [laughter]. My granddad showed me just a little. We've stayed there a lot of nights. At least I've stayed there for weeks at a time.

passages.q: What mountain is that that they're at? / McGowan. / What did the river sound like when you were sitting under the –
passages.t: McGowan Mountain. There used to be a fire tower around on top of us here. Then camp rocks were right under below that. But it's a longways to up there. Yes. She could have never made it up there. I never heard anything like it before. It was just unbelievable. Just like half a dozen freight trains or I don't know. It was, well, probably even more than that. It just roared all night until you nearly had to yell so that we could hear each other. It was just really loud. Plus, all those things breaking up. Once we heard a really loud explosion and we imagined that it was our gas tank, the heating gas. I had about probably 350 gallons of gas in the tank. We thought that it might have been that, but I don't know. It may have been a gas line over in Hendricks or somewhere that blew up. But you could just hear things just crashing all night long. So, we were sure Hendricks was totally gone. We were right, most of it was [laughter]. But the next morning as soon as it got daylight, we crawled out of there and went back to the house. We kept seeing this green roof and I said, "My goodness, the house is torn apart." Norman said, "No, the house is still all there." I said, "Well, what is that green roof? Did your barn have a green roof on it?" He said, "No." When we got a little closer, we could see it was the old, big house that we used just to store things. Had totally passed our house and turned completely around and was down on the neighbor's property. It was not on my place. So, I mean, tear it down as quick as I can. [laughter]

passages.q: [laughter] / Did you build your house?
passages.t: [laughter] It was unbelievable that it stayed all together and washed all the way down there, that big, old house, until it was below. Yes. They have two boards broke down. It was above our house and now it's below our house. It passed right by. No, honey. It's been there for about seventy-five or eighty years. Dad's eighty-six years old. He said that house stood there for a long time. He said that's the first he ever saw water up to it. He was raised up here at the mouth of Otter Creek.

passages.q: Is your dad still alive? Your dad is still alive? Is he?
passages.t: Well, he is in better shape than I am in [laughter]. He still walks off Fork Mountain. He lives on top of that mountain. He tells me to move up out of this sand and I'll live a long time. That's what he told me the other day. He walks 3 miles into Parsons and carries stuff up in a sac on his back. He'll pick his sack of flour and ride up there with it.

passages.q: What's his name? / Ry? / Well, Joe must have kept him from me [laughter]. / No, I never met him. / I will have to meet him. I hadn't heard his name. I've heard a lot about your grandmother. That's who I've heard the most about. / That's right.
passages.t: Ry Long. Riley. Yes. He's older than Joe was. He's brother to Joe. But he's older than Joe. He's the oldest one. You never met Riley Long? You're going to have to go up and meet him. My grandmother, Indiana? I wish I had my album down here. I'd show you her picture. You can see why I can make us a good den [laughter]. They lived in a house all the way on top of Fork Mountain. They don't have electricity. Just in the past year they've had water in the house and just the past year they've had a bathroom. But he's eighty-six and she's eighty-seven.

passages.q: Your mom is still young.
passages.t: Basically, they're healthy. They do their farming with an old, white horse shit. The Lord only knows how old that horse is. I tried to get him to trade him off and get him a young one. He says, "Which one will last long as my old bell?" So, he still got him. It was raining so hard while we were out there in that fodder shock. We had matches, but you couldn't get a fire started at all. Norman even pulled some stuff out from under rocks and so forth, that were dry and cut shavings. But it was raining so hard that it would put the fire out. You just couldn't get one started. Anyway, the next morning I was worried about my stuff. I've got stuff up there that I wouldn't take anything for, but I thought it took nothing for it that night. I mentioned this one machine I have. I've had it for years. She said, "I hope you never find that thing again." That was the first thing I found when I went in the barn. It was just sitting up there with the lid on, just as pretty [laughter]. But don't mention what it was [laughter]. It was more comparable. [laughter]

passages.q: [laughter] / Were you thinking about people or things as you walked back to your house? / Everything.
passages.t: [laughter] But he hasn't used it [laughter]. I took it and I put it back there where I know it's safe keeping it now, the water won't get it. I was just thinking of everything. I just couldn't imagine. All night long he kept thinking maybe the horse would walk out and come to us or something. I hardly thought of anything else. Once we heard something making a noise, it must have been one of the dogs. The one got in the fodder shock with us rode in my [inaudible]. He licked himself dry and then he tried to lick me dry [laughter]. That we heard something making a noise once and he crawled out to see. He was sure it was a horse out there, but it wasn't. I don't know what was making the noise. Probably just the wind. The wind started blowing really hard too in addition to all that rain. I've got a big bear trap that I wouldn't take anything for it blowing to my granddad. Never did use it or nothing, but I just keep it for a keepsake. I was worried about that. I looked for three days for it. Joy over here was walking up through one of those big sandbars. There was just the ring on top of the sand and he pulled that up out of there. That tickled me more than anything else. I took that and put it with my steel [laughter]. [laughter] I got them both hid back there. No one knows where it's at except me and dad. They're both illegal [laughter].

passages.q: The bear trap's illegal? / What did you see in the morning when you looked across the river at Hendricks?
passages.t: It's illegal to use. See, all that stuff been going down to the family. [talking simultaneously] I have made him a lot of drink in that machine [laughter]. Just like the steel, they're illegal to use. They'd be wrong and dangerous. They got him a new one and he gave me that. We really couldn't tell that it was even Hendricks. We thought for a minute that we've gone somewhere where we're not supposed to be or something because it didn't look like across the river at Hendricks normally. Well, tell them what I argued with about there. When we came down the road that comes out close to the Denison property up there, I thought that we were coming into the main road. Norman said, "That isn't the road. The road there." He said, "That's those fields." I said, it couldn't be because it just looked like it had washed sand up on the roadbed. But really, we were where there had been great piles of old brush and stuff where they had cut timber and left all these. All that was gone and it was just like a sandy bottom like we were coming out into the road. But it was unbelievable. Hendricks, it just looked like another place. It really didn't look like it would. We got to look at the houses over here. Buzzy Turner, he's a good friend of ours, and I got to argue with her. She said, "That's Buzzy's house laying in there, tilted up here on the side." I said, "No, it's not." I said, Buzzy's house was white." But it was. Buzzy had his house painted last summer and I didn't notice it. It was just different. You couldn't recognize. Then a few nights after, I was back here coon hunting again in the mountain. I looked across there and it's just the little streak of lights through Hendricks and Hamilton. They're not half as big as they used to be.

passages.q: But you were coon hunting a couple of days later.
passages.t: Oh, yes. That's my life. Yes [laughter]. Sooner coon hunting and anything. Luckily, the coon dogs didn't drown [laughter]. I'll be right in after the dog gets here that night [laughter]. If he hadn't have gotten out [laughter]. But the good part is she can swim good and I can't swim a licking. I had to take her out of the water [laughter].

passages.q: Your grandma didn't teach you that, huh? / But you lived on the river all your life and didn't swim at all.
passages.t: She couldn't swim either. I did. But see, she lived back on top of the mountain there all her life. He can wade up to his chin because he can't swim a lick. On above Uncle Paul's in there around top of the mountain. That's where her home was. That's where she raised her family. She was 105 when she died. She's buried up there.

passages.q: Was that Indiana? / Indiana? / Up at what house? Your house? / You still had stuff in the house? / Aren't you lucky?
passages.t: Huh? Right. I've got a picture up at the house there, a picture of her. Yes, upstairs. I've got what I had upstairs. I had it upstairs. I go up every once in a while and look things over. I'm figuring someday really soon I'd like to build back up there. I like it there so well I can't leave it. We still have one bedroom suit upstairs and I had a little electric organ up there and a rollaway bed. That was it [laughter]. Downstairs, the muck and mud was just about that deep. I just took a shovel and went in there and started and shoveled it out there. The mud was even in – Floors were just all buckled up with that. If I ever do fix it up, I'm going to have to put floors in it. But hopefully, I can build a new house. The mud was even in the freezer on my refrigerator and there was mud even in that. It would be impossible to get everything cleaned up, I think. I don't see how those people downtown are getting those houses cleaned out. Deep freeze it was all then [inaudible].

passages.q: Well, I'll tell you downtown is a lot more accessible than your place was. / Volunteers come in, they can get to Main Street and they don't think about the house up Elk Lick.
passages.t: Well, probably. They might have some high-pressure cleaning things too that they could do something with. But I really don't see how you could possibly get that mud cleaned out of things. We've washed and washed. Some of the stuff they hosed it down and it still has just like a muddy film on it that I don't know how you would get off. I guess you –

passages.q: Yes, everybody says that.
passages.t: I don't think it can be cleaned up. I don't think it can be. I thought maybe I had a lot of things made of wood and I thought that they would be all right. But the legs are splitting and they're coming apart. Even the old antique things, I thought that they would hold together [laughter] but they're not. They're just falling apart. Both of our porches are gone. It washed the foundation from under two corners and then washed through under the house. So, evidently something must be gone in the middle. The floor is kind of sagged like this. Then we got a letter from FEMA saying that we were eligible for $1,200 in minimal repair [laughter] so that we could get back in our house. The fellow came when we weren't even here. Joe went up with him. He drove a rental car as far as he could go. Then he walked on in. He really paid close attention to the house because he thought that we had a pump and a well rather than the spring and reservoir. Because on the paper it tells you that this money must be spent for these specific purposes. We don't even have a pump or a well. We got a reservoir in the mountain. They're about 400 feet above the hollow there. I don't how they determine those things so I called them then.

passages.q: $1,200, would that pay for a new floor? / That hardly would. / So, this guy came up to appraise the damage? What type of – / Did he leave a paper for you? / Why did he mention a pump and a well?
passages.t: [laughter] That won't put a floor around it. I doubt it. $1,200 we'd rather buy the material with price of stuff now. Supposedly. We weren't here. No, he took Edith's grandson up with him and he just looked around the outside and left. I have no idea. I don't believe he was at our place. I believe it was some other place and looked at it. But Joe took him up. Joe said he just looked around a little bit and said, "It's pretty bad, isn't it," and turned around and left. We didn't know how they determined that. So, I called and she said, "Well, he was there. He walked in. It says there's no roads or a very narrow path and no electric poles or anything. So, she said he must have been there." I said, "Well, he certainly wasn't in the house because the house was locked up." Norman fastened the doors back and put the window back in that was broken out and locked it out because we've had so many people going up there just to look. Well, there was a path into it because I took a D6 in there those two days before and plowed the road in. There still isn't any road, only what he did. He was sent out and got the wrong place wrote down [laughter].

passages.q: So, what do you think? You have this little road and you're really thinking about going back and building a house, even though. / Is there still the little flat?
passages.t: Well, we hope that they will put a road back up there come spring anyway. Oh, I'm going to build back there. There isn't no doubt about it. I was just born just the next farm up there and all. I'll always be there. There's a little flat. Oh, yes. The little flat up against the hill, yes. Our garden is still there. It didn't wash the topsoil off of it. I pushed a 6 foot. I measured the sand that was on that. It was just 6 foot of sand down in the lower side of the chair. I got a D4 dozer the other day and worked up there all day and I didn't get it all pushed off. Off the garden. I was always kind of fast with one of them. I built all the roads back through here on the Forest Service and everything. I couldn't get all that sand moved. It was just like pushing water. You get a blade full and it just slides off of the ends. I'd never pushed sand before in my life [laughter]. It's really deep.

passages.q: You wonder where it all came from, all that sand.
passages.t: Oh, the river is a hundred feet deeper than it used to be. It cleaned that river out until it's just way deeper than it used to be. Our meadow just looks like the riverbed. Up above our house it looks like a bomb's been dropped. It's devastating. But if you go up there and look, there's a rock pushed out of the river on top of the sod. It can be cleaned off and pushed back in. But it'll take a lot of topsoil with it when they do. Oh, yes, it's going to take a lot of it. Then a lot of places the topsoil is just gone. I was just getting them bottoms build up until it could raise something on them.

passages.q: Did you have any kind of a premonition about this flood? Any sense that it was going to happen?
passages.t: No. People would say to us, "Why don't you get out of that place?" Because the water came over the road down at Elk Lick three, four times a year and would wash out the bridge. If we saw the river coming up, we would hurry into town and buy groceries, whatever we needed and go back. Because as long as we were at home, we were fine. We would rather be caught in than caught out because at least if we were in, we knew the water wasn't going to come in our house. It never had before. We had done that, that day. We had gone out and got a little grocery and brought it back in. I had washed clothes and then we hurried back in because we knew it was going to come over the road. But that didn't concern us because as long as we were in, we were all right. Even in 1954, the water only – and there was a major flood that covered all these bottoms down below. Of course, it didn't wash anything away except little chicken houses or hog pens or something like that. But even in [19]54, it didn't come above the pine trees that stood in front of our house. So, when we saw it coming up on the porch, it was just something really unbelievable that it could come up there. Then to break through behind the house and come down behind the house yet and to do the things that it did, because our house was on a raise. It was probably what? How many feet were we from the river? Oh, goodness. It was about 300 feet from the river.

passages.q: Over but not up.
passages.t: We were probably 30 feet above the river level. Yes. At least 30, maybe 40 feet above the river level. Yes. Because there was a nice, little level. I guess on the way at the end of the back over there about 20 feet on the other side of the house. That little calf barn is probably another 300 feet, isn't it – Yes. – from the house. Plus, up against the hill a little bit. It went just about 20 feet up against the hill on the other side. It didn't wash the little calf barn away that it was up in it. Then it pushed the floor out. It must have raised it up and took the floor. In our house – this was really strange – we had these big, old pine trees beside the house. All these years we've been worried that they might blow out and fall down on the house. So, we were going to have them cut down. They were the only thing that saved the house. All the other outbuildings and the other buildings washed away. The barn and the garage and all of the meat house and the corn crib and everything just washed away. But those trees caught all that debris and broke the water from the house. That's the only reason that we even had the house left there. When I built that barn, I didn't think water could ever move it. I set poles and a nail to them. The poles were the frame. Set them in concrete. I cemented them in. It was pretty near a solid cement floor. They were great locusts. They weren't poles. They were locust logs [laughter] being carried in on his back and put up there too. Oh, I skidded them in there. Well, but I mean you'd put them up. The three of them, Robin, and his boys, had to help me set. You put them up. I didn't think water could ever move that. Oh, I dug holes down there about 8 feet and had them down in the ground and cement poured around. Now there's just a big hole there. There are big holes where every one of those post pulled out. I know a big dozer wouldn't upset that. Someone said that they clocked the river at one point when they could get down to it going 40 miles an hour. I believe it because it was really going fast.

passages.q: How could they clock it?
passages.t: I guess with some sort of instruments that they have at the timber and watershed lab, they can – I don't know what they measure it. They just guess the same as I do. I spent thirty some years [laughter]. Well, no. The timber and watershed, they have something that they can measure the speed of the water when they could get to it. But after they, of course, started coming up in the bottom. But now that's what someone said that they had the velocity of it. I bet you a lot because you're doing 30 mile an hour and he went through the bottom. So, he was just a fighting or trying to come out. [laughter] Oh God. He couldn't make her though. He couldn't get turned around in it. He'd try to turn around and he'd turn him back around. I don't figure he went very further if something hit him. We've never heard or saw anything of him or the barn or none of the hay or anything. We've never even found a scrap that looked like the barn. I had a set of hornets in there I'd give $185 for, and I can't find them even. I had them special made out here at Oakland. He was so big. He weighed more than 1,700 pounds. You'd have thought that he would have been strong enough to have come out of it. But he must have gone right in the mainstream of the river. He was one of the strongest horses I ever seen. I drove a team for a long time in the woods, but I never had a team that could move the load he could. I hope I can replace him this week, but I know I can [laughter].

passages.q: Will you bring it here? / Do you think it could flood that bad again?
passages.t: No, I'm going to bring him here until I get me a barn build up down the hill. Never put another one in that bottom again [laughter]. I never passed another horse in that bottom. I'll be afraid of that as long as I live now. Yes, I believe it could the way the river's filled up, up there. The river is filled up right on the upper end of the bottom there to this current level. It probably will if they don't reach ten in the – A winter night or two whenever the winter rain and everything, there's water that come back down through the bottom there. I was up there watching it. There's water that comes back down through there. It washed our road out again. Down below they had just put culverts in. I guess they don't turn the river out there. They place them with a nickel there. They had just put culverts in and gotten us a road. We'd only had a road for two days when it came up and washed it out again. I sat there and watched it come down through there again. Oh, it only got about that deep. But that was deep enough. It will as long as it's like it is because it just has a new course down through there. It doesn't even have to raise all that much now to come down through. There's nothing there to stop it. It's just straight through like this bottom down here. If you're here in the daylight, you could see what happened down there.

passages.q: We did see what happened. / I was curious to thinking Scott and I about a week after the flood, and we had talked a lot to Joe when he was alive about when he logged when he was about sixteen, and they clear cut these woods when it was virgin timber. I'm wondering about what happened at that point when they had stripped all the big trees off.
passages.t: It just filled a mouth of Green Hole up there, the entrance where it goes out, and pushed it down through the bottom. I don't know whether they'll ever take that out or not. Well, the difference was they logged with horses some days. They didn't build all these roads like we have today. These roads are what's carrying the water off. I built hundreds of miles of those roads. When we first started the Fernow Forest up here, I skidded that with a team. We started out with horses there. They didn't have no dozer or nothing. As soon as they could afford to get a dozer, they started building these roads. I've noticed Elk Lick out here, it used to stay all just a normal stream. Now it looks raised and it goes clean and dry, then the water just runs off as fast as it comes. They have to clear so much more land now.

passages.q: To get the same amount.
passages.t: Yes, right, to get the same amount of timber off to make it big enough with a tractor. Now, I can take you back to Green Mountain there. That place has never been logged. I'll show you where they logged with horses. Dad and all of them worked in there. Those old, logged roads are there. You can walk them and follow them. But they're not roads like these where they're built with dozers. I always have been against that. But I made a lot of money, I don't [laughter]. That was my bread and butter back in those days and I had to do it or stay there. Tell them how long you worked for the Forest Service. I was with them thirty-two years. What did you do when you started? When I started, I started driving team and cutting. Then he cut timber for them. With the cross-cut saws, me and Daniel Hardy laying over here in Bretz. Now, he's dying with cancer. Me and him were to the heart at first. We cut the first tree on that job and skidded it with a team of horses. One of them was mine, one was my brother's. They made him a real nice book when he retired and put pictures of all the different things that they had done on the Fernow, the different experiments that they had tried. I wish we had it to show it to you all. Come up when we get back home [laughter] if we ever get back home. They come out there one time with upsetting the tree. It was leaning back this way. Just they wanted to fall it the other way and they came out with a hydraulic jack to do that [laughter]. Cut a notch in it up here and a notch down here and set the jack in. Naturally full of meanness, I couldn't pump it with a jack handle. I took a peavey and stuck in there. I said, "I believe I can lift her with this. Boy, I just made the fluid fly [laughter]. They went and got another jack and had done the same thing. They quit with me [laughter].

passages.q: Tell me about the Long people. / Ashamed of it.
passages.t: Now what do you want to know about them? Been the onerous thing this ever was [laughter]. Cleta could tell you that better than I could. I was sort of ashamed of it [laughter]. Yes. Could you talk about the Longs? About the Longs? She wrote a story on them. [laughter] Oh, no [laughter]. No. This you don't need to put down.

passages.q: Well, just put down what you know.
passages.t: I just want you to know, don't do that. I'm not going to say it. I'm going to say that I don't have some – Mr. Grumble, he did say, he said it to be true, that he could do more work in a day than his wife could do in two. So, Mrs. Grumble, she did say, and she said it to be true, well, if you can do more work in a day than I can do in two, then you can do the housework and I'll follow the plow. So, she said, "Now, don't you forget to watch that speckled hen unless she goes astray. Don't you forget to have that spun of yarn that I spun yesterday. Don't forget to have the dinner right on time. Don't forget to churn the butter and get the milk out to the cooler or something," she said. Then he said he forgot to watch the speckled hen. She did go astray. He forgot to have the dinner right on time. He forgot the skin of the yarn that his wife spun yesterday. Then in the end of it, he said, "I swore by all the stars on earth and all the stars in heaven, my wife could do more work in a day than a man could do in seven. [laughter] That's the end of it. I used to know it all but I've forgotten a part of it. Might get it together if I get mad.

passages.q: Changed his mind after he walked in her shoes.
passages.t: Yes. There are too many things for him to do. "Envy me and the chance of sounding ungrateful, I must say my peace do or die. When I overheard folks talking envy, for the life of me I can't see why. The lady was saying, "These flood folk, they sure do have it made. They're getting free food, housing, clothing, and even not working as paid." Well, I had to walk on when I heard her not trusting my temper to keep. But when I laid down in a friend's house in bed, I found that I just couldn't sleep. So, I got up and wrote down my feelings, the one thing in this world that's free. Lady, if you read this story, I'm a flood victim, don't envy me." Then I went on to tell about what all I hadn't gotten that they promised [laughter].

passages.q: Go ahead. / Can you do the one about the flood that you published? / What'd you call it?
passages.t: Well, no. It's [laughter] not quite up to par. But I started it [laughter]. As soon as I find it. I'll have to have my glasses here. She wrote the title. She put "Thankful for a Fodder Shock. "It was just an ordinary evening when the river was running quite high. For so many times I've been flooded in. But my house there was snug, high, and dry. I'm safe, I said, it's been before to the trees that stood out from my door, but never in, not even when the storm of [19]54. Then just at dark, a strange new sound with a roar unreal like a train, we peered through the windows and wondered if could that be the sound of the rain. We grabbed our coats, ran out with the light, then stared in horror at the terrible site of water washing our car down the lane. Up to the porch, the rushing waves came. So helpless we watched as our beautiful horse admired by all folks passing by with strong muscle legs and his huge body weight drifting by like a leaf on the tide. We tied fast the car and the truck to the trees, grabbed the blanket and untied the dog. Then off to the hills lying back of the house through water now floating with logs. We sat in the calf barn, bare minutes passed by until water rose even to floor. Again, up the mountain we hurried away while rain like a spigot did pour. No shelter up here, so we must travel on to an aunt's house in old Brooklyn Heights. If my crippled old legs will last until then, we'll be safe from the storm in the night. But the rugged, old mountain seems steeper in dark. Rambles caught and I fell many times. My husband's strong arm pulled me back from the grasp of a stream that threatened great harm. We heard crash of houses and trees going down and the snap as the bridge cable gave.

passages.q: Go ahead. / Can you do the one about the flood that you published? / What'd you call it?
passages.t: We heard crash of houses and trees going down and the snap as the bridge cable gave. I thought how we worked to save the old span and my tears mingled in with the rain. We crossed over the mountain to old Rebel Run. Alas, there's no way we could cross. Though we searched up and down, the calm, little stream was a torrent both rushing and wide. Oh, where could we go from the wind and the rain that chilled us right down to our bones? Then we thought of a fodder shock left in the field way back on the mountain we'd come. So, we turned and went back and with fingers now numb, built a shelter, and quickly crept in. Not a dry thread remained. The dog shivered too as he crouched by my side from the rain. He licked off his fur and then licked at my coat. Though in vain, the poor dog did try. Our last spite of all for I knew if I didn't, I'd surely break down and cry. We prayed that the rain and the wind first would stop. Then we prayed for the light of the day, not knowing the path the destruction took while we waited the long night away. With day's first drill light, we stretched our stiff legs and hiked back to our house to see. But the site turned us cold for the water still ran. The rest you wouldn't believe. It looked not our farm. The meadows were gone and the house so curiously stayed. Three vehicles wrecked, barn and buildings all gone. Great holes marked the place of their grave. So, back around the mountain we trudged once again. By now, we could wait for every run. But when we saw Hendricks, no one could describe the whole town laying to ruin how thankful we are that we have folks who care. When we got to a house warm and dry, they gave us their clothes and they warmed us with food and their love brought tears to our eyes.

passages.q: Go ahead. / Can you do the one about the flood that you published? / What'd you call it?
passages.t: When we got to a house warm and dry, they gave us their clothes and they warmed us with food and their love brought tears to our eyes. We'll never forget that night on the hill in a fodder shock, shivering and wet. But how lucky we were that we had mountains near. When I read of what others have lost, we still have our lives, thank God for that, and how little the rest of the cost. I pray God will help those who suffered so great in the flood that November eve. May we not forget them in our prayers all this year in the winter so meager and bleak. It doesn't quite rhyme [laughter].

passages.q: It doesn't have to rhyme. / Yes. / I was going to check that out.
passages.t: Did you read the one I wrote about her husband, about Joe? You did. Oh, did you [laughter]? I'll tell you; they were both about frozen when they got there the next day to my house. We came to her house and she wasn't at home. We were looking for you. I didn't want to come. I was afraid you'd gotten into the water. I was trying to get to your place. But the door was unlocked and we went on in and shook up the fire. When she came, she got us some dry clothes and made us some coffee and we stayed over there for better than a week. I think I slept all afternoon recuperating [laughter].

passages.q: Do you have a copy of that poem about Joe in that book over by the bridge?
passages.t: No, I don't have it. I have it at home, but I don't up the house in my – She gave me a pair of Joe's pants. I had to roll about that much of them up. Joe is so tall. I was going to put it in the paper. I just want to change some of it. But it still sounds a little silly. But I finally wrote a book about Cheat Mountain. He calls it The Mountain Speaks. So, I wrote this one about "The Bridge Speaks. It's kind of sad too [laughter]. Maureen said, "Oh, don't put that in the paper. It makes me cry. "I am an old, old swinging bridge built back in [19]17. For many years, I stood so strong. But now, I sway and lean. Once children ran across my span and lovers strolled and tarried, there was no thought of breaking down. My peers were firmly buried. But years took toll. I lost one pier. My cables rusted then. The tower posts that held me tall began to sag and bend. Then on a sad November eve in 1985, a mighty wall of water caught me with a grave surprise. High water splashed upon my floor. At this I only laughed. I'll hold on tight, I told myself, this torrent too shall pass. But soon my laugh became a groan. As waters higher rose above my floor and then some more, the mighty onrush closed. I shook in fear as trees passed by. Oh, will I fall this night? I must hold on. So, many folks depend upon my fight. The Woman's Club has worked so hard to try and keep me here. If I fall down, a few will cry. But many folks won't care. I feel my eye pins giving now as huge trees beat my span. Rocks batter at my cement piers. Oh Lord, I cannot stand. One cable gives, my timbers crack as house roofs scrape me by. I'm going now. All hope is lost. All hope is gone. I tremble with a sigh.

passages.q: Do you have a copy of that poem about Joe in that book over by the bridge?
passages.t: I tremble with a sigh. The many friends who walked each day across my mighty brow will have to travel many miles to get to Hendricks now. When deafening snap and history's gone along with all the rest, my cables lie on either side, although I did my best. Oh, will they build me up again like good friends did before? Or will they leave me lying here and close another door on all that stood for what was free to travelers passing by with steady feet across my span? Or am I doomed to die? A week goes by and now it's two. I hear a rumor spoke, we will rebuild the swinging bridge, say many friendly folks. The mayor of Hendricks sees my need. He knows of those who care. The DNR comes down to look if I can be repaired. If you'd help by writing them to let them know you care, soon I will stand again so strong and beautiful and rare. If you like my photograph and if you like my story and if you can, please help me stand again in all my glory. I was going to put a photograph and this in the paper to see it. But from what I hear, the Army Corps of Engineers has supposedly appropriated something like $30,000 to rebuild our swinging bridge. So, if that's true, I won't have to [laughter].

passages.q: Was when was the original bridge built? / Who rebuilt it then?
passages.t: In 1917. Then it broke down again in the flood of [19]54 and was rebuilt. Bob White and Joe Long and – Pastor Jordan. Did you help that? No. Baxter and Willis built it originally. Oh, what was it? Willis Spencer and Baxter Jordan built it in 1917. Then in [19]54 when it broke down, Joe and Brian Sponagle, and Bob White and Norman and Jim Sponagle, I believe, rebuilt it. Then in 1958, a big tree fell across it and broke it down again. The same bunch helped to – Our Old Bridge just threw them off. The same bunch helped to rebuild it. But see, they've used the same materials. Every time they've used the same cables. Those are original cables and they've just put smaller ones on to reinforce it. It's a wonder they didn't spread pieces though in all that water. But they just strung down on the side. Those cables are still lying down this side. They're still there, yes. But they're on the other side. There's a cable on that bridge that me and Joe put together. After we let the weight of the bridge on, you couldn't tell where it went together at. That's where I first learned to splice cable. They showed me right there how to do it. But you couldn't tell where that cable was together, I hardly could.

passages.q: Did you see the swinging bridge up at our creek after the army fixed it up? / Because we went up there and it seemed like it was going to be really heavy if the snow would fall. / [laughter] / What do you mean?
passages.t: No, I never went up to see it. I did. That's what I thought too. There was no way for the snow to get down. Now, the little bridge over there across Otter Creek. Boy, I tell you the biggest sassafras and that bottom was worn out on me one morning over that. [laughter] There's where I started to school at. I was a little smart ELIC and grandma would go down there and she'd put wood ashes on that so as we could cross it. Now, it wasn't a bridge then. They called it a what? A foot log. I just went down there and grandma was hollering at me and on across that aisle went just to skate. Then boy, she got me stopped to her and she walked me back across there. She wore the biggest switch out she could find in that bottom [laughter].

passages.q: [laughter] / Which house did you live in at up there?
passages.t: You were supposed to wait until she put the ashes on [laughter]. She made me walk across that, as she said, like a gentleman [laughter]. [laughter] You remembered that. I remember that as well as if it happened yesterday. Boy, she did give me a [inaudible] [laughter]. It was all around this way up from where her cabin is, around here on the hill. Right straight across from (Store Jordan's?), isn't it? Yes. Right up on that hill in there. You know why they're called the Bill Long place over from where the cabin is and then it's along beyond that. That's where I was born. I was nine years old when we left there and went to the top of the Fork Mountain. Left up there about 5:00 p.m. one evening, we could end up at home there about 2:00 a.m. the next morning. But the people came in here. Pop cut trees down that big to get the wagon turned. Couldn't even get into the house. That was mom's home place and all of them had left there years before and moved in there. There's where they still live. Strange how you remember things when you were – He had a little mule and a bay mare when he moved in there. Had to cut his way in. There were no roads. Everybody over there calls him the wire mesh because he went in there like that.

passages.q: [laughter] Was that whole track your family's? / That whole track of land up there, your family's at that time? / John said there was an old coal mine on top of that mountain he came across one time, like a little hand dug.
passages.t: Huh? That belongs to my two brothers now. Yes, they made it. John and Rob. Oh, it's on this other mountain. Fork Mountain, it's got no coal mine. This is up on the mountain where Mandy Teeter used to live up on there. Yes, up there. Yes, on that mountain. There's where boy went up there and died, wasn't it? They had to bring them off from wars [inaudible]. Yes. I don’t know where there's three mines in Turkey Run. I don't know where those two mines on Otter Creek where they got coal off the log trains. There are three mines in Otter Creek. I don't know where's that. They got coal off the log trains in there. I know where every log camp was from the mouth up here, clinging to the alpine. I've been to every one of them. They were numbered. We went up there one time to – we went camping, is what he calls it. Were they numbered? They were numbered. I thought they were numbered. That's what I heard Joe say, they were numbered. Joe said those camps were numbered. Starts here at Camp One and goes clean through. Camp Eleven was the last one.

passages.q: How old were you when they were doing that? / Yes. / Just a boy? You were not even a boy? / He was still a twinkle in his daddy's eye. [laughter] / But he took you up to show you where they were? / Your dad made you live in the woods?
passages.t: Me? I wasn't thought of then [laughter]. Pop was just a young boy, I believe. He wasn't even thought of then. Pop was just a young boy at that time. Mighty young. Oh, he showed me a lot of times through there and made us live in the woods back in there. Well, yes. He'd take us and go for weeks at a time. We wouldn't go home. Well, I could thrive in the woods. Just stay in the woods sang and hunt. Norman said whenever they started to play, that he would find him something to do. He wouldn't allow him to play that night. No, we weren't allowed to play around. He said he'd work him six days of the week on one side of the mountain and on the seventh day, he'd take him over on the other side so they couldn't hear the church bells ring [laughter]. [laughter] That's right. One time he ran out of work back in there in the Elk Lick side, got over there on the other side of East Parsons. Those church bells went to ringing and he reared up. He looked at us boys, he said, "Boy, it must be a quarter going on downtown [laughter]. Your pops didn't know the difference, huh? That's the truth [laughter]. He didn't know the difference. I don't want to repair it and tell out on him, boy, he'd get mad at you [laughter]. Well, I'll tell you what, my grandmother and grandfather raised me. But we worked too. We worked all week, but when Sunday came, we all went to church. Don't you think we didn't. Oh, we didn't know when Sunday came. I took my shoes off and walked down and I could see the church. Many a time when we get outside, we took them off and went barefooted home too. I only got one pair a year [laughter]. Did you know that Edith was born in the cellar? No, I was born in the barn. Born in the barn. Yes, on the second day of January.

passages.q: How old were you when they were doing that? / Yes. / Just a boy? You were not even a boy? / He was still a twinkle in his daddy's eye. [laughter] / But he took you up to show you where they were? / Your dad made you live in the woods?
passages.t: Yes, on the second day of January. Didn't she take you to the cellar then? Yes, I was hid [laughter]. Her mother took her to the cellar and hid her. She didn't get in the house until you were, what, nine days older? Well, it was something like that? I don't remember [laughter]. I think it was quite a – Oh, you know what they did. Well, I do know that my mother told me that she had me out of wedlock and she was afraid to take me in. Well, my grandmother was a very strict woman. Of course, she had to know that that girl had a baby. She had to know that, that's all. No mother could be around a girl and know she wasn't going to have a child and be with her all that time, I don't think. She probably ignored it [laughter]. So, she went out to the barn. When she went out there, she was sick and she had me out in the barn. She didn't have no clothes. She didn't have no blanket. So, she took off her underskirt. She had to cut the underskirt halfway one and wrapped me up in that and laid me down in the manger. Well, now my aunt said she knew something was wrong. Her name was Stephine. My mother's name was Aldell. That was her sister, said she knew there's something going on. She went out there and said she heard something grunting down in there and it scared her and she left. But then she went back later and mama took me to the cellar. But she kept the key around her neck and if they wanted anything out of the cellar, she went and got it. She didn't let nobody go in. One of the rats had eaten me up, isn't it [laughter]? Then finally, on Sunday they went to church. As I say, they always went to church. Mom was sick. She stayed home, took me to the house, and found some of her little sister's clothes and that was my first bath and the first clothes I had on. That must have been about a week or nine days, I suppose, after I was born. But I thrived. I'm still here [laughter]. She's seventy-five years old now. It was in 1909 when I was born.

passages.q: Where was that? / Who were your people?
passages.t: At Gladesville. At Gladesville. Teeter. My mother was a Teeter. Yes, she was Andrew Teeter's daughter. He was my grandfather. I have his picture and I have her picture too at the house. I have his picture and Clark's picture. Here's Arthur. Brian recognized them down here. All of them except two, I believe. There's four of them, Jacksons, and Clarks and what's that other one's name? Patterson's. Two of the girls too. Yes, and two of the girls. But now, Brian wasn't sure about the girls. It was Alley and Corey and Liz and – Virginia. Yes, Virginia. You never forgot them. Boini was one of the grandfathers. You should make me go "Uh-huh." You have to go "Uh-huh." We did that for the seniors. Well, now when I sing two stanzas, you go uh-huh. Now you do it. Now, I'm not going to say "Uh-huh." You can say "Uh-huh."

passages.q: [laughter] Kick me when I'm supposed to. / No, it's all right. Just turn it off. Froggy went-a courting and he did ride, a sword, and a pistol by his side. He rode up to Miss Mousy's door where he had often been before. He knocked at the door of the Mousy's door, said, "Hey, Pretty Miss, are you within?" Oh, Mr. Frog got card and spin to slip the latch and walk right in. Well, the frog took the mouse up on his knees, said, "Hey, Pretty Miss, will you marry me?" "I cannot answer that until I have seen my Uncle Rat." Uncle Rat came riding home who's been here since I've been gone. Fine gentleman has been here, asked for me to be his dear. Uncle Rat just split his sides, thinking of a mouse being a bride. Uncle Rat rode off to town to buy his niece a wedding gown. Where will the wedding supper be? Way down under in a hollow tree. What will the wedding supper be? Piece of bread and butter and black-eyed peas. Who will be our wedding guests? All our friends that we love best. First to come, this little moth, she spread on the tablecloth. Next to come is a big black bug on his back with a whiskey jug. Next to come was a big, black snake. He brought in the pound cake. Next to come is a bumblebee when his corn stock fiddle up on his knee. Next to come is Missy Tick, she ate so much that it made her sick.
