passages.t: They haven't quite decided. I think it's going to be a combination of the two. I think part of it will be accessible as like a strip to pull in, you know, near, and some will be enclosed. They aren't sure yet. I mean it's just still, I think, on the board on that. But I think the new, the Food City is going to relocate, which I think would be good to have that as an anchor store, you know, because, you know, anybody who goes to buy groceries, if there's other stores around--Terry Trivett and I were talking about it this morning, about how, you know, if we all get in a cluster it helps everybody's business. I mean, you know, here we have this little strip down here that people, you know, shop together, you know.

passages.q: / Especially if you got a 600-car garage.
passages.t: On this side, this street on 460. And I think it would be so nice if we had a good parking area where more people could park, and just run in, and, you know, go in Jackson's, come in here, go to the Family Shop. We think that side-by-side businesses feed off each other, definitely. Right. Um hmm. Instead of a place for two cars. Yeah.

passages.q: What do you think about the argument that it's just not going to flood here anymore?
passages.t: Oh, I think that's a real fallacy that few people really believe. It will flood here again. Yeah. We've even had some people say, "Well, the water table is low." No, that makes no difference. It's our terrain. I mean if we have the rain, we're going to flood. Definitely. Just like I say here, we're at the intersection of Slate Creek and Levisa River. We're going to flood again. It's just a matter of when. We've had several high waters that seemed threatening since '77 that we used to, you know, evacuate. But we just decided, you know, we got tired of that, you know. Carry everything upstairs. You have to take it down the street and up the steps. We do have some storage up there. Damaged a lot of things that way, so we decided to sit through it. But we will flood again if we stay here long enough.

passages.q: And even if you don't flood, what's happening to the coal reserves here? How much more- -How many more years is... active coal industry? / Twenty percent. / Any parting thoughts? / Thank you very much.
passages.t: I think there's lots of years of coal left here. I think it might be different types of mining techniques that recover it, but I don't think the coal is gone here. I mean I don't think the coal industry is dead. Looks a little bad right now, twenty percent unemployment I heard on TV last night. Twenty percent in Buchanan County right now. But it's a lot of shifting of ownership of these mines and things. See A.T. Massey just came in and bought United Coal, and they laid a lot of people off. They're redirecting their personnel. I mean, you know, they're switching around to, I guess see who's going to work and who's not. So I think that's maybe not a true unemployment picture right now. I think that will reverse. But I do think there's some coal reserve left here. I think that's why A.T. Massey's coming in here. And United got tired of the coal business. They've moved on to other things. They raise tomatoes. They're the second largest tomato producer in the United States, I think, something way up there. Right. And they're into golf courses, other things. No, I just hope they get this done in time for me to enjoy it! Uh huh.

passages.q: Full name? / Your middle initial? / Frank. I met your dad one time down there. / I'm sorry. / What's his name? First name? / Russell. / His wife?
passages.t: Danny Hebb. Yes, F, Frank. That's my uncle. Yes. Shoot. Ora. I just call [laughter] her aunt. She used to cook out there at school when I was in grade school. We were in school. They wouldn't let us call them by their first name. There she was, my aunt, and I had to call her Mrs. Hebb. [laughter] [inaudible]

passages.q: Who's your dad? / Your granddad? / I see. But this was your great granddad's place out here. / What was his name? / He must have farmed this whole hillside, did he?
passages.t: Charlie, Charlie Hebb. Elwood. He and Russell are brothers, Russ' older brother. Yes. Burley. Burley, yes. I don't know. He worked in the mine. See, they was originally from Benbush. They was coal miners, and they moved down in here. My Uncle Russ, that's where he stayed up. But he come down here and live and grew up a little bit. But he originally from [inaudible] and they mined coal up in there.

passages.q: You work in the mines now? / A power plant. / Up in Mount Storm? / Are you an electrician? / How long have you worked there? / Well, at first, I guess, I heard about the experience you went through probably from Hank. / Yes. / What do you remember best about that? Had it been raining all that week? / Well, I was at work that day. I had to take a road trip. They take labors and send them, if they got errands, like errands to run or something to pick up in places. They send to take us out and send us on the road for road trips. I had to go to Oakland for a road trip and pick up the paper. When I went out, it'd been raining about all week. I reckon about five days in a row. When I went out, the creek was getting pretty high up here, but they weren't flooding the banks or anything. I was [inaudible] out there, maybe an hour, 45 minutes. So, I came back, and it just looked like the lake is out through there on both sides of the road. I knew then there's going to be some flooding. That was about, I'd say, I come through there, probably about 2:30 p.m. back through, coming back to the plant. So, when I came home from work, I didn't come here at home. I just went on down to the river. I was checking the river to see how fast it's coming up. I put a stick down, and it was coming up – just steady coming up on the stick when I was watching it. I knew then it was going to flood. I was going to run to town. My brother and sister-in-law lived down the Pulp Mill Bottom in Parsons. I come up over the hill out here, and I've seen Bobby Spano. I asked him if he'd seen the mayor. He said he had. I asked him if he'd call the mayor and get him to evacuate them people down there. He said he would. So, I come on to town. When I come to town I called the emergency squad and tried to get them to evacuate people. They said they was out like in more places trying to get people out. They weren't really worried about the big rivers. Just the small streams they said was flooding. So, I went on over Pulp Mill Bottom. I told my sister-in-law and them about it. Her husband kind of laughed at me. She said when I left, he [laughter] kind of said, "Well, the water isn't getting up here." He just kind of laughed at me. So, when I left, I come on back at Hendricks. I've seen the water was coming up in the streets. Well, it was up where the Hick fairground was, the water was. I'd asked the deputy sheriff – that was Hank Thompson. Jim Blosser, he was a foreman and a chief. I reckon he was a chief foreman who was down there. I asked him if they'd got my uncle and aunt out of their house. They've lived on the lower street there, right next where Blackwater comes into Dry Fork area. They said they didn't. So, I told him I was going on down. They told me they'd get down with me, Jim and Hank did. So, I told them to walk on one side of the street, and I'd go on the other side. We'd try to check the rest of them houses up there and make sure there wasn't anybody else there. So, we walked up there, and we was checking them. They got down there. We could see there was already some people trying to get my uncle and aunt out of their house, and there wasn't nobody in other houses. So, I started to cross the road. I was wading water probably up to my chest when I crossed the road. We got across. I knew it was too deep for her to get out. Because she had – she's got arthritis and stuff real bad. She hadn't been very well. I knew we couldn't walk her out. That water's just blue cold. So, I asked him if he had a rope. We'd go out. I'd try to tie a rope to a pole and take it across and tie to another house where we can grab a whole rope and take ourselves across on it. I got a rope out. I went out and tried to go across it. Shoot, I hit the middle of the street, and the water just took me. I pulled myself back up with the rope. I told him, I said, "We couldn't get out." So, my father-inlaw was a state policeman. So, I wanted to call the emergency squad and see if they'd pass me onto him and maybe we get a boat in to us. So, I tried calling the emergency squad. They wouldn't let me talk to him. They said that he was busy over there. I asked them if they'd get a boat into us. Tell the fire department to get a boat into us because there wasn't no way we could get out. The water was coming into the house then. It was just barely coming [inaudible] coming over the floor. So, we waited there a while on them, well, about as long as we could. The water come up in the living room. It was coming up pretty close to the phone. I thought, well, if I'm going to make another call, I better try it to see if the phone is still working. I picked up, and it was still working. So, I made another call. I told them that there wasn't no chance to even get a boat into us then. Because there's too much debris and stuff coming down the river. There was buildings and everything else, trees and stuff coming down through there. So, I asked them if they'd send a helicopter into us to get us out. Because it was eight of us in the house. They said that they couldn't pass me through my father-in-law or nothing because they was all busy on the phone lines, and everything was tore up. She said she'd call me back. I told her, I said, "Well, you'll not call me back on the phone." I said, "It's just a wonder it's working now." It went dead on us then. So, I knew then that we had to get upstairs, get out of the water. So, I took and helped my aunt upstairs. Then told the rest of them to come upstairs. When we went upstairs, we put her to bed. I've seen the water. There wasn't no chance for us getting out. So, I just asked them all, if they'd come into one room, we'd have a word of prayer. So, we all come in one room. I asked them to get in a circle. We grabbed hands, and I prayed for them, prayed for all of us. It wasn't too soon, I said amen, boy, I heard kaboom and underneath it was – our house started shaking. I hear a building or something come through the side of the house right underneath where we're standing. So, we took her over and put her in another bed. My aunt, we put her in another bed in another room. Then we all went in over in the other room. Then about every twenty minutes or so, we'd go over in the one room where we was standing, where it had a window where we could look up to see the people who was trying to get us out of it. I had a flashlight where I keep flipping at them and let them know we're still in there. We went back. I just figured myself, man, the water was way up there. I could reach out the window, and you could – the water will hit your hands from reaching out the window, the upstairs window. So, I figured that we was going to be – I figured the river's just going to take us down. So, when I knew if them fellas wasn't right with the Lord, and they'd be killed at night, I just felt the Lord hold me responsible for. So, I went, and I asked to -- went and took the fellows off by their selves one-on-one and I asked him if they'd been saved. Hank told me he never. He kind of broke down. He told me he'd like to be. So, I led him in a word of prayer. I just went to each – to the other ones. Jim Blosser, the foreman, and he wanted me to pray for him. So, we took – me and him went together off and prayed. But the rest of them, they didn't want me to – they didn't want to say they wanted to be saved, but they asked me to pray for them. Maybe every ten minutes or so, one of them asked me to pray for them. So, it was going – the house was staying pretty good. You could hear stuff smashing into it and roaring. It just sound like a train coming through it, just a steady roar. You couldn't hear. There was two boys across the street in another big house that come down. They tried to bring a boat to us, one, to foreman. I told them to get in another house across street from us. They was pretty saved. It was a big old house. There was another house blocking the debris from them. It was just right across street. They couldn't holler. We couldn't holler and hear each other. So, we went in. I knew that the water was deep and stuff, but the house, it was staying pretty good. Then it started raining a lot harder. I reckon it's about 11:30, 12:00. The house started shaking a lot. There was trees. You could hear a lot of trees and stuff coming down, going through it. Something come in the other end where we was in that one room. It was behind us. It sounded like tree stuff coming through there. The house started shaking really bad then. The wind started rattling everything. I figured that that was time the house was going to go then. So, I just started praying so hard and everything. I just started getting scriptures back. It was in the Bible about faith. I just tried to block everything from my mind and just have faith in the Lord, and the old house quit shaking. It wasn't no sooner when I quit praying, the windows stopped shaking. The water kept raising, but the house stopped shaking. I reckon we sat there about 1:00 a.m. We had a Coleman lantern keeping us warm. Well, I was soaked. I was coming across street and something come down through and knocked me down. I went in and clear my head. I was all wet. So, he gave me a blanket and wrapped around me. The rest of us had blankets. Because we're just all pretty cold from being out in the water. So, we just laid there with that Coleman lantern. I'd go to the window, and they tried to bring a – I heard a loud noise, just like a roar. I knew it was something they was trying to bring in to get us out there then. It was the big loader. All them guys was hollering that they was going to get out. I thought maybe they'd get us out too. I've seen it was a loader. I told myself, they ain't going to get nothing down here with rubber tires. I said, it'll get down. But that guy wouldn't quit trying. Every time he'd try there, you'd see the loaders start to get down the stream. They just backed up and give up. They give up on the loader. But then I reckon they just kept praying for us. But the water receded then. It kind of quit raining. Then the water started going down. The next morning, I was getting daylight then. The water – it just felt like somebody pulled the plug on a bathtub or something. The water went out so fast. It went down. Then they brought a canoe in and got us out with a canoe then. They brought some boys down there with a rope, and they took us out in the canoe. But it was something. [inaudible] again. / Are you a preacher?
passages.t: No, I work in West Virginia Power. Yes. Yes. Just TA electrician. It's just a temporary assign, a labor, but a TA. If we get outages and stuff going on, you get TA for them. Two years and about five or six months. I used to work construction for Armstrong before that. Thompson? Yes. No. I go to First Baptist Church in Parsons. We're Christian people,

passages.q: But you said that you felt the responsibility for the souls of those people was on you.
passages.t: Yes. I felt if they didn't know the Lord, if they haven't heard the word, it was my job to minister to them, to go and talk to them about. Because I knew it because I'm a Christian, that I knew the way to be saved. The Lord tells you to come on to me through my son, Jesus Christ, and accept Him, and you will be saved. That's what you've got to believe. I felt if I wouldn't have done that and they'd have died, and they wouldn't have known Christ, they went to hell. That had been on my head.

passages.q: How long have you been a Christian? / What was your own salvation like or conversion?
passages.t: Since I was 18 years old. I'm 24 now. So, it's been six years. Well, I used to do body work, and I met another fellow. I used to work at a garage in Parsons at Lambrecht Chevrolet. This other fellow, he was a carpenter, but he had a garage he built. Me and him used to do work on the side. He was a Christian. He'd talk to me all the time about going to church. I went to the Methodist church, but I was far from being a Christian. I just went to church more or less to be there. But I didn't have the understanding. I didn't have the Lord in my heart then. But he talked to me, ministered to me a lot. They had a prayer chain going there. I didn't know about it. I just found out about it here just a few months ago. But he and these other fellows, they got together, and they was praying for me. Of course, I didn't know it then. But I was down one night working on a car for him. We got to talk about again – he'd come and talk about it. I'd talk about being a Christian. He was always trying to get me to come to the Baptist Church with him. So, I was down there one night. He was to tell me about getting saved. It had been bothering me for a while, about if I die, where would I go? That night, I was back there standing in the car, and I just got real hot. I started sweating. But I was just cool, but I just felt real hot. It was just like a cold sweat broke out. I started shaking so bad. I couldn't even hold any tools in my hands. I knew then the Lord was calling me. So, I told him. I said, "I'd like to go up to church," up to the Methodist church I was going to at the time. So, he told me, he said, "Go ahead. He knew what I was going through, but I didn't know that he knew so much about it. But when I left, he went in the house and called the guys that was having a prayer chain. He called them, and they got together and was praying again. I went out and got the preacher out and told him I'd like to be saved. He took me over and explained to me and prayed for me. I feel in my heart that I was saved that night. The Lord saved me.

passages.q: So, it was just you and the minister? / In the church? / You were in a state of spiritual crisis. / Have you felt that power growing inside of you?
passages.t: Yes. Yes. I woke him up. He was in bed, I believe. I got him out of bed. It was about 10:30 p.m. It's kind of a funny feeling [laughter]. I'd never done that, just be going out and getting somebody out of bed and do it. But it's just – Yes, just a movement, you just can't explain. Yes.

passages.q: I mean, it just seems to me what you did over in that house that night was pretty amazing. Because I know the comfort that you brought to Hank, for example. I know that. He described his own conversion. He described how it made his body feel better. I mean, he just felt completely different. He felt transformed. There was a lot of some kind of good juices flowing through you that night.
passages.t: It's something. I was scared. I was scared of – I just got married, and I thought that night that I was going to die because of the way the house and stuff was. I didn't want to leave my wife. We were just getting married and things. I was worried about her. I was worried about the other people in the house. But I wasn't so much scared as of dying itself, with just dying, but I was scared of if other fellas would have died, where they was going? I was sure that if I would die then, I'd be with the Lord that night. But I was kind of scared of when we hit the water, how bad we was going to be tore up before we would die or something like that or have to watch somebody else to die. I was scared of that. I knew that the Lord was there. He put the flood there. I'm sure that he could calm it. So, it's up to Him whether we went or stayed. But it was up to me whether them fellas got heard the word or not. But I'm not a person that really go out and minister to people, just to go out and be ministering to them. But I'm not afraid to talk about Lord because I'm not ashamed of Him. I love him. But that night, when they started up the steps, and I was helping her up the steps, the Lord was just talking to me there, that I'm leaving this up to you. Just putting it on my heart like I was the only Christian in the place and as far as I knew I was. I asked my uncle if he had a Bible. I just want to read some scripture and stuff at night. He said, well, he thought he had one. But he looked for one, he couldn't find it. That was kind of disappointing to me. Because I was looking for something, but seemed like the Lord was putting it in my mind, out of his mouth to say, instead of me reading it out of the book. But a lot of scripture come back to me. I read my Bible a lot, but I don't – I can't remember scripture a lot, but it come to me that night and everything.

passages.q: Is that maybe a sign to you that you're going to be called to do more, more preaching, more ministering?
passages.t: Well, I don't feel that I could be a preacher. But I wouldn't stop anything that the Lord had me to do. He's put me up there to work up the power plant. If he don't want me there – I took tests for another job here. It wasn't too long ago. But I just put it in Lord's hand. I just prayed about it and said, "If you want me here, put me here. If you don't, then I'll stay where I'm at." He's put me where I'm at. I got a letter from another job that said the job has been filled, but they appreciated my time and effort of coming down there and calling them. But the job I got is okay. I like it pretty well. It's something you can look forward to in the future. But if the Lord would call me to do something, I wouldn't stand back to wait for somebody else to do it.

passages.q: What did you see when you got back to the bank? Had a lot of people been praying? How did the community turn out there?
passages.t: Down here? Yes, my wife, she said – well, I was worried about her that night because I was afraid maybe she'd tried it to do something kind of stupid, try to get down there to us somehow or something. She'd come home and went to bed. She said she'd prayed. The Lord just put it on her heart that I was going to be okay. She said she just went to sleep. Just wasn't very long at all, and she was sleeping. She's asleep and good. The Lord was taking care of her the same time he was taking care of her. He was just easing her mind. When we got out, the people met us up there, and I felt more emotional me then. I held myself pretty good down there. Well, I felt calm and in my heart and the will to talk to those other men, the other people down there. But that morning, when we got out, it just felt like it just broke loose. You just felt like a lead bone hit my heart or something. I just let go then. But it just seemed like it scared me then, worse than it did when I was in there that night. But the people never stopped trying to get down to us that night. I found out later that there was people trying them boats and everything else to get down to us that night to get us out of there. But if that was the only way, maybe those two was the only two saved down there in that night, maybe that's the Lord saying, but that was the only time they could have been reached. If two souls are saved out of the flood, maybe it's worth it. But it's awful. But I think the people should open their eyes to the things that is going on around them, that the Lord is – I think, people going too much of an ease. I feel that the Lord is showing us he's still in command.

passages.q: What did you see when you got back to the bank? Had a lot of people been praying? How did the community turn out there?
passages.t: I feel that the Lord is showing us he's still in command. He can put that rain here, he can dry it up, or he can cause an earthquake, whatever it is. I feel that time has grown short, but the Bible tells you that things will happen, these times. But the people should stand up and take a note and take a look at what is around them. I know a lot of people got a lot of things – people never got their loved ones or their selves killed or hurt in it, but they lost everything. Maybe they hold a big grudge for it. But they're still here. They're living. There's a lot of people that just like to be here, that people in these big cities and stuff are sleeping on the streets and what have you. But people around here, they're – maybe they don't have all that much money, but they're living pretty good. The Lord tells you to live day to day. Don't look for the things, riches for tomorrow, and things like that. Live for the day. "Live for Me," He tells you.

passages.q: How's it been for you since that night? Have you thought a lot about it?
passages.t: I think it's made me stronger as a Christian. Because in church, I'd stand up and give my testimony. I'd stand up and testify a little bit, but not like I will now. The Lord kind of opened my eyes and opened my heart to it. You went through this. What can be the most that something can happen to you? If you stand up in church, it isn't going to be – nobody will send a flood on you there in church. If you've got something in your heart you want to say, stand up and say it. If you want to say something to people, say it. Do what you feel is right to do. Don't hold back and wait for somebody else to do it right. Take it on yourself to do it. I feel it just made me stronger.

passages.q: Have you got worried though or dreamed at all about the flood? Or do you fear water in any way?
passages.t: No. I always swim. I swim around here in the summertime. That was all for us to do as kids, go swimming, fishing, and things. I'm not afraid of water or anything, like I said. I haven't had no dreams or anything like that about it. I've worried a lot about the other people that's been in it that, the people that hadn't been reached – the people we haven't reached out – you can't reach out to them and talk to them and help them, like my aunt and uncle down there. Now, they bought another house. He's 76 years old, and they're fixing that house. It needs quite a bit of work done to it. I've been going down evenings and helping him. If it wouldn't been for me – he had another fellow down there helping him one day, and he was kind of a drunkard. He had my uncle to give him some money. Then he left and never come back. But I can get down and help him, and I don't mind doing it. I wouldn't take any money from him from doing it. I just love to help him. But the old people like that, they don't have nobody to help them and don't have nobody to talk to them how they're feeling about it. That worries me a little bit. [end of transcript]

passages.q: You probably don't even know what day of the week it is, do you? / Where do you work? / How long have you been up there? / Twelve years. Can you tell me your full name? / You were raised here in Tucker County. / Where? / Tell me a little bit about your people. / Who's your dad? / Who is she? / She's a Poling. Where did your dad go? / Pretty good-sized family. They all stay around here?
passages.t: It's Monday. I have no work. Firefox [inaudible]. Probably about twelve years. Darrell Lynn Heckler. [affirmative] [inaudible] and Parsons mostly. I don’t know. I don’t know about it. Durl Heckler, Dub Heckler, they call him. My mother is Beulah Heckler. Poling. In Parsons. My mother lived in Parsons too. I've got four brothers and one sister. [affirmative] In the area.

passages.q: All of them? / That's unusual. You might find a few but [inaudible] them all. You've lived up here for how long? / But mostly around the St. George area here. / What do you remember about November 4th? / How long had it been raining? / When did you notice that it was getting bad? / Down in St. George?
passages.t: (Randall?) Oh, (Randall?). He [inaudible] around. About four years. Yes. Been in St. George for about ten years. Thirteen. Thirteen years. It's a lot of water. [laughter] Four to five days of rain. About 9:00 p.m. It was the neighbor who called us down. The neighbors called us down to get on the basement, help in the basement. [inaudible] [affirmative]

passages.q: So, tell me about it. What happened?
passages.t: The basement started getting water and we started pumping it out. We see the losing battle when suddenly the water quickly started coming on us. [inaudible] came down. We got out on the floor and everything started [inaudible] the house. The basement [inaudible] we got out there. Then what we did we do? We moved everything out. We moved everything out of the basement in front of the garage. Then we moved everything out of the garage and put them on the front porch. [laughter]

passages.q: This was [inaudible] the neighbors.
passages.t: Yes. [inaudible] in the store. Yes. It was (Harry Parson?). We were helping them until about, what 9:00, 10:00, 11:00. Then we came back up here. We went over to the grocery store across the river and see if they need any help. They were up in the stairs and water is up about waist deep down there. So, we moved the food down there in a boat. I tried to get down to communities and they wouldn’t. They didn’t think the water was going to get that high. So, they stayed. We told them we'll call about 10:00 p.m.

passages.q: This was who now?
passages.t: Bob and (Rita?) Jones. When we tried to call them, the phones were out. So, we're going down to check on them. Something is going on. So, back to St. George we went again. That's when we saw the water was coming up. I mean it was coming up so fast. It was unbelievable. Someone said that (Lillian Town?) was still in their house. Danny – Johnson? Yes. Danny Johnson. He said he's still around the house.

passages.q: So, what did you do when you heard they're still in their house? / How did you start to go? / Is there any way you could [inaudible]?
passages.t: [inaudible] over because the water is too deep to go across. Swim, walk through it. Everything you see that's out of the house was taken out. So, we thought that was too deep. [laughter] So, we took off and come back up here. I got (Jeraimus?) He had a boat up here and along the plumps. They plumped long too, so we took the boat and come back down. [inaudible] got in the boat and took off and went up.

passages.q: Can you give me a little more detail about that night? I mean, what kind of a boat was it? / Two brooms.
passages.t: Just a boat and we had two brooms we used for row is what we have, paddles. Yes. We used for paddles, two brooms. So, we went up and tried to walk in the water to [inaudible] back down. So, back up front and tried again and [inaudible] down again. This time, we're [inaudible] St. George, walked up this side and tried it again and [inaudible]. So, then we made it that time over the house. Then we tried again going upstairs [inaudible] down the river flow straight at us. I yelled, "Get us out and help." He yelled, "No." So, I kicked the window out on top of the house. I wanted to [inaudible] stayed out in the boat, and meanwhile I brought the broom. So, we finally got them out of the house and into the boat. She didn’t want to go because the dog was there and she couldn’t find the dog. It was up in the attic and she wouldn’t leave the dog. So, I went up to the top of the attic and kicked a couple cabinets apart and take the [inaudible] off him and [inaudible] come back. That's all the work to it. [laughter]

passages.q: What did the trailer do?
passages.t: Hit the house. [inaudible] I was inside and Joe with us. He had just said that he was hanging on to the side of the house. He said whenever the trailer hit, his arm went clearing the house like that. He split the corner of it off. It's ripped and torn apart. When we got in the mountain, [inaudible] George there. The house is [inaudible] and no one's starting down the river. He went down and [inaudible] George and got wedged and stopped.

passages.q: So, while you were still on the boat coming back with them, their house begins to float? / There must have been more to it than that. Were you scared?
passages.t: [affirmative] They were nuts, weren't they? [laughter] There's been worst to it. [laughter] No. I wasn’t scared. I was. I was petrified because there were electric poles falling. Our house that we used down in St. George, it come out. I mean, it just disintegrated right in front of our eyes. In five minutes time, it was gone. I was petrified.

passages.q: You didn’t care? / What did the force of the water feel like against that little boat? / You went out in the main part of the river? Strike at anything. / Where did you get the brooms?
passages.t: [laughter] She does that to me. That's why I go back [inaudible] the boat does. That's all. He just wants [inaudible] at the boat. So, [inaudible]. We didn’t do it the way I see it. It was [inaudible] swift really. [inaudible] Yes. I think it's come off [inaudible], didn’t we? Yes. [inaudible]. She has [inaudible] going through the same brooms. [laughter] Those are her brooms. She rigged and [inaudible]. [laughter]

passages.q: You kept the brooms when you took the boat. / It never would have occurred to me. / Always takes a broom whenever he goes out probably. / That's the most bag on courageous thing I ever heard of. I can't imagine. How far from where you launched the boat was it actually out to the house? / Yes.
passages.t: Yes. We were down at the basement to find something to paddle with. We found two brooms she had. Maybe Joe thought about it. Joe does a lot of boating. No, he usually has paddles and a motorboat too. You know, St. George, don't you? Well, that's when it goes down and past post office. About half an hour or so, I don’t know.

passages.q: What did you use for a light? / That's all you had. Was it a real dark night? / How could you see? / You could recognize the houses by their tops because you could tell where you were?
passages.t: I had an old beam light, something like that. Yes, it was dark and raining. You can see on an [inaudible]. You close that if you see stuff. The top of the houses [inaudible] taking the boat [inaudible] going. Some of them I could. A couple of town [inaudible] were there. No one [inaudible] sets for you. That's when you saw the light at [inaudible] and down this house too. Yes, we got trapped there. Because they’ve got [inaudible] in this house. Then we got [inaudible] and we can't get out. So, I got on top of the house [inaudible] and got back in. We started to comeback because we dominated line to continue [inaudible]. Now, she's right up in the attic. My house calls for the [inaudible], please come to the room. So, we tried their [inaudible] shut down by the [inaudible] water took down the house.

passages.q: Did you have this fancy talking to get them to crawl out into that boat?
passages.t: [inaudible] second. [laughter] He tried once before and tried to get him to go with this because the water was coming up in the downstairs part then. And we tried to get them to leave. They said, "No. The water is not going to get that high. We'll just go upstairs and we'll be fine." So, we went ahead and left. Then when we went back down, we saw the water wasn't that fine. I went over and come to the window. I said, "You want to go out now or you want to wait an hour longer?" He said, "I want to go right now."

passages.q: What about her? / Then it comes back [inaudible].
passages.t: Oh, she's hunting for the dog. She wouldn’t go without that dog. We had even tried giving [inaudible]. So, that's when I went inside. She's up in the attic. I just go, "[inaudible] if I had to get her out." Finally, she did go with the dog. That's about it. I went down and got the other woman out. Marry Hab didn’t got out too.

passages.q: Marry Hab, I didn’t hear about her. Tell me about her. / How old is she? / You didn’t ask if she want to come? You just went in and got her?
passages.t: She [inaudible] we're there. The water was up to her waist and she wouldn’t come out. So, I just come down her door and made her come. She broke that door. Because we screamed at her and tried to get her attention. About sixty-five years, sixty, I don’t know. I told her. We also asked if [inaudible] get in there. What the hell. Well, she was afraid of the water was one thing. She didn’t want to get in the water. There were some other guys with me. No, it's just you and a couple of boys that got Mary. [inaudible] with me. There was even a boy about twenty years old. Well, that might have been (Connie Jones?). I don’t know who it was who went to follow with me. He said she wouldn’t come out.

passages.q: So, you don’t think of this at all as an act of heroism or anything. / What do you think about it? / Is that the kind of what he always does? / He doesn’t wait around. / That's a great story. But you were involved earlier in the rescue of the police officers. / You forgot about that. You forgot you were a hero too. Hang on. Your full name? / Joan.
passages.t: I think we had a boat and I offered for them. I'm proud of him. Thank you. He does. It's just the kind of a guy he is. [laughter] He doesn’t think. I'm the one [inaudible] and thinks [laughter] and worries. But he's like that. He's someone [inaudible]. He's always been like that. Oh, yes. Joan Ellen Heckler. Ellen Heckler.

passages.q: Ellen? / Ellen. What's your maiden name? / Wiles. Where were you raised? / [inaudible] / Nice. / You're making some big changes here. / Did your dad build this house? / What would he think about these changes? / Oh, he does. / He approves? / We just came from talking to the sheriff and the trooper about their little adventure in the [inaudible] charges. Can you tell us what you remember about that? That all happened before this.
passages.t: Ellen. Wiles. Right here in the south. [affirmative] Yes. [laughter] Oh, yes. It had to be. I mean, the house was a mess. [affirmative] He lives with us. Yes. My mom died about four years ago. He didn’t at first. Now, he does. [laughter] Well, you do [inaudible]. [laughter] Yes. We see the water started over the road. Because Darrell and I just come back from checking on Bob and Dodd. Well, (Gary Lipscomb?) and – I can't think of the state trooper's name.

passages.q: (Keith Cordial?).
passages.t: Yes, Cordial. They started back through it. Darrell thought he was going to lose his truck because he started to come back across. When they got about halfway into the water, their truck, I mean, it just went sideways. What stopped though – and they had this rope and they threw it at us. Trina and Steve and I and (Connie Jones?) grabbed the rope. They got across that some way but then the cruiser went on down the river.

passages.q: But where did they throw the rope from? Were they inside of it? / Tell me the whole story.
passages.t: No. They were on top of it. They had just crawled out of the vehicle and got on top and started hollering help. It's funny now, it wasn't then. But to look at it now, it's funny. But we just took off running. I mean, Trina and I and Steve, we were standing there on the other side of the road. We just took off running over on the back. When they threw the rope, we grabbed it. Then we tied it off on a fence post which is washed away by now, but we just pulled them. I mean, all four of us grabbed to hold the rope and they come across it. That was about it.

passages.q: Did you wrap the rope around yourself?
passages.t: I don’t even remember. I don’t know. I was on the tail end of it, so I may have. [laughter] Are you sure you did? [laughter] I could have. I really don’t remember. [laughter] I mean, there was a lot that went on that night that was brain boggling. No one expected it. I mean, it was something that no one expected. To see the water that high and to take that old bridge out, there was plenty of water.

passages.q: There hadn't been any warning in the forecast.? / It is hard to imagine. / St. George, you think of it as being well off and away from the river. / There it was up in the second storey, 4-feet up in the second storey of the town.
passages.t: No. Darrell and I talked to Gary and another state trooper. They said that they hadn't even thought of St. George. I mean, they had had a 20-minute warning in Hendrix. But they said that St. George just didn't even cross their mind. It didn't. I mean, they had no warning whatsoever. It is. Right. Yes. Well, over there at Bob Jones was a 16-foot because there was a mark around the top of his ceiling how high the water was. I mean, to think about it now, you still can't imagine. I mean, you know what happened. I mean, you can see it all around you. But it still doesn't seem real.

passages.q: Have you had any dreams about what happened up there? / What did you dream about? / Really?
passages.t: Oh, I did. I don't know, I ended up with an ulcer. [laughter] I worked day and night you may as well say. I worked in St. George two weeks helping the people get the mud and stuff cleaned out. Darrell took a week off mark too and helped. Then they were fixing meals at the Parsons at the grade school up there. They were feeding over 1,000. So, the third week, I start up there now work three weeks up there. But I mean, it was something I couldn't imagine. Because I can remember the flood back in [19]54. It took (Center Cassidy's?) house. But this, I mean, it was nothing compared to this. I mean –

passages.q: What time was it when the trooper threw the rope? / Because what the trooper told us and the sheriff told us same thing and about four weeks ago, a fireman told us the same thing. They said that a wall of water came down. The farmer told us the same thing in an unrelated incident. They were down there trying to save [inaudible].
passages.t: About 9:00. I left because we were trying to get them near, and Jay can't. See, they weren't out yet. Bill died right after the flood, not long after flood. But we went over and were trying to see if we could help them and get them out, get Bill out mainly because he was in a wheelchair. So, after we got to troopers over, I mean, we just went over there, or I did. [inaudible] was very high, it was. [inaudible] water got up to take on [inaudible]. Well, I don’t know how long it's set clear though. Well, they tuck behind us, they can cause it.

passages.q: They said like a wave of water hit them and knock them off. / You don’t remember saying anything? / It was Steve and Trina or were they behind you? / Because they said they lost control of their truck too. / So, you worked five weeks all together?
passages.t: It may have then. No, I don’t. That truck went sideways so we may have come across it. It was swift going across that. [inaudible] they may have come behind me. I think they were behind us, weren't they? Yes. Yes. Well, I cleaned for two weeks down here, then went up to the school and started cooking. But I would sleep two hours a night. I mean, it just seemed like I had more energy than I knew what to do with. I couldn't relax. I go to sleep. I get to think about those people that were homeless, in the mud. Boy, I know John saw the mud. I mean it was a mess. What all they lost and everything and it really got to me.

passages.q: Were you paid to work out at the school? / How many hours did you work a day?
passages.t: Oh no. No. Oh, most usually I go in – I'd get the kids off where they started – have they started school back yet? They hadn't, had they? The last week they'd started back. So, it was probably about 7:30 a.m. when I go in. Normally, it'd be probably about 3:00 p.m. when I'd leave. But I got my pay. [laughter]

passages.q: What was that?
passages.t: Just I knew I was helping. I was doing something that the people needed. When I went up there, I mean, those cooks, (Peneway Bright?] and (Sarah Nest?), I mean, they were exhausted. Sarah had been there well, from the time the floods started. She's one of those in the school up and brought everyone up there. She was asking when I could get to school. So, when I went in, it was two weeks later, I went up and started helping. I mean, you could just see, they were literally exhausted. Then we all worked together and we made it.

passages.q: You think it has been a real spirit all over the county of people helping each other?
passages.t: I do. I really do. I mean, it has brought a lot of people together. I can remember when I was a kid. I mean, it used to be people help neighbors help neighbors. But you don't find that anymore. But when this flood happened, you did. I mean, everyone chipped in and helped and was able to. I'm glad it's over.

passages.q: Do you think that spirit will carry on now? / I think that's great. I think you're both heroes. / Well, that's what heroes always do. / You'd like to everybody – / Joan, can you think of anything?
passages.t: I hope it does because I think people need it. It's going to take a long time. It is. Yes, it is. I don't feel like a hero. I just did what I thought needed to be done. I don't know. I'm no hero. [laughter] No, no. [inaudible] you're doing. Because these are stories that need to be told, and they do. I mean, not just for me and Darrell, but everybody. I mean, you wouldn't believe the people that come into St. George and helped, come in to Parsons and helped. I mean, they were people from Weirton all over. I mean, they came in and they worked just to get things straightened up.

passages.q: Do you think it's important that these stories be told? / Why is that? / The boat over there? / That was (Don Goss?). / They also got [inaudible] out of the river. Don took what seven people out of the attic window. / Don is seventy years old.
passages.t: I do. Just to let people know that there are people around that care. [inaudible] Have you heard anything about that? Yes. Somebody could go on people out there – The (Don Goss?). I head they placed they placed [inaudible] after we did. I heard he is. They played [inaudible] told me wouldn't go out there. [inaudible] he told me.

passages.q: Don is not afraid of anything, another hero. / [inaudible] power motors with two brooms. / What in the world do you think were they after? You didn't see him or anything? / You can swim?
passages.t: Another hero back home. [inaudible] I bet you're nuts. [laughter] Yes. [laughter] Here they come back with two tuba (force?). [laughter] You couldn’t see nothing. No light, nothing. Trina and Steve were with me. I was nervous wreck. You have to talk [inaudible]. He can't swim. He can't. [laughter] [inaudible] I mean, I've been out in the water all my life. [inaudible] the difference. I mean, [inaudible] other people would. To me, I couldn’t hardly got hurt. But Joe, he can't swim. It makes a difference. He was there. But he didn’t hesitate one minute. I mean, he was ready to go. He was. He was even in bed when Darrell went up. Darrell had let out [inaudible] and he said, "Joe, we need the boat. Come on, there are some people trapped down there." Right down the steps he come, got the boat and they took off. But I was nervous wreck, I'm not kidding. [laughter] I was.

passages.q: How long was he out? / No.
passages.t: A good hour. Yes. It was a good hour. But now, (May Bowens?) is another one. Have you talked to her? Now she stayed in her house through the whole thing. When Darrell comes back, they had told him that someone from the other end got May out. Though they were going to go back after her. I can't remember who it was that they got May out. Keith. Was it Keith? [affirmative] Then come to find out she had spent the whole night there. But of course, she was okay. The water can get to [inaudible] deep. It was up in the downstairs of it. Up at the school –

passages.q: You noticed what?
passages.t: The older people are the ones that would come in. I don't know. Every time they would come in, they would want to tell you about it, what happened to them. I know a couple of people they were just so sick of hearing it. But still, it was something they had to talk about. Because they had lived through it. I guess they had to talk about it until they finally got it talked out. But I know that was different with the older ones, like they'd lost their home or something like that. And it was just something they –

passages.q: Like grieving or something?
passages.t: It was, yes. They were more or less like in a daze that I found. They didn't know what they were going to do. I'd probably been the same way if I had been in it. I mean, they didn't know where to start. They want to talk about it. I mean, what they had been through and what they lost. Like their pictures, that was the main thing they talked about was the pictures.

passages.q: Did you get sick of hearing it?
passages.t: No. I still don’t. I mean people still come out and talk to me about it. I'm a good listener. I think if you want to talk about it, you go ahead and talk, because I'm good talker too. [laughter] Well, I can keep a conversation going anyway. [laughter] But no, I don't get tired of hearing it. Yes, it helps him to talk about it.

passages.q: What about your own children? What has been their reaction to it? / Were the kids at all troubled by it?
passages.t: They were fantastic. They worked right along beside me. We clean dishes. We clean mud. We mop floors. We clean malls. Didn't we? [laughter] But we all worked together. We set up a laundromat. That was something else we did. He's wearing the shirt that got bleached. [laughter] I think just from seeing their friends' things destroyed, things like that, they would have to be bothered by it. But still with them helping, I think that relieved a lot it. Doing good of a lot of stuff [inaudible] down here and brought them back to them. Yes. Even these two are my foster children. I've got another foster daughter. She must be up in the bedroom. This is my son. But my foster son and my son found – how much money did you find? [inaudible] 50 cent pieces and they gave it back.

passages.q: You guys are great. / How did you find out who owned it? Somebody from St. George. / That's great. So, you feel a lot of growth has come out with people?
passages.t: So, I was really proud of them. Because there were a lot of them that would have taken it. They would never say one word about it. [inaudible] I think so. I really do. I mean, you know, it's going to take years. Probably in my lifetime, I'll never see it the way it was. But still, I think the people have learned a lot from it. I have. I think Darrel has.

passages.q: What have you learned? / What caused that to dry up or fall off? / Why? Why would people all of a sudden stop? / That's okay. [end of transcript]
passages.t: Well, it was more like it used to be. I mean, everyone helped the other one. Well, people forget that. I think people just stop caring. Care too much about yourself, I guess. Maybe it took something like that to shake them out and say, "Hey." People always [inaudible] St. George. [inaudible] and everybody always comes to help you. You don’t need to ask them. Well, that's true. But with this, you didn’t have to ask. I mean, everyone was there. That's the way it should be. I mean, when you see somebody in trouble, you shouldn't have to ask. I mean, you should just go help. And that's what we did. [laughter]

codes.label: Environmental cues
codes.def: The narrator noticed the flood coming from the environment itself: rain, the river or creek, water on the road, sounds.
codes.inc: Watching the river rise, rain that would not stop, water in the road or yard, hearing a roar, debris in the river.
codes.exc: Being told by someone else (F2) or by an official source (F3).

codes.label: Social and informal warnings
codes.def: The narrator learned of the danger from other people or local signals: neighbors, family, firefighters or police at the door, the fire whistle, scanners or CB radio.
codes.inc: Phone calls, people knocking or shouting, door-to-door evacuation by local responders, the fire whistle, listening to the scanner.
codes.exc: Forecasts, flood watches or warnings from the Weather Service, and broadcast warnings (F3).

codes.label: Official warnings, forecasts and their absence
codes.def: Forecasts, flood watches and warnings, broadcast bulletins, or the narrator's statement that no warning came.
codes.inc: The Weather Service or Weather Bureau, flood watch or warning, radio and TV warnings, 'there was no warning', officials caught off guard.
codes.exc: Neighbors and local responders acting on what they saw (F2).

codes.label: Risk perception and the decision to act
codes.def: How the narrator judged the danger and decided whether to act: expectations from past floods, disbelief, false alarms, reluctance to leave.
codes.inc: 'It never got that high', staying because it never flooded before, cry-wolf talk, refusing or hesitating to leave.
codes.exc: Memories of past floods with no link to this decision (F8).

codes.label: Protective action
codes.def: What the narrator or household did as the water came: leaving, going up the hill or upstairs, moving vehicles, animals or belongings, or staying put.
codes.inc: Evacuating, sheltering at the school, moving to the second floor, moving cars, getting relatives out.
codes.exc: Rescuing others from danger by boat or rope (F6); cleanup afterwards (F10).

codes.label: Rescue and response
codes.def: Rescues and attempted rescues, by neighbors, firefighters, police, the Guard or boats; people trapped; bodies recovered.
codes.inc: Accounts by rescuers and by the rescued, failed rescues, recovering the dead.

codes.label: Information, rumor and trust
codes.def: What people heard, believed or doubted during and after the flood, and how they judged officials, agencies and the media.
codes.inc: News blackouts, rumors, conflicting reports, lost phones and radios, confusion among agencies, trust or distrust of officials, the Corps, FEMA or the press.
codes.exc: Simply receiving a warning, with no judgment about it (F2, F3).

codes.label: Past floods, local knowledge and explanations
codes.def: Earlier floods, high-water marks, how the river behaves, and local explanations of why floods happen or are getting worse.
codes.inc: The 1888, 1930s, 1950s or 1977 floods; 'she comes and she goes'; blaming mining, timbering or dams for worse floods.
codes.exc: Using past floods to decide whether to act this time (F4).

codes.label: Damage, loss and displacement
codes.def: Losses of homes, belongings, land and livelihoods, and being forced to move, whether by the flood or by a dam or flood-control project.
codes.inc: Houses washed away or gutted, mud to the ceiling, losing everything, families who left and did not return.
codes.exc: Cleanup and aid (F10); what a place meant to people (F15).

codes.label: Recovery, relief and aid
codes.def: Cleanup, rebuilding and the aid that came or did not: agencies, churches, volunteers, loans, donations, temporary housing.
codes.inc: FEMA, Red Cross, Salvation Army, Mennonite volunteers, SBA loans, vouchers, trailers, mucking out.
codes.exc: Neighbors helping each other with no organized aid (F11).

codes.label: Community and social support
codes.def: Help between neighbors, family, churches and strangers; the community pulling together or pulling apart.
codes.inc: Sharing homes and food, schools and churches as hubs, conflict over aid or over the dam.

codes.label: Emotional aftermath and mental health
codes.def: Fear, grief, stress and how the flood stayed with people, including the work of counselors.
codes.inc: Nightmares, fear when it rains, anxiety, depression, counseling, crying, 'I'll never forget'.
codes.exc: Physical damage with no emotional content (F9).

codes.label: Faith and meaning-making
codes.def: How narrators make sense of the flood through faith, providence, prayer or a sense of purpose.
codes.inc: 'The Lord was watching over us', prayer during the night, the flood as a sign or a test, church as spiritual support.
codes.exc: Churches as places that gave food and shelter (F11).

codes.label: Flood control, dams and relocation programs
codes.def: Dams, floodwalls and other structures, and the programs that buy, condemn, flood-proof or relocate homes and towns.
codes.inc: The Corps of Engineers, condemnation and appraisal, forced removal, buyouts, flood-proofing, moving a downtown, floodplain rules, flood insurance.
codes.exc: Natural changes in the river with no project involved (F8).

codes.label: Place attachment and loss of place
codes.def: What a place means to people, and what is lost when a homeplace, farm, town or community is flooded, moved or erased.
codes.inc: Homeplaces, family land and graves, the old town, 'born and raised', 'it will never be the same'.
codes.exc: Property value with no attachment (F9 or F14).

codes.label: Children, schools and institutions
codes.def: Children's experiences and the part schools and other institutions played as shelters, hubs or casualties.
codes.inc: Children's own accounts, adults on children's reactions, schools as shelters and relief centers, school closures.

codes.label: Livelihoods and local economy
codes.def: Work, income and the local economy as they shape and are shaped by floods and flood control: coal, gas, farming, timber, hunting, local business.
codes.inc: Mining and drilling, farms and land use, businesses lost or moved, jobs after the flood.
codes.exc: Work history with no link to the flood, the dam or the place.

questions.q: Where did the water come up first, and how fast?
Which bridges, culverts and debris made flooding worse?
How did people find out, and what warnings failed?
What did earlier floods teach people, or mislead them about?
What do people say makes flooding worse here?
Who was cut off, and for how long?
What happened when homes and businesses were bought out, flood-proofed or moved?
What helped recovery, and what got in the way?

cards.title: A low bridge caught debris and pushed water back up the river
cards.place: Hoot Owl Bridge, near Grundy, VA
cards.note: The narrator blames the depth of flooding at his home on trailers lodging against a low bridge downstream.
cards.verify: Bridge location and low-chord height against the 1977 high water; whether the bridge was raised or replaced.
cards.ask_next: Which bridges in your jurisdiction catch debris, at what river level, and what has been done about them?

quotes.text: The bridge is low, and debris got in there and dammed it up, and the water was coming back up the river.
quotes.speaker: Harold Trivett

quotes.text: Because there was a couple of house trailers washed down.
quotes.speaker: Harold Trivett

cards.title: Debris at the railroad crossing dammed the water in Parsons
cards.place: Parsons, WV
cards.note: Two narrators describe debris piling against the railroad bridge and backing water into town. One also thinks the railroad bridge shielded the Route 219 bridge. The transcript's 'Blackport bridge' may mean Black Fork; someone local should confirm which bridge each narrator means.
cards.verify: Bridge locations and 1985 damage reports; photographs from the days after the flood.
cards.ask_next: Where do debris jams form in town, and which structures are at risk when they let go?

quotes.text: It just put a complete barrier across there. It built a dam. It built its own dam.
quotes.speaker: Forest Blume

quotes.text: That formed a big dam in here because the water couldn't go down through under the bridges.
quotes.speaker: Ona Hovatter

quotes.text: I think that railroad bridge saved the town bridge.
quotes.speaker: Ona Hovatter

cards.title: The forks rose at different times, and the water came back up in the night
cards.place: Parsons, WV, where the forks meet
cards.note: Narrators describe one fork rising first, a drop during the night, then a second rise, and water backing up where the forks join.
cards.verify: Stream gauge records for the forks and the Cheat River for November 4-5, 1985.
cards.ask_next: In your experience, which stream comes up first, how long until the next one, and where does water back up?

quotes.text: It seemed like every five minutes, it was up another foot.
quotes.speaker: Bryan King (junior firefighter)

quotes.text: The Dry Fork came up first.
quotes.speaker: Jim Blosser (junior firefighter)

quotes.text: Then it started rising again.
quotes.speaker: Jim Blosser (junior firefighter)

quotes.text: where Black Fork and Shavers come together and the Cheat that was forcing it to start backing up
quotes.speaker: Steven Craig Wilfong

cards.title: Upstream knew first
cards.place: Harman to Parsons, WV
cards.note: A call from upstream reached Parsons, and a driver from Harman saw the river at Parsons still down that afternoon. Upstream observers may have been the earliest warning anyone got.
cards.verify: Times in these accounts against gauge records and NWS warning times for November 4, 1985.
cards.ask_next: Who upstream do you call, or who calls you, when the water starts coming up?

quotes.text: I understand that somebody from Harman did call and tell them
quotes.speaker: Forest Blume

quotes.text: So, I looked over to the river. It wasn't up.
quotes.speaker: Steven Craig Wilfong

cards.title: A warning whistle nobody had learned to read
cards.place: Tucker County, WV (community not named in the passage)
cards.note: A whistle sounded, but people took it for a fire call. The same narrator says earlier high-water alarms had worn down belief.
cards.verify: Which communities had sirens or whistles in 1985, what they signaled, and what they signal now.
cards.ask_next: How does each community you work with get the word out, and do people know what the signal means?

quotes.text: I understand they had sounded a warning whistle. But they had never been prepared for floods. So, nobody knew what the whistle was for.
quotes.speaker: Forest Blume

quotes.text: So, I think it had been hollered wolf too many times.
quotes.speaker: Forest Blume

cards.title: Grundy's warning chain ran through the mayor and the radio station
cards.place: Grundy, VA
cards.note: An alert on a wire service reached the mayor, who phoned merchants; the civil defense director had the local station announce the flood.
cards.verify: NWS warning products and times for April 4-5, 1977; who relayed them locally.
cards.ask_next: Who are the relays in your area today, and what happens when the power and phones go out?

quotes.text: Had been picked up on some sort of wire service that they had through here. And she had been calling the merchants.
quotes.speaker: Sue Branham

quotes.text: So he asked me to go open the radio station and begin to announce to people that we were going to have this flood
quotes.speaker: Ronald Cole

cards.title: Heavy rain on saturated ground
cards.place: Buchanan County, VA
cards.note: The narrator's rainfall figures are a recollection, given twenty years later.
cards.verify: Rain gauge totals for April 4-5, 1977 in and around Buchanan County.
cards.ask_next: What rain, on what ground, gets your streams out of their banks?

quotes.text: That heavy rain came in a wet season. The ground was already saturated.
quotes.speaker: Ronald Cole

quotes.text: We had between three and seven inches of rain in, I think, a five-hour period.
quotes.speaker: Ronald Cole

cards.title: Water depths at one building across two floods
cards.place: Downtown Grundy, VA
cards.note: The owner moved to what he thought was high ground after 1957. Depths at a known building are the raw material for a flood impact statement.
cards.verify: The building's location and floor elevation; recorded high-water marks and crests for 1957 and 1977.
cards.ask_next: Which buildings or landmarks do you use to judge how high a flood got, and do you have photos or marks?

quotes.text: So I knew it would never get flooded here!
quotes.speaker: Lodge Compton

quotes.text: In '77 we had the basement completely filled and about two feet of water on our street floor.
quotes.speaker: Lodge Compton

cards.title: A family benchmark: the rock on the hill
cards.place: Grundy, VA
cards.note: Her father sited buildings by a rock he had watched for years; she kept photographs of three floods. Personal records like these are worth collecting with the interview.
cards.verify: The photographs, with dates and locations, against recorded crests.
cards.ask_next: What files, photos or maps do you keep that nobody else has?

quotes.text: he had a big rock over on the side of the mountain that, or side of the hill that he had watched for years.
quotes.speaker: Helen Johnson

quotes.text: And I've got pictures from three different floods that have come, and they've all gotten higher.
quotes.speaker: Helen Johnson

cards.title: Measured against the flood of 1888
cards.place: St. George, WV
cards.note: A family story kept the 1888 flood as the benchmark for nearly a century.
cards.verify: Historical crest records on the Cheat River near St. George.
cards.ask_next: What is the flood people in each community measure against, and how high was it?

quotes.text: just about six foot more water than the [18]88 flood
quotes.speaker: John Anvill

cards.title: Flood-proofing came with a deed restriction
cards.place: Tug Fork and Levisa Fork valleys
cards.note: The Corps describes why it moved to non-structural measures and what homeowners signed.
cards.verify: Corps program documents for the Tug Fork and Levisa Fork projects; local permit records.
cards.ask_next: Which past projects worked, which did not, and what would you tell whoever designs the next one?

quotes.text: It was not cost-effective.
quotes.speaker: Gene Barr (speaking for the Corps, Huntington District)

quotes.text: It also places a restriction on their property against future development below the [19]77 flood level.
quotes.speaker: Gene Barr (speaking for the Corps, Huntington District)

cards.title: A backed-up culvert held people up before the river rose
cards.place: Tucker County, WV
cards.note: Small drainage failures slowed people down early in the event, before the main river came up.
cards.verify: Culvert and road locations; road closure records.
cards.ask_next: Which culverts and low crossings flood first, and who gets cut off when they do?

quotes.text: they were delayed by about an hour because of their culvert backing up and their road flooding.
quotes.speaker: Susan Schmitt

cards.title: Building in the channel pushes the current somewhere else
cards.place: Grundy, VA
cards.note: A resident's account of encroachment, in his own words.
cards.verify: Fill and building permits along the channel since 1977.
cards.ask_next: Where has fill or building changed how water moves, and how did permits handle it?

quotes.text: when you put an obstruction in the river channel, even if you make it strong enough so that it doesn't wash away your structure, that's going to throw the thrust of the current against something else.
quotes.speaker: Ronald Cole

quotes.text: since the flood we have more filled lots where people are pushing more debris toward the natural river channel
quotes.speaker: Ronald Cole

cards.title: Flood insurance did not pay for the cleanup crew
cards.place: Grundy, VA
cards.note: Volunteer crews filled a gap insurance left. Coverage rules may differ today.
cards.verify: Current NFIP coverage for cleanup labor.
cards.ask_next: What did people assume insurance covered that it did not?

quotes.text: flood insurance does not cover help in time of flooding. Does not cover hired help.
quotes.speaker: Marie Williams

cards.title: The assistance center closed before people stopped needing it
cards.place: Tucker County, WV
cards.note: An outreach worker on the FEMA crisis-counseling project found people still without housing after the center closed.
cards.verify: Disaster recovery center dates for the 1985 declaration.
cards.ask_next: How long were people still showing up for help, and who was there for them?

quotes.text: Hindsight, someone should be there.
quotes.speaker: Ruth Ann Toth

cards.title: Why these streams flood: debris stored since the last big one
cards.place: Headwater streams, Tucker and Pendleton Counties, WV
cards.note: A stream ecologist interviewed in the collection explains the mechanism: steep tributaries flood first, flush out decades of stored rock and timber, and dump it where they meet the gentler main stream. His transcript came through OCR, so stray typos are the scanner's, not his.
cards.verify: Post-flood sediment and debris surveys for the 1985 event; channel maintenance records since.
cards.ask_next: Which channels have been accumulating debris since the last flood of record, and who checks them?

quotes.text: Really they've been accumulating that debris, since the last flood ef this magnitude.
quotes.speaker: Jim VanGundy (stream ecologist, Davis & Elkins College)

quotes.text: In effect you're putting a series of little ponds in the main stream.
quotes.speaker: Jim VanGundy (stream ecologist, Davis & Elkins College)

cards.title: The rain gauges sit in the valleys; the rain fell on the ridges
cards.place: Pendleton County and southern Tucker County, WV
cards.note: The same scientist points at a measurement gap: recorded totals over 10 inches in 24 hours were probably undercounts because the heaviest rain fell at elevations with no gauges. OCR typos are the scanner's.
cards.verify: Gauge network coverage then and now against terrain; the official 1985 storm totals.
cards.ask_next: Where do you believe the rain actually falls hardest, and is anything measuring there today?

quotes.text: there were some parts of Pendleton County that the weather bureau recorded 24 hr. rainfall in excess of 10 inches
quotes.speaker: Jim VanGundy (stream ecologist, Davis & Elkins College)

quotes.text: for the most part there aren's rain gauges at the higher elevations, they are down in the valleys
quotes.speaker: Jim VanGundy (stream ecologist, Davis & Elkins College)

cards.title: The Levisa rises and falls inside forty-eight hours
cards.place: Levisa Fork at Grundy, VA
cards.note: A Grundy merchant contrasts the Levisa with slow Midwest rivers: there is no time for sandbags, only flood doors and evacuation. This is the operational argument for short-fuse warnings in steep terrain.
cards.verify: Hydrographs for the Levisa Fork at Grundy: time from rise to crest to recession.
cards.ask_next: On your streams, how many hours pass between first rise and crest, and what can actually be done in that window?

quotes.text: Within forty-eight hours, she can come and she can go. You don't have time to put sandbags up.
quotes.speaker: Chuck Crabtree (Grundy merchant)

quotes.text: When she starts rising and the water doesn't start coming down, you'd better shut your flood doors and pull out.
quotes.speaker: Chuck Crabtree (Grundy merchant)

cards.title: For a while, one radio was the only link out of Parsons
cards.place: Parsons, WV
cards.note: A fire-and-rescue volunteer kept the only working link to the Elkins operations center after power and phones failed; inside town, an EMT's walkie-talkie reached people trapped at the jail.
cards.verify: Emergency communications plans of record for Tucker County in 1985 and today.
cards.ask_next: When phones and power go, what is the real backup link in each community, and who holds it?

quotes.text: After the power went off and the phone went out, that was the only contact in and out of Parsons was what I had there
quotes.speaker: Forest Blume (fire and rescue volunteer)

quotes.text: Do you have contact with anybody in the jail?
quotes.speaker: Forest Blume (fire and rescue volunteer)

cards.title: Scanners and ham radio carried the news
cards.place: Tucker County, WV
cards.note: Fire-service scanner traffic was how families tracked the flood in real time, and ham operators relayed personal messages out of the shelter for days.
cards.verify: Amateur radio logs for the 1985 operation, if clubs kept them; who monitors scanner traffic today.
cards.ask_next: Who in your communities still listens on scanners and amateur radio, and are they in the warning loop?

quotes.text: She said people had scanners and stuff that had been hearing what's going on.
quotes.speaker: Michael Parsons (junior firefighter)

quotes.text: It took me fifteen minutes to get two blocks down to get to the shelter to send out a message by the ham operators up to Morgantown
quotes.speaker: Susan Schmitt (Parsons clinic)

cards.title: The school shelters were not equipped to be shelters
cards.place: Parsons, WV and Grundy, VA
cards.note: Both towns sheltered people in schools that had never been provisioned for it. In Parsons the battery lights burned out by morning.
cards.verify: Current shelter agreements and provisioning for the same buildings.
cards.ask_next: Which buildings would shelter people tonight, and what is actually stocked in them?

quotes.text: Certainly, the schools were not equipped for this. We had emergency lighting from batteries in the gymnasium
quotes.speaker: Bob Klein (mental health worker)

quotes.text: they did set up emergency shelter over at the junior high school, what's now the law school, and served food
quotes.speaker: Sue Branham (Grundy merchant)

cards.title: The crest came after dark; by 3 a.m. the water was falling
cards.place: St. George and Tucker County, WV
cards.note: Independent accounts put the worst of it in darkness, with recession visible between 2 and 3 a.m. Night crests change what warnings and rescues have to accomplish.
cards.verify: Gauge traces for the night of November 4-5, 1985.
cards.ask_next: How do your communities get warned and moved when the crest comes after dark?

quotes.text: At about 3:00 a.m. that morning, the water began to recede.
quotes.speaker: Vittie Lipscomb

quotes.text: about 2:00 a.m., I looked out. I'd seen the water had gone down in the road some.
quotes.speaker: Helen Sites

cards.title: By the weekend, sightseers were in the way
cards.place: Parsons, WV
cards.note: Crowds of onlookers slowed movement between the clinic and the shelter within days of the flood.
cards.verify: Access-control measures used in 1985; current county plans for post-disaster traffic.
cards.ask_next: How do you plan to control sightseer traffic in the first week, and who enforces it?

quotes.text: It was gawkers in a line.
quotes.speaker: Susan Schmitt (Parsons clinic)

cards.title: Coal equipment and a pass system cleaned up Grundy
cards.place: Grundy, VA
cards.note: Local industry supplied end loaders and coal trucks; access downtown ran on passes. Private heavy equipment was the de facto debris-removal fleet.
cards.verify: Debris-removal arrangements in the 1977 recovery; current mutual-aid or contractor agreements.
cards.ask_next: Whose heavy equipment would clear your streets now that the mines have thinned out, and is it under agreement?

quotes.text: If it hadn’t been for the coal companies here, I don’t know if we’d have ever gotten Grundy cleaned up or not.
quotes.speaker: Roger Powers (coal operator)

quotes.text: they would allow anyone in that had a pass to get downtown
quotes.speaker: Roger Powers (coal operator)

cards.title: Straight bleach burns and a strep wave: cleanup health
cards.place: Parsons, WV
cards.note: A clinician describes the cleanup-era caseload: chemical burns from undiluted bleach, then strep and viral waves through a doubled-up population. Flooded-home cleanup guidance is a health product, not just a housing one. The clinic also gave two to three hundred tetanus shots in the first week (as recalled).
cards.verify: Health department records for the winter after the flood, if any survive.
cards.ask_next: What cleanup guidance actually reaches people, and in what form, in the first week?

quotes.text: We gave two- to three hundred tetanus shots the first week we were open.
quotes.speaker: Susan Schmitt (physician, St. George clinic)

quotes.text: So, people use straight bleach and they burn themselves.
quotes.speaker: Susan Schmitt (Parsons clinic)

quotes.text: We just saw a lot of strep.
quotes.speaker: Susan Schmitt (Parsons clinic)

cards.title: The trailers arrived after people had scattered
cards.place: Blackman Flats, Tucker County, WV
cards.note: A member of the trailer-siting crew: by the time a sixty-five-unit court was ready, displaced families had already settled elsewhere and would not move twice. Temporary housing is only temporary housing if it comes fast.
cards.verify: FEMA temporary-housing occupancy figures for the 1985 declaration.
cards.ask_next: How fast did temporary housing actually arrive in your floods, and where did people really go?

quotes.text: Sixty-five units already built and ready to move in with not a trailer or one in it.
quotes.speaker: Forest Blume (on the FEMA trailer-siting crew)

quotes.text: once the fellows got settled down somewhere else and settled in, they weren't about to pack up and move their life around again to get in a FEMA trailer
quotes.speaker: Forest Blume (on the FEMA trailer-siting crew)

cards.title: Outreach workers found the people the system missed
cards.place: Tucker County, WV
cards.note: FEMA-funded 'crisis counselors' worked as door-to-door outreach, finding households living over flood-damaged floors a year on, and walking them back into the aid system.
cards.verify: The crisis-counseling program grant records for the 1985 declaration.
cards.ask_next: A year after your floods, who was still living in damaged housing, and how were they found?

quotes.text: FEMA's term for us is crisis counselors, but we like to term ourselves outreach workers
quotes.speaker: Ruth Ann Toth (flood recovery outreach worker)

quotes.text: The one we found was living in an apartment that the floor was falling in.
quotes.speaker: Ruth Ann Toth (flood recovery outreach worker)

cards.title: The flood-proofing program's rules, in the Corps' own words
cards.place: Tug Fork and Levisa Fork valleys
cards.note: Eligibility ran on a design flood (the 1977 event), a twelve-foot raise limit, floodway locations forced acquisition, and homeowners paid a cost share. Program design details like these rarely survive anywhere but in participants' memories and scattered files.
cards.verify: Corps project reports for the Tug Fork and Levisa Fork non-structural projects.
cards.ask_next: Which program rules worked, which pushed people out, and what would you change in the next one?

quotes.text: we have a design flood, which is that of the [19]77 flood
quotes.speaker: Gene Barr (speaking for the Corps, Huntington District)

quotes.text: We will not flood proof houses greater than twelve feet.
quotes.speaker: Gene Barr (speaking for the Corps, Huntington District)

quotes.text: a rough average is anywhere from 2,500 to $5,000 out of pocket
quotes.speaker: Gene Barr (speaking for the Corps, Huntington District)

quotes.text: Anyone located in the regulatory floodway that is eligible would have an acquisition as their only option.
quotes.speaker: Gene Barr (U.S. Army Corps of Engineers, Huntington District)

cards.title: Pikeville's cut-through was the model Grundy watched
cards.place: Pikeville, KY and Grundy, VA
cards.note: Grundy people cite Pikeville, where the river was moved through the mountain, as proof a town could engineer its way out. Precedent projects shape what communities will accept.
cards.verify: The Pikeville cut-through project history and its measured flood outcomes.
cards.ask_next: Which nearby project do your communities point to when they imagine their own fix?

quotes.text: they drew up this project to put the river through the mountain, did a cut through. They moved the river, and it's wonderful.
quotes.speaker: Sue Branham (Grundy merchant)

quotes.text: he got federal assistance, and people thought he was crazy in the '60s. It's a boom town now.
quotes.speaker: Sue Branham (Grundy merchant)
