cards.title: Landowners slowed condemnation one square yard at a time
cards.place: West Fork valley, Lewis County, WV
cards.note: Opponents deeded square-yard parcels to supporters across the country, forcing the Corps to condemn each one. Any future acquisition program should expect organized, creative resistance and understand why it happened here.
cards.verify: Federal court records in Elkins for the square-yard condemnations.
cards.ask_next: What did the agency misread about this community, and what would have earned cooperation instead?

quotes.text: They condemned it one square yard at a time.
quotes.speaker: Matthew Snyder (landowner in the take area)

quotes.text: President Carter, I think got three or four square yards. Pope got one square yard.
quotes.speaker: Francine Snyder (landowner in the take area)

cards.title: Condemnation awards fell short of replacement
cards.place: Lewis County, WV
cards.note: Narrators say awards were sometimes below what owners had paid, and that even good awards did not replace a farm. Fair market value is not replacement value, and the gap is what people remember.
cards.verify: Award amounts versus assessed and purchase values in the court records.
cards.ask_next: In buyouts you have run, did the money actually rehouse people at the same standard, and where did they land?

quotes.text: even the ones that have done well in condemnation barely get enough to buy them a tract house or a trailer and a lot
quotes.speaker: Matthew Snyder (landowner in the take area)

quotes.text: They condemned it for less than what you paid for it.
quotes.speaker: Francine Snyder (landowner in the take area)

cards.title: Easements reached land the water will never touch
cards.place: Above the Stonewall Jackson pool, Lewis County, WV
cards.note: A dairy farmer describes building restrictions on easement land at the edge of his place, outside the pool itself. Project footprints are bigger than their maps of water.
cards.verify: Easement deeds and restriction terms in county land records.
cards.ask_next: What restrictions ride on land around your projects, and do owners understand them before signing?

quotes.text: they took an easement on a little bit of it right at the lower edge of it. But you can't build nothing on it or anything like that
quotes.speaker: Aubrey West (dairy farmer in the take area)

cards.title: The dam's justification shifted as arguments failed
cards.place: Stonewall Jackson Dam, WV
cards.note: A sitting congressman who opposed the dam walks through the cost-benefit history: flood-control claims reaching to Pittsburgh, then pollution control, then recreation. A record of how one project's math was argued, from inside the fight.
cards.verify: The project's authorization documents and successive benefit-cost analyses.
cards.ask_next: Which of your projects' justifications would survive a recalculation today?

quotes.text: for every dollar you put into a dam, you have to get more than $1 benefits out
quotes.speaker: Bob Wise (then a U.S. congressman, dam opponent)

quotes.text: this dam is 100 miles from Pittsburgh, and yet it was portrayed as stopping torrents of water pouring through Pittsburgh
quotes.speaker: Bob Wise (then a U.S. congressman, dam opponent)

cards.title: Power out three to four days; water out with it
cards.place: Grundy and Buchanan County, VA
cards.note: The outage timeline from two narrators: town electricity back on day three or four, households without power and water for days. Restoration time is the clock every other recovery task runs on.
cards.verify: Utility restoration records for April 1977, if the companies kept them.
cards.ask_next: What are realistic restoration times for power and water in your valleys today?

quotes.text: there was no regular electricity restored before, I think, the third or fourth day
quotes.speaker: Ronald Cole (local radio broadcaster)

quotes.text: But we were without power and water for a few days, but we made out.
quotes.speaker: John Fleenor (Grundy florist)

cards.title: People lined up at the radio station to say they were alive
cards.place: Grundy, VA
cards.note: With phones down, the AM station on generator power became the welfare-message channel: residents broadcast 'I'm okay' to relatives. A reunification function emergency plans now assign to official systems ran through one local broadcaster.
cards.verify: Whether the station or its successor still exists, and what the welfare-information plan is now.
cards.ask_next: Where would 'I'm okay' messages flow in your counties if phones failed for three days?

quotes.text: People were coming in and using that as a form of public communication.
quotes.speaker: Ronald Cole (local radio broadcaster)

cards.title: Slate Creek rises within hours; coincident Levisa crest backs it up
cards.place: Mouth of Slate Creek at the Levisa Fork, Grundy, VA
cards.note: Slate Creek responds within a couple of hours of heavy rain, the Levisa more slowly; the worst downtown flooding came when both crested together, as in 1957 and 1977. When Slate Creek fell before the Levisa crested, near-disasters were avoided.
cards.verify: USGS stage records for Slate Creek and Levisa Fork at Grundy for the 1957 and 1977 events, comparing crest times.
cards.ask_next: In the floods you remember, how many hours apart did Slate Creek and the Levisa crest, and what did downtown look like each time?

quotes.text: Slate Creek has such a steep pitch, the runoff, my gosh, just a couple hours after a heavy rain you already see the creek is on the rise.
quotes.speaker: Lodge Compton (editor, Virginia Mountaineer)

quotes.text: If you have a crest, Slate Creek crests at the same time Levisa does, then you got yourself a backup situation.
quotes.speaker: Lodge Compton (editor, Virginia Mountaineer)

quotes.text: That particularly happened in '57 and '77.
quotes.speaker: Lodge Compton (editor, Virginia Mountaineer)

cards.title: Leaf-off and frozen ground made winter and spring floods worse
cards.place: Levisa Fork and tributaries, Grundy, VA
cards.note: Compton recalls both damaging floods came with no foliage, while heavy midsummer rains gave a big river but not devastating floods. He says that after freezing, very little rain gets the creeks running.
cards.verify: Flood-peak dates and seasonal timing in the Levisa Fork gauge record at Grundy; antecedent temperature and soil-frost records.
cards.ask_next: Have summer storms with similar rain amounts ever flooded downtown, or does it take a leaf-off season to do that?

quotes.text: Our--You know, our--The two that I'm more familiar with, one came in January when there was no foliage at and one in April when nothing really was out.
quotes.speaker: Lodge Compton (editor, Virginia Mountaineer)

quotes.text: But certainly in the wintertime, especially after you've had freezing and such, you know, it takes very little rainfall to start those creeks running.
quotes.speaker: Lodge Compton (editor, Virginia Mountaineer)

cards.title: 1957 water rose from mid-morning to crest by noon, gone by dark
cards.place: Lower Main Street newspaper office, Grundy, VA
cards.note: Compton recalls no warning in 1957; water entered around 9 a.m., neared crest by noon and fell fast enough to return before dark (as recalled). Once water reached floor level it overwhelmed door-blocking in under an hour; Wilfong describes a similar knee-to-waist rise in Parsons.
cards.verify: Levisa Fork gauge hydrograph at Grundy for the 1957 event; Cheat/Black Fork stage records at Parsons for November 4, 1985.
cards.ask_next: How much time passed between water at the doorsill and water too deep to work in, and did anyone tell you it was coming?

quotes.text: Oh, I don't know, by noon we were getting close to crest I guess, because it must have really started into our place like nine o'clock in the morning or something.
quotes.speaker: Lodge Compton (editor, Virginia Mountaineer)

quotes.text: And it just, in a matter of, you know, probably less than an hour, it just overwhelmed.
quotes.speaker: Lodge Compton (editor, Virginia Mountaineer)

quotes.text: We went back down another time to check on somebody else and crap, it wasn't even knee deep when I was down at the store, around the back but that time it was waist deep.
quotes.speaker: Craig Wilfong (volunteer firefighter, auto-parts owner)

cards.title: Depot Bridge held but caught mobile homes on its upstream side
cards.place: Old Depot Bridge over the Levisa Fork, Grundy, VA
cards.note: Water overtopped the railroad-built Depot Bridge but it stood; in the afternoon mobile homes lodged on its upstream side. Compton places the crest around 5:00-5:30 p.m., near dark (as recalled), and has photographs.
cards.verify: Compton's Virginia Mountaineer photographs ('A Couple of Hours Before Crest'); VDOT or railroad bridge records for the Depot Bridge; gauge crest time.
cards.ask_next: Where did the mobile homes that hit the Depot Bridge come from, and are there still homes upstream in that spot?

quotes.text: The bridge stayed, but somewhere along in the afternoon a couple of mobile homes washed in this upper side.
quotes.speaker: Lodge Compton (editor, Virginia Mountaineer)

quotes.text: I'm saying along five o'clock or something, 5:00, 5:30 in the evening.
quotes.speaker: Lodge Compton (editor, Virginia Mountaineer)

cards.title: Oil drums and gas cylinders floated in from riverside storage lots
cards.place: Downtown Grundy, VA (newspaper building basement and neighboring shop)
cards.note: Oil company storage lots flooded and drums floated through town; a neighboring cinder-block shop broke apart and the pressure broke through the paper's basement doors, filling the basement with debris including oxygen tanks while power was still on.
cards.verify: Locations of bulk fuel and gas storage in the Grundy floodplain (permit files, 1977 photos); post-flood damage survey of downtown buildings.
cards.ask_next: Which businesses store fuel, drums or gas cylinders in the floodplain today, and are they anchored or moved before a flood?

quotes.text: My gosh, one of the, a couple of the oil company storage lots got in.
quotes.speaker: Lodge Compton (editor, Virginia Mountaineer)

quotes.text: You had sixty-gallon drums floating everywhere.
quotes.speaker: Lodge Compton (editor, Virginia Mountaineer)

quotes.text: It was block, cinder block, and it was pretty poor construction.
quotes.speaker: Lodge Compton (editor, Virginia Mountaineer)

cards.title: Road damage, not utilities, kept Grundy businesses shut
cards.place: Grundy, VA and US 460 corridor
cards.note: Compton says the paper could have printed elsewhere (Richlands) without power or phones if roads were open, but blockages and bridges out made short trips take hours. A few days later sightseers jammed the streets, and state police turned traffic back.
cards.verify: VDOT road and bridge closure logs for Buchanan County, April 1977; state police deployment records.
cards.ask_next: After the '77 flood, which road or bridge closures cut you off the longest, and how long did it take to get a through route open?

quotes.text: If you got there, you might go to the lower end of town, you might be two or three hours getting back, you know.
quotes.speaker: Lodge Compton (editor, Virginia Mountaineer)

quotes.text: You got to keep curiosity seekers out, because, you now, a couple three days afterwards when we pulled everything out of here the street was a constant line, just people out looking.
quotes.speaker: Lodge Compton (editor, Virginia Mountaineer)

cards.title: Cleanup needed pumps, gasoline, generators and water, not donated food
cards.place: Downtown Grundy, VA; Hendricks, WV
cards.note: Compton learned in 1957 that silt sets quickly, so in 1977 he put a pump in the river and washed out while water still stood; he says what was needed was pumps, gasoline and generators. In Hendricks, Sponangle heard the same: give a meal, then help shovel mud.
cards.verify: Relief-agency supply logs (Red Cross, National Guard) for Grundy 1977 and Tucker County 1985, compared with what businesses requested.
cards.ask_next: In the first week after the flood, what equipment did you most need and couldn't get, and who finally supplied it?

quotes.text: So we did get access to a pump, put it in the river, and by the time the water was, while it was still had water standing in places we were washing it out.
quotes.speaker: Lodge Compton (editor, Virginia Mountaineer)

quotes.text: We need pumps, and we need generators. And we'll make it if we get those things.
quotes.speaker: Lodge Compton (editor, Virginia Mountaineer)

quotes.text: It was like, if you want to give me something, give me a couple meal and then help me shovel mud.
quotes.speaker: Martha Sponangle (school staff, Hendricks)

cards.title: 1977 storm brought three rain bursts, up to 15.5 inches
cards.place: Levisa Fork basin upstream of Grundy, VA
cards.note: A narrator in the Grundy project video says rain began April 2, increased on the 3rd, and came in three heavy bursts on the 4th and 5th. He gives a storm-center maximum of about 15.5 inches and 8-10 inches over the basin above Grundy.
cards.verify: NWS storm reports and Corps Huntington District post-flood report for April 1977 (isohyetal map, storm-center total).
cards.ask_next: Where did the official 1977 rain totals come from, and are there gauges in the upper Levisa now that would catch bursts like that?

quotes.text: Then three heavy bursts of rainfall occurred over Western Virginia during the fourth and then also over the fifth.
quotes.speaker: Unidentified male narrator (Grundy project video)

quotes.text: It resulted in about a fifteen-and-a-half-inch maximum rainfall at the center of the storm event with about eight to ten inches of rainfall over the whole drainage basin in upstream of Grundy.
quotes.speaker: Unidentified male narrator (Grundy project video)

cards.title: Corps found Grundy floodwalls and dams unaffordable after 1986 cost-sharing
cards.place: Grundy, VA (Corps Huntington District project)
cards.note: The Corps studied reservoirs, floodwalls, channels and diversion tunnels from 1982 to 1986; after 1986 cost-sharing, no option was affordable for the town. The project moved to nonstructural measures and to routing US 460 through town as a levee with VDOT.
cards.verify: Corps Huntington District Grundy feasibility reports (1980s-1990s) and the VDOT/Corps combined US 460 project agreement.
cards.ask_next: When the local share went to 25 percent, what options did the town look at, and who finally became the non-federal sponsor?

quotes.text: We looked at reservoirs, flood walls, open-cut channels, diversion tunnels, and channel-improvement projects.
quotes.speaker: Jim Twohig (Corps of Engineers project manager)

quotes.text: In 1986, under the Water Resources Development Act of that year, cost sharing was required for flood control projects.
quotes.speaker: Jim Twohig (Corps of Engineers project manager)

quotes.text: And then when the funding formula changed it just--You know, when you have to come up with twenty-five percent local money, it just more or less killed the project.
quotes.speaker: Lodge Compton (editor, Virginia Mountaineer)

cards.title: Weston's US 33 strip was built on swamp filled with mine spoil
cards.place: US 33 commercial strip, Weston, WV (Stonecoal Creek / West Fork)
cards.note: Snyder says the swamp along US 33 was filled with dirt hauled from strip jobs and now holds a shopping strip, so Stonecoal Creek no longer spreads out when high. He says people were still dumping fill in the stream channel at the time of the interview.
cards.verify: Historical aerial photos and USGS topo maps of the US 33 corridor at Weston; county fill or floodplain permits; Corps Section 404 records.
cards.ask_next: Where along US 33 was the swamp, and has anyone mapped how much fill went in and whether it was permitted?

quotes.text: When they were stripping out there, they'd haul the dirt off the coal job at night and evenings and weekends and fill the swamps.
quotes.speaker: Matthew Snyder (contractor and farmer)

quotes.text: There's no place for the water to go.
quotes.speaker: Matthew Snyder (contractor and farmer)

quotes.text: I can go out there right today and there's somebody dumping dirt in that stream channel filling the dent.
quotes.speaker: Matthew Snyder (contractor and farmer)

cards.title: Small Polk Creek dams credited with cutting Weston flooding
cards.place: Polk Creek and Skin Creek, Lewis County, WV
cards.note: West says the small Polk Creek dams did Weston more good than anything else, and that in the 1936 cloudburst Town Run, not just Skin Creek, flooded the town. Francine Snyder says no agency other than the Corps, such as the Soil Conservation Service, was allowed to study alternatives to the big dam.
cards.verify: SCS/NRCS PL-566 watershed project records for Polk Creek; Weston flood history before and after the dams; Stonewall Jackson Dam alternatives analysis.
cards.ask_next: Since the Polk Creek dams went in, which streams still flood Weston, and was a small-dam option ever studied for Skin Creek or Town Run?

quotes.text: Whenever they put in those small dams out at Polk Creek, that did Weston more good than anything that they've ever done yet.
quotes.speaker: Aubrey West (retired dairy farmer)

quotes.text: It wasn't all Skin Creek.
quotes.speaker: Aubrey West (retired dairy farmer)

quotes.text: Had the Soil Conservation Service maybe been allowed to have done a feasibility study to have demonstrated that there were alternatives – as it was, it was just our word against the Corps of Engineers' word.
quotes.speaker: Francine Snyder (Upper West Fork Watershed Association)

cards.title: Dam relocation gave farmers 60 days amid zero vacant housing
cards.place: Stonewall Jackson Dam take area, Lewis County, WV
cards.note: Snyder says the county had no vacant housing, so displaced owners had to buy fast, sometimes before condemnation money was paid. Redabaugh, a dairy farmer, was first given 60 days and says a dairy cannot be moved in the fall. Buyout timelines need to fit local housing and the farm calendar.
cards.verify: Corps real estate relocation files for the Stonewall Jackson project (offer, payment and vacate dates); Lewis County housing vacancy data, 1984-85.
cards.ask_next: For people bought out, how long did they get between payment and move-out, and where did they find housing?

quotes.text: I mean, you've got a zero vacancy rate in the county.
quotes.speaker: Matthew Snyder (contractor and farmer)

quotes.text: There's no housing available other than low-income compartment or something, and there's not much of that.
quotes.speaker: Matthew Snyder (contractor and farmer)

quotes.text: I can't move in the fall of the year. You just can't do it.
quotes.speaker: John Redabaugh (dairy farmer)

cards.title: Washed-out bridges blocked outside rescuers from reaching Parsons overnight
cards.place: Parsons, WV, and approach routes from Elkins and Fairmont (Clover Run)
cards.note: The National Guard could not start until morning, and DNR boats from Elkins were turned back by a bridge out. A Barbour County officer who knew the back roads scouted a route via Clover Run and led the Fairmont crew in; DNR boats arrived at daybreak.
cards.verify: WVDOH bridge damage inventory for November 1985 (Tucker, Barbour, Randolph); National Guard activation times; DNR deployment logs.
cards.ask_next: Which routes into Parsons stayed open that night, and is there now a pre-planned back-road route for outside crews?

quotes.text: She told me the National Guards couldn't start until in the morning.
quotes.speaker: Forest Blume (DNR conservation officer)

quotes.text: So, a half hour to forty-five minutes later, they called back and said they can't get there either because the bridge is out of Billington.
quotes.speaker: Forest Blume (DNR conservation officer)

quotes.text: But he'd made a dry run into Clover Run there and turned around and went back to the top of the mountain to pick them up to lead them through.
quotes.speaker: Forest Blume (DNR conservation officer)

cards.title: Fire truck sent to rescue had only a 25-foot rope
cards.place: Holly Meadows, near Parsons, WV
cards.note: Ropes had been moved to the rescue truck sent to Hendricks and Hambleton, so the engine at Holly Meadows had about 25 feet of rope. A wall of water released from fences and debris upstream then swept the truck into the current. Blume adds that the fire hall was the usual equipment source and most firefighters were hospitalized or cut off.
cards.verify: Parsons VFD incident reports and apparatus inventory for November 4, 1985; hospital admission records for firefighters (counts only).
cards.ask_next: When the department split between Hendricks and Holly Meadows, what water-rescue gear did each truck carry, and what is standard now?

quotes.text: They took all the ropes out and put them in the rescue truck when they went to Hendricks and Hambleton to try and get the people out from up in there.
quotes.speaker: Craig Wilfong (volunteer firefighter, auto-parts owner)

quotes.text: Evidently somewhere on up the upper end of the fields with the fences and the debris and stuff holding the water back and it broke over.
quotes.speaker: Craig Wilfong (volunteer firefighter, auto-parts owner)

quotes.text: This was where we've always depended on for equipment, the fire hall, really.
quotes.speaker: Forest Blume (DNR conservation officer)

cards.title: Parsons firefighters discounted a 3-feet-over-flood-stage call
cards.place: Parsons, WV
cards.note: Wilfong heard a forecast of 3 feet above flood stage and did not think it unusual because past forecasts had crested and dropped before reaching town. In Parsons, a neighbor without a scanner told Wampler she would only get water in the grass, shortly before her house was destroyed.
cards.verify: NWS Pittsburgh flood statements and stage forecasts for the Cheat at Parsons on November 4, 1985, versus the observed crest.
cards.ask_next: When you heard '3 feet above flood stage,' what did that number mean to you on the ground, and what would have made you act differently?

quotes.text: I said we're calling for 3 feet above flood stage.
quotes.speaker: Craig Wilfong (volunteer firefighter, auto-parts owner)

quotes.text: It's always crested before it got there and went down.
quotes.speaker: Craig Wilfong (volunteer firefighter, auto-parts owner)

quotes.text: I think that youre okay where you are. I think that it will be just, you know, water in the grass
quotes.speaker: Juanita Miller Wampler (Parsons resident)

cards.title: Parsons flooded first from behind, via railroad ditch backwater
cards.place: Railroad ditch and pond dike near 1st Street, Parsons, WV
cards.note: Wilfong saw water entering from the back of his store while the river had not yet topped the bank in town; he attributes it to backwater where Black Fork and Shavers Fork join the Cheat, then a break at the pond dike. He measured a 10-foot mark on his house and recalls about 12 feet at a nearby service station.
cards.verify: Post-flood high-water mark surveys (USGS/Corps) in Parsons; location and failure of the pond dike; photos of the railroad ditch area.
cards.ask_next: Where is the pond dike that broke, and has the railroad ditch backflow path been mapped or closed off since?

quotes.text: I don't think we got that much water that came this way until it broke over at the dike at the pond.
quotes.speaker: Craig Wilfong (volunteer firefighter, auto-parts owner)

quotes.text: We measured 10 on the house over there where the mark was.
quotes.speaker: Craig Wilfong (volunteer firefighter, auto-parts owner)

cards.title: FHA-required flood insurance paid off a Parsons mortgage, not contents
cards.place: Parsons, WV
cards.note: Wilfong had flood insurance only because his FHA loan required it; it paid off the mortgage but he had no contents or business coverage. He was working to sell the house to the government rather than rebuild in the floodplain.
cards.verify: NFIP policy and claims data for Parsons (1985 event); Tucker County acquisition/buyout records after 1985.
cards.ask_next: Who in town had flood insurance only because a lender required it, and how many took a buyout instead of rebuilding?

quotes.text: FHA loan required – lived in the floodplains – it was a requirement that I had to have.
quotes.speaker: Craig Wilfong (volunteer firefighter, auto-parts owner)

quotes.text: Didn't have nothing on contents, but it paid off what I owed FHA.
quotes.speaker: Craig Wilfong (volunteer firefighter, auto-parts owner)

quotes.text: I'm working on a plan with the government to sell it back to the government.
quotes.speaker: Craig Wilfong (volunteer firefighter, auto-parts owner)

cards.title: Remote SBA and FEMA processing stalled aid for months
cards.place: Tucker County, WV (Parsons, Hendricks)
cards.note: Four months after the flood Wilfong knew no one with SBA money in hand; paperwork went by mail to Atlanta, and records needed for applications had washed away. Klein heard that homes not listed as destroyed got repair grants of $900-1,200.
cards.verify: SBA disaster loan disbursement dates and FEMA individual assistance grant amounts for DR-WV November 1985, Tucker County.
cards.ask_next: How long after the flood did your first aid check arrive, and which documents were hardest to replace?

quotes.text: I don't know of anybody that has got SBA money in hand yet for a business or a home.
quotes.speaker: Craig Wilfong (volunteer firefighter, auto-parts owner)

quotes.text: A lot of times, I ask for stuff that you couldn't provide.
quotes.speaker: Craig Wilfong (volunteer firefighter, auto-parts owner)

quotes.text: You're going to get $900 or $1,200 to repair it.
quotes.speaker: Bob Klein (mental health counselor, Parsons)

cards.title: Relief services sat on one side of the river from stranded areas
cards.place: School relief center across the Black Fork from Parsons (Hamrick school, as transcribed) and Parsons, WV
cards.note: Klein and his wife opened a school center with no heat; its battery emergency lights died by morning. Red Cross and FEMA set up on the Parsons side, so people stranded across the river or in St. George could not reach them. Most people on that side went to relatives, and Hambleton went two to three weeks without phones.
cards.verify: Red Cross shelter and service-center locations and dates for Tucker County 1985; telephone restoration records for Hambleton/Hendricks.
cards.ask_next: Which shelters in the county have backup power and heat, and is there a plan to open services on both sides of the Black Fork?

quotes.text: People on the other areas and even down St. George that were stranded wouldn't have been able to get to these services.
quotes.speaker: Bob Klein (mental health counselor, Parsons)

quotes.text: Like Hamilton, they didn't get any telephone over there for good, maybe two, three weeks.
quotes.speaker: Bob Klein (mental health counselor, Parsons)

cards.title: Everyone underestimated the forecast rain; a gauge network was proposed
cards.place: Eastern WV highlands (Dry Fork, Harman, Canaan Valley, Pendleton County)
cards.note: VanGundy says the heavy rain was forecast but everyone underestimated it, and that the recorded 10 1/3 inches in 24 hours was likely a minimum for the hardest-hit areas. Elsewhere in the same interview he mentions a proposed remote rain-gauge warning system for the eastern counties.
cards.verify: NWS forecasts and warnings issued November 3-4, 1985; storm rainfall analysis; records of the eastern WV IFLOWS/ALERT gauge network installation.
cards.ask_next: Do you now have upstream rain or stream gauges that would tell you the Dry Fork is coming up, and who watches them at night?

quotes.text: It was clear that we were going to get a lot of rainfall. But I guess everyone underestimated it.
quotes.speaker: Jim VanGundy (stream ecologist, Davis & Elkins College)

quotes.text: So probably 10 and a third inches in a 24 hr. period is kind of a minimum rainfall in the areas that received the heaviest rainfall; like Pendleton County and southern Tucker County.
quotes.speaker: Jim VanGundy (stream ecologist, Davis & Elkins College)

cards.title: Reported bridge losses were often approaches cut around the span
cards.place: Black Fork bridge, Parsons; Hendricks bridge; St. George bridge, Tucker County, WV
cards.note: At Parsons the bridge was rumored out, but the river had cut a new channel around its end; in Hendricks the far end of the bridge was gone and residents walked the railroad bridge. At St. George a culvert on the bridge approach gave way under the sheriff's vehicle. Damage reports should say whether the span or the approach failed.
cards.verify: WVDOH bridge damage reports for Tucker County, November 1985, distinguishing span and approach failures; repair dates (Hendricks bridge reopened about two days later per Sponangle).
cards.ask_next: For each bridge you lost access to in 1985, did the span fail or the road leading to it, and how was the approach rebuilt?

quotes.text: It wasn't the bridge, but it was the river creating new channel.
quotes.speaker: Bob Klein (mental health counselor, Parsons)

quotes.text: We couldn't get over the bridge because the other end of the bridge was gone.
quotes.speaker: Martha Sponangle (school staff, Hendricks)

quotes.text: So, they went across, checked on it, and coming back, the culvert gave away or whatever and washed them downstream and that thing.
quotes.speaker: Forest Blume (DNR conservation officer)

cards.title: Thin soils over bedrock slid when saturated in 1985
cards.place: Highland hillsides of the Monongahela National Forest area, WV
cards.note: Brashler says highland slopes have only inches to a few feet of soil over bedrock and became unstable when saturated, producing major slides. She notes the slides showed how large boulder piles in the valleys were formed.
cards.verify: WV Geological Survey and WVDOH landslide inventories for November 1985; road-closure logs near Elkins.
cards.ask_next: Where did slides block roads or hit homes in 1985, and have those slopes moved again in later heavy rains?

quotes.text: They've got a few inches to a few feet of soil overlaying the bedrock of the mountains.
quotes.speaker: Janet Brashler (Forest Service archeologist)

quotes.text: When that all gets saturated, it becomes very unstable and particularly in some kinds of soils.
quotes.speaker: Janet Brashler (Forest Service archeologist)

cards.title: Jenningston river rose two feet in about five minutes
cards.place: Jenningston, Tucker County, WV
cards.note: A Rhodes family member got home from the school bus to pack and recalls the river rose about two feet in five minutes. The family drove out through water crossing the road, and the bus driver left the bus because he could not get home.
cards.verify: School bus route and dismissal times for Jenningston on November 4, 1985; Dry Fork stage records at Hendricks.
cards.ask_next: What time did the school buses run that day, and who decided whether to send children home along the river?

quotes.text: The river had rose two feet.
quotes.speaker: Rhodes family narrative (Jenningston)

quotes.text: And we started down the road and the river broke through across the road And almost stalled the engine
quotes.speaker: Rhodes family narrative (Jenningston)

cards.title: Homeowner cost share varied by state sponsor
cards.place: Mingo County, WV; Pike and Martin Counties, KY; Grundy, VA
cards.note: In Mingo County the 5 percent local share was passed on to homeowners (roughly $2,500 to $5,000 out of pocket, as recalled), while Kentucky state and local governments absorbed it; in Grundy the 25 percent share was to be covered through VDOT's highway relocation. Who pays the local share changes what a voluntary program costs each household.
cards.verify: Project cooperation agreements with Mingo County, Kentucky sponsors and the Town of Grundy/VDOT; homeowner payment records.
cards.ask_next: Did the cost share passed to Mingo County homeowners lower sign-up compared with Kentucky, and who covered it in the end in Grundy?

quotes.text: In the Pike County and Martin County areas of Kentucky, the state and the local governments have assumed that 5 percent, so that none of that is passed on to the individual homeowners.
quotes.speaker: Gene Barr (U.S. Army Corps of Engineers, Huntington District)

quotes.text: In the case of Grundy, the cost share requirement in that area is 25 percent versus the 5 percent that's required in Mingo County and Kentucky area.
quotes.speaker: Gene Barr (U.S. Army Corps of Engineers, Huntington District)

cards.title: Flood-proofing a house displaces the family 30-90 days
cards.place: Tug Fork Valley, WV/KY
cards.note: Raising a house takes about thirty to ninety days and the family must move out the whole time. Temporary housing costs are paid in the single joint check at the end, so the contractor normally has to advance the rent money. Programs should plan bridge funding and nearby rentals.
cards.verify: Flood-proofing agreements and temporary housing payments in Corps Huntington District files.
cards.ask_next: Where did families live during the raise, and did any contractor refuse to advance the temporary housing money?

quotes.text: During that period of time, you have to be out of your house, actually, vacate the house due to safety reasons.
quotes.speaker: Gene Barr (U.S. Army Corps of Engineers, Huntington District)

quotes.text: The contractor and the homeowner should work on this prior to entering their construction contract because, normally speaking, the contractor will have to give them that money up front so they can rent a place.
quotes.speaker: Gene Barr (U.S. Army Corps of Engineers, Huntington District)

cards.title: Grundy floods come from small steep streams, not groundwater
cards.place: Levisa Fork and tributaries, Grundy, VA
cards.note: A Corps emergency manager said the 1989 Grundy flooding was all on small streams, with none on the Levisa Fork main stem, and that a lower water table does not reduce the flash flood threat. A downtown merchant gave the same answer to the 'water table is low' argument.
cards.verify: USGS gauge records for Levisa Fork at Grundy and tributary high-water marks for the 1989 event; NWS storm reports.
cards.ask_next: Which hollows and tributaries in Grundy flooded in 1989 while the Levisa stayed in its banks?

quotes.text: When I was down there in [19]89 in the last Grundy flooding that we had, the flooding there was all in the small strips, all in the small streams.
quotes.speaker: Carl Miller (Chief, Readiness Branch, Corps of Engineers, Huntington District)

quotes.text: Basically, it wasn't on the Levisa Fork, the main stream.
quotes.speaker: Carl Miller (Chief, Readiness Branch, Corps of Engineers, Huntington District)

quotes.text: No, that makes no difference. It's our terrain.
quotes.speaker: Sue Branham (owner, The Corner, downtown Grundy)

cards.title: Out-of-county radio stayed on air when Grundy's went dark
cards.place: Downtown Grundy, VA
cards.note: When power and the local radio station were out, residents followed the flood on Elkhorn City Radio (Kentucky). Warning plans should name a backup broadcaster outside the flooded valley.
cards.verify: Station logs or recollections from the Elkhorn City station and the Grundy station for April 4-5, 1977.
cards.ask_next: Which station do people in Grundy count on now when local power and broadcast fail?

quotes.text: The radio station was out. We listened to--Elkhorn City Radio stayed on the air, and they kept us updated, you know, as to what was happening as much as they could.
quotes.speaker: Sue Branham (owner, The Corner, downtown Grundy)

cards.title: Calling off school kept children off flooding roads
cards.place: Grundy Junior High School, Grundy, VA
cards.note: Schools were closed on the morning of the flood, so students and teachers were at home rather than in town or on buses when the water came through about 2:30 p.m. (as recalled). Early school closure decisions are a protective action worth tying to forecasts.
cards.verify: Buchanan County school board minutes and closure records for April 4, 1977.
cards.ask_next: Who made the school closure call that morning, and what information was it based on?

quotes.text: And they had called off school that day.
quotes.speaker: Sue Branham (owner, The Corner, downtown Grundy)

quotes.text: And that's why that we were all, you know, at different locations rather than being in town, which was really smart that they didn't have us all over here at this school with all the kids on the road.
quotes.speaker: Sue Branham (owner, The Corner, downtown Grundy)

cards.title: Bridge timber burst through a storefront at Slate Creek's mouth
cards.place: The Corner, Slate Creek and Levisa Fork intersection, Grundy, VA
cards.note: A span of wood from a bridge broke through the front door and water pressure blew out a back window, emptying the store; heavy potting-soil bags were carried roughly 300 yards from Food City (as recalled) and mud was about three feet deep inside.
cards.verify: 1977 damage photos of Main Street at Slate Creek; bridge inventory showing which Slate Creek bridge lost its deck.
cards.ask_next: Which bridge did that timber come from, and has that crossing been rebuilt to pass debris?

quotes.text: Because what happened was, as far as where we're located here, some wood from a bridge, a big--I don't know, I guess--What would you call it a span of wood, came through this front door, you know, burst through the door.
quotes.speaker: Sue Branham (owner, The Corner, downtown Grundy)

quotes.text: We had mud like up to three feet deep in here.
quotes.speaker: Sue Branham (owner, The Corner, downtown Grundy)

cards.title: Day-after access stopped at Mountain Mission School
cards.place: Mountain Mission School to downtown Grundy, VA
cards.note: The day after the flood, debris and torn-up roads meant private cars could get no closer than Mountain Mission School; only emergency vehicles went into downtown and merchants walked in with shovels.
cards.verify: Town or VDOT road closure records and photos for Route 460/Main Street after April 4, 1977.
cards.ask_next: How long was downtown closed to private traffic, and who decided when owners could drive back in?

quotes.text: And we could only come as far as Mountain Mission School and park.
quotes.speaker: Sue Branham (owner, The Corner, downtown Grundy)

quotes.text: They had emergency vehicles only, you know, coming through.
quotes.speaker: Sue Branham (owner, The Corner, downtown Grundy)

cards.title: Repeated false alarms led merchants to stop moving stock
cards.place: Main Street (Route 460), downtown Grundy, VA
cards.note: After several threatening high waters since 1977, a downtown merchant stopped carrying stock upstairs because moving it was costly and damaging. Warning fatigue is shaping protective actions in the business district.
cards.verify: NWS warning history for Grundy after 1977 compared with gauge crests that stayed below flood stage.
cards.ask_next: What would a warning have to say for you to start moving stock again?

quotes.text: We've had several high waters that seemed threatening since '77 that we used to, you know, evacuate. But we just decided, you know, we got tired of that, you know.
quotes.speaker: Sue Branham (owner, The Corner, downtown Grundy)

quotes.text: Damaged a lot of things that way, so we decided to sit through it.
quotes.speaker: Sue Branham (owner, The Corner, downtown Grundy)

cards.title: Polk Creek watershed uses eight small dams, one dry
cards.place: Polk Creek watershed, Lewis County, WV
cards.note: The Polk Creek PL-566 project has eight structures on tributaries; one is kept dry because large gas lines run beneath it and is only used in extra heavy rain, under an agreement between the gas company and the West Fork district. Local watershed groups later petitioned for a PL-566 alternative to Stonewall Jackson Dam.
cards.verify: NRCS (formerly SCS) PL-566 structure inventory for Polk Creek; West Fork Conservation District agreement with the gas company.
cards.ask_next: How often has the dry Polk Creek structure held water, and is it still maintained by the district?

quotes.text: A series of eight dams that are on various tributaries.
quotes.speaker: Barbara Heavner (Roanoke Nursery; Upper West Fork River Watershed Association)

quotes.text: One of them is the dry one, because of the fact there are very large gas lines that go in underneath of the soil.
quotes.speaker: Barbara Heavner (Roanoke Nursery; Upper West Fork River Watershed Association)

cards.title: Residents' count found three times the official population
cards.place: Stonewall Jackson Lake area, southern Lewis County, WV
cards.note: Watershed volunteers split the map into blocks and counted houses, farms, businesses, churches, schools and cemeteries, reaching eighteen hundred-plus people where the official figure was about six hundred (as recalled). A local door-to-door count can correct the baseline for a relocation or mitigation project.
cards.verify: The 1973 watershed request on file with NRCS and the Upper West Fork River Watershed Association; Corps relocation counts for Stonewall Jackson Lake.
cards.ask_next: Which places and households did the official count miss, and how were farms defined in each count?

quotes.text: We took the map of that end of the county and we blocked it off so that no one person would overstep the other's boundaries, and we counted.
quotes.speaker: Barbara Heavner (Roanoke Nursery; Upper West Fork River Watershed Association)

quotes.text: We came up with eighteen hundred plus in the Stonewall Jackson Lake area where the court said it was only around six hundred at the time.
quotes.speaker: Barbara Heavner (Roanoke Nursery; Upper West Fork River Watershed Association)

cards.title: Holly Meadows family got no warning and false reassurance
cards.place: Holly Meadows, below Parsons, WV
cards.note: Nobody came down to warn the family; the water was not up at 6:30 p.m., and when they called the man who sold them the land he said all of Parsons would wash away before they flooded. By about 8 p.m. water was near the back door (as recalled).
cards.verify: Cheat River gauge at Parsons for the evening of November 4, 1985; county warning and door-to-door notification records for Holly Meadows.
cards.ask_next: Who is responsible for warning the houses down in Holly Meadows now, and how would they get word?

quotes.text: So, there had been nobody down to tell her.
quotes.speaker: David Humphrey (Parsons resident, volunteer rescuer)

quotes.text: He said not to worry about it because all of Parsons would have to be washed away before we got flooded down there, and we didn't.
quotes.speaker: Amy Moore (Holly Meadows resident)

quotes.text: Mom had checked it at 6:30 p.m. and it wasn't up at all.
quotes.speaker: Amy Moore (Holly Meadows resident)

cards.title: Holly Meadows road went from dry to impassable in minutes
cards.place: Holly Meadows road, below Parsons, WV
cards.note: The road was dry when Amy drove it, ankle-deep five minutes later, and too deep for the jeep moments after that; the jeep was swept over. When the fire truck pushed in, its wake lifted the jeep again.
cards.verify: Rate of rise at the Parsons gauge 7-9 p.m. November 4, 1985; fire department run reports for Holly Meadows.
cards.ask_next: At what point should Holly Meadows residents stop trying to drive out and go uphill instead?

quotes.text: He went and looked on the road that I just came down five minutes before, and there was water up to his ankles.
quotes.speaker: Amy Moore (Holly Meadows resident)

quotes.text: But I guess when the water came up by them, it caused the water to pick the jeep up again.
quotes.speaker: Amy Moore (Holly Meadows resident)

cards.title: Three rivers meet below Parsons and sent a wave down
cards.place: Confluence below Parsons and Holly Meadows, WV
cards.note: Narrators describe Shavers Fork joining the combined Black Fork and Dry Fork just below Parsons, and a 3- to 4-foot wave (as heard from firefighters) rolling the Moores' jeep in Holly Meadows. Forecasts for Holly Meadows and St. George depend on timing the crests of both forks.
cards.verify: USGS gauges on Shavers Fork at Parsons and Black Fork/Cheat at Parsons for crest timing; post-flood high-water mark surveys at Holly Meadows.
cards.ask_next: Did the Shavers Fork crest and the Black Fork crest reach Parsons at the same time, and who saw the surge come through?

quotes.text: Then right below Parsons here, it all intersects in the three – there were three rivers, into one river.
quotes.speaker: David Humphrey (Parsons resident, volunteer rescuer)

quotes.text: They said it was about a 3- or 4-foot wave.
quotes.speaker: David Humphrey (Parsons resident, volunteer rescuer)

cards.title: Boat rescue snagged downed lines and needed upstream anchoring
cards.place: Cheat River at Holly Meadows, WV
cards.note: Volunteers in a private 16-foot boat caught downed telephone or power lines on the motor and dragged poles downstream; they then tied off to a tree upstream of the victim and let rope out to drift down to her. The fire department's 400-foot shore rope was not long enough.
cards.verify: Parsons fire department and ambulance run records for November 5, 1985; utility records of downed lines at Holly Meadows.
cards.ask_next: What boats, ropes and lights does the county have now for night swiftwater rescue, and who checks for downed lines first?

quotes.text: They were telling us that we – the telephone lines or the power lines had got up around the motor on the boat, and we were dragging the poles down the river.
quotes.speaker: David Humphrey (Parsons resident, volunteer rescuer)

quotes.text: I told the Humphrey boy, "I'm going to get up next to that tree there, up above her, you snatch this rope around the tree, when I holler you let it off a little bit."
quotes.speaker: Don Goss (boat owner, Parsons)

quotes.text: As we got in beside the tree, they had a 400-foot rope on us.
quotes.speaker: David Humphrey (Parsons resident, volunteer rescuer)

cards.title: Debris hit Parsons, Holly Meadows and St. George bridges
cards.place: Parsons town bridge, Holly Meadows bridge and St. George bridge, Tucker County, WV
cards.note: A fifth-wheel camper struck the town river bridge and was torn off its frame, debris hit the Holly Meadows bridge through the night, and the old St. George bridge was taken out; trailers and campers from riverside parks made up much of the debris.
cards.verify: WVDOH bridge inventory and post-flood inspection reports for the Parsons, Holly Meadows and St. George bridges; photos.
cards.ask_next: Were the replacement bridges at St. George and Holly Meadows raised or lengthened to pass trailers and logs?

quotes.text: I'd seen it hit the town bridge down at the river bridge.
quotes.speaker: David Humphrey (Parsons resident, volunteer rescuer)

quotes.text: They had stuff hit that Holly Meadows bridge down while we were down at the bottom looking for her.
quotes.speaker: David Humphrey (Parsons resident, volunteer rescuer)

quotes.text: Well, it took the old St. George bridge out.
quotes.speaker: David Humphrey (Parsons resident, volunteer rescuer)

cards.title: Upstairs refuge at St. George nearly failed as water rose
cards.place: House by the St. George bridge, Tucker County, WV
cards.note: Older residents went upstairs expecting to be safe; rescuers had to break out a second-story window to take them by boat, and on the last trip water was above the window and beds were floating. Going upstairs is not a safe plan in that reach.
cards.verify: High-water mark on the St. George house relative to its second floor; rescue records.
cards.ask_next: How do you reach older residents in St. George early enough that they leave before going upstairs is their only option?

quotes.text: I guess they thought that if they would just go upstairs they would be safe.
quotes.speaker: Don Goss (boat owner, Parsons)

quotes.text: Then after going to St. George and seeing them have to break the upstairs window and let 8 to 12 inches of water go in the upstairs window of that house, you wondered just how many people were caught unaware of it and left in their house that panicked or actually got caught in the water with the house still standing there.
quotes.speaker: Forest Blume (game warden, Parsons)

cards.title: Floodwater reached Pulp Mill Bottom from behind first
cards.place: Pulp Mill Bottom, Parsons, WV
cards.note: Water crossed the road at the next crossing behind riverfront homes before the river came over its bank in front, so a resident watching the river did not know he was already cut off.
cards.verify: Post-flood high-water marks and topography for Pulp Mill Bottom; route of overflow along the railroad.
cards.ask_next: Where does water first cross the road into Pulp Mill Bottom, and at what river level?

quotes.text: By the time I'd left here and went up on the hill and came back to get my boat, the water was coming across the road down here, just at this next crossing.
quotes.speaker: Don Goss (boat owner, Parsons)

quotes.text: He didn't know the water had come in behind him.
quotes.speaker: Don Goss (boat owner, Parsons)

cards.title: Rebuilt dikes and channelized reaches worried locals
cards.place: Fortney Mill bottom and Cheat/Black Fork between Harman and Parsons, WV
cards.note: Residents doubted the rebuilt dikes would hold, reported that the river runs straight into the new Fortney Mill bottom structure at high water, and worried that straightened channels and lost bank vegetation will speed future floods; a CCC wall on Clover Run from the 1930s was cited as still standing.
cards.verify: Corps and NRCS post-flood emergency stream work records (Section 14, EWP) for Tucker and Randolph Counties; inspection of the Fortney Mill structure.
cards.ask_next: Who designed and maintains the rebuilt dike at Fortney Mill bottom, and has it been overtopped or damaged since?

quotes.text: I understand from people that should know at the one they built in the Fortney Mill bottom, when the water is up high, it's coming straight into it and this could go at any time.
quotes.speaker: Forest Blume (game warden, Parsons)

quotes.text: Several people have told me with the way they've channeled the rivers between here and Harman, if we ever get a hard rain, we have never seen nothing yet to what we're going to see.
quotes.speaker: Forest Blume (game warden, Parsons)

quotes.text: These dikes they rebuilt up there, I don't think that will hold either.
quotes.speaker: David Humphrey (Parsons resident, volunteer rescuer)

cards.title: Riverside garage told to rebuild several feet higher
cards.place: Harper's garage, beside the river, Parsons, WV
cards.note: A long-standing garage beside the river was swept away; the narrator understood it might not be allowed back, and if it were, it would have to be built 4 to 6 feet higher, which is hard for a floor carrying heavy trucks.
cards.verify: Parsons floodplain permit file and substantial damage determination for the Harper property.
cards.ask_next: What elevation did you require for commercial rebuilds next to the river in Parsons, and did any owners give up?

quotes.text: Harpers over there, I don't think they're going to let him rebuild back because it's right beside the river.
quotes.speaker: David Humphrey (Parsons resident, volunteer rescuer)

quotes.text: If they do let him build it back, they want him to build it 4 or 5, 6 feet, whatever, higher off the ground than what it was originally.
quotes.speaker: David Humphrey (Parsons resident, volunteer rescuer)

cards.title: Eight inches of rain versus five in 1954
cards.place: Canaan Valley and Elkins, upstream of Parsons, WV
cards.note: Residents say they would have moved faster had they known 8 inches of rain fell upstream, compared with 5 inches (as recalled) in the 1954 flood they remembered. Stating rainfall against a known local flood gives people a usable benchmark.
cards.verify: NWS/cooperative observer rainfall for Canaan Valley and Elkins November 3-5, 1985, and for the 1954 flood.
cards.ask_next: Which past flood do people here compare to, and would a rainfall number compared with it have changed what you did?

quotes.text: I've heard several people since say, "Well, if I had known there'd been 8 inches of rain in Canaan Valley and Elkins, I was here in the [19]54 flood, I'd have been moving a lot faster than I was."
quotes.speaker: Forest Blume (game warden, Parsons)

quotes.text: For the [19]54 floods, there were 5 inches of rainfall compared to this.
quotes.speaker: Forest Blume (game warden, Parsons)

cards.title: Rural families refused group trailer sites outside their community
cards.place: Brushy Run, Roaring Creek and Seneca group site, Pendleton County, WV
cards.note: Families in the Northfork area resisted moving to a group site three miles away in Seneca and fought to place trailers on friends' land; few needed government trailers because most moved in with relatives. Temporary housing that keeps people in their own hollow is more likely to be used.
cards.verify: FEMA temporary housing records for Pendleton County: private-site vs group-site placements.
cards.ask_next: How many private-site trailer placements were approved in Pendleton County, and what made FEMA agree to them?

quotes.text: When the government said, "Well, we're building this group site and it's only three miles from your home and it's just right down the road in Seneca," they didn't realize that Seneca was another world to these people in a sense.
quotes.speaker: Michael Smith (counselor, Appalachian Mental Health Center)

quotes.text: In fact, there weren't really that many people in Pendleton County that actually required the temporary housing in the forms of the mobile homes from the government.
quotes.speaker: Michael Smith (counselor, Appalachian Mental Health Center)

cards.title: No word between Parsons and Hendricks; shelter had no information
cards.place: Parsons school gym shelter and Hendricks, Tucker County, WV
cards.note: An officer stranded in Hendricks from about 7 p.m. lost phone service as water reached the house; his family at the school shelter got no news overnight and evacuees were not allowed to leave. Shelters need a way to pass status information to families of responders and residents.
cards.verify: Telephone company outage records for Hendricks; county dispatch radio logs for November 4-5, 1985.
cards.ask_next: How would dispatch reach an officer or residents in Hendricks today if phones and roads went out?

quotes.text: Then the phones just went dead.
quotes.speaker: Hank Thompson (law officer, Tucker County)

quotes.text: The next morning, no one knew anything.
quotes.speaker: Denise Thompson (sheriff's residence, Parsons)

quotes.text: This day and age, with all the computers and telephones and all the equipment, and no one could get from Parsons to Hendricks to find out if he was all right.
quotes.speaker: Denise Thompson (sheriff's residence, Parsons)

cards.title: Water at the parking meters meant walking out was too late
cards.place: Tucker County sheriff's residence and jail, Parsons, WV
cards.note: Busy dispatchers upstairs did not tell the family in the sheriff's residence how bad the flooding was; by the time water reached the parking meters she could not carry two small children out, and rescuers led her out in chest-deep current.
cards.verify: High-water mark at the Tucker County jail and courthouse block; dispatch logs.
cards.ask_next: Who tells families living at the jail and dispatch building to leave, and at what river level?

quotes.text: But they didn't even tell me that it was flooding that bad.
quotes.speaker: Denise Thompson (sheriff's residence, Parsons)

quotes.text: Because I knew when I saw – when I realized out the window that it was hitting the parking meters.
quotes.speaker: Denise Thompson (sheriff's residence, Parsons)

quotes.text: It was up to my chest.
quotes.speaker: Denise Thompson (sheriff's residence, Parsons)

cards.title: Long Bottom's single low bridge cuts the neighborhood off in floods
cards.place: Long Bottom bridge over Slate Creek, Grundy, VA
cards.note: Long Bottom had one way in and out, a low bridge level with the roadway that was buried in debris for days in 1957; in 1977 drivers were still crossing it when water was over the deck, on a neighbor's word. A single at-grade crossing is both an isolation point and a drive-through-water hazard.
cards.verify: VDOT/Buchanan County bridge inventory for the Long Bottom (Slate Creek) crossing: deck elevation, rebuild dates after 1957 and 1977; photos Helen Johnson holds of the washed-out approach.
cards.ask_next: Is the Long Bottom bridge still the only way in, and has its deck been raised since 1977?

quotes.text: There's only one bridge in and out here, and it was–Wasn't it a low water bridge, mom?
quotes.speaker: Patrick Johnson (Grundy paralegal, later attorney)

quotes.text: It was a fairly low water bridge, and it was covered up with debris for several days.
quotes.speaker: Patrick Johnson (Grundy paralegal, later attorney)

quotes.text: I rolled the window down, and he said, "You can make it. It's only a couple of inches over the bridge."
quotes.speaker: Patrick Johnson (Grundy paralegal, later attorney)

cards.title: Bridge decks stood while their approaches washed out
cards.place: Long Bottom bridge, Grundy, VA; Parsons and Hendricks area bridges, Tucker County, WV
cards.note: In both floods, narrators saw the bridge structure survive but the fill approaches scour away, so a standing bridge was still impassable. Damage assessment and reopening plans should check approaches, not just spans.
cards.verify: WVDOH and VDOT post-flood damage reports listing approach-fill versus superstructure repairs; post-flood photos of the Long Bottom and Tucker County bridges.
cards.ask_next: After the flood, which bridges here reopened late because of approach washouts, and were the approaches rebuilt any differently?

quotes.text: The bridge was standing, but you, the approach was all just rocks.
quotes.speaker: Helen Combs Johnson (Long Bottom resident)

quotes.text: None of the bridges were destroyed.
quotes.speaker: Unidentified man (participant, Hendricks children's workshop)

quotes.text: But the approach up to the bridge itself –
quotes.speaker: Unidentified man (participant, Hendricks children's workshop)

cards.title: Grundy water rose from in-bank to inside stores by noon
cards.place: John's Flower Shop and downtown Grundy, Levisa Fork, Grundy, VA
cards.note: As recalled, the river was high but in its banks at the start of the workday, inside riverfront buildings by noon (about 42 inches in the flower shop), and the managing partner of a law firm sent staff home around noon. The warning that moved people was informal and came within hours of flooding.
cards.verify: USGS Levisa Fork at Grundy stage record for April 4, 1977 (hourly if available); NWS warning issuance times for Buchanan County.
cards.ask_next: On the morning of April 4, 1977, what was the first official word you got, and how many hours before water reached the stores?

quotes.text: We came out to work that morning, and of course the water was high, but it wasn’t out of the banks or anything.
quotes.speaker: John Fleenor (owner, John's Flower Shop; Grundy mayor)

quotes.text: But by noon it was up getting in the building, and we had to evacuate the building, get out of it.
quotes.speaker: John Fleenor (owner, John's Flower Shop; Grundy mayor)

quotes.text: "You all better go home. It looks like we're going to have high water, and we don't know what the extent of it's going to be."
quotes.speaker: Patrick Johnson (Grundy paralegal, later attorney)

cards.title: Mountains left Grundy with one radio station, which failed
cards.place: Grundy, Buchanan County, VA
cards.note: Terrain blocked outside radio signals, so the local Grundy station was the only source, and it appears to have stopped transmitting; phones and TV were also out. Warning dissemination that depends on one local broadcaster has no backup here.
cards.verify: Station log or FCC records for the Grundy AM station in April 1977; current NOAA Weather Radio coverage maps for Buchanan County.
cards.ask_next: During the 1977 flood, did the Grundy radio station stay on the air, and what do people here rely on today when power and phones go out?

quotes.text: We lived in an area where, at that time anyway, no matter what kind of radio you had you couldn't pick up any other radio station other than the Grundy station because of the mountains.
quotes.speaker: Patrick Johnson (Grundy paralegal, later attorney)

quotes.text: And I believe the radio station had even, was failing to transmit.
quotes.speaker: Patrick Johnson (Grundy paralegal, later attorney)

quotes.text: Again, there was no phones.
quotes.speaker: Patrick Johnson (Grundy paralegal, later attorney)

cards.title: Route 460 four-lane had missing sections and no barricades
cards.place: U.S. 460 between Deal and Shorts Gap, Buchanan County, VA
cards.note: The night after the crest, whole chunks of the main highway out of Grundy were gone with no signs or barricades yet, and drivers detoured into the oncoming lanes. Early post-flood road closures and marking were a gap.
cards.verify: VDOT damage and repair records for U.S. 460 Deal to Shorts Gap, April 1977.
cards.ask_next: Who is responsible for closing and marking washed-out roads the first night, and how fast did that happen on 460 in 1977?

quotes.text: And we got up there on the four-lane highway between Deal and Shorts Gap, and there were just like huge chunks of road missing.
quotes.speaker: Patrick Johnson (Grundy paralegal, later attorney)

quotes.text: There hadn't been enough time to put anything, any signs, or have anybody up there, any barricades, or anything.
quotes.speaker: Patrick Johnson (Grundy paralegal, later attorney)

cards.title: Coal company heavy equipment did much of Grundy's 1977 cleanup
cards.place: Downtown Grundy, VA
cards.note: Two narrators credit locally owned coal companies and their heavy equipment with the speed of the 1977 cleanup, and both say that capacity is gone now that the mines have closed or sold out. Recovery plans should not assume the 1977 private equipment pool exists today.
cards.verify: Buchanan County and VA Department of Emergency Services 1977 recovery records on contracted and donated equipment; current county mutual-aid and equipment inventories.
cards.ask_next: If Grundy flooded like 1977 tomorrow, whose heavy equipment would clear the streets, and is that written down anywhere?

quotes.text: And all these coal companies, they had a lot of heavy equipment in here, and they moved in and took over.
quotes.speaker: Patrick Johnson (Grundy paralegal, later attorney)

quotes.text: And they're the ones that helped clean Grundy up. If we have another one, they're out.
quotes.speaker: Helen Combs Johnson (Long Bottom resident)

cards.title: Raising a house 7.5 feet still left 4.5 feet inside
cards.place: Marie Williams home, Grundy, VA
cards.note: After 1957 flooded her old house, the owner rebuilt it seven and a half feet higher in 1963, yet in 1977 water came about four and a half feet into the new house, as recalled. Elevation set by the last flood of record was not enough.
cards.verify: Survey of the first-floor elevation against the 1977 high-water mark and the current Grundy FIRM base flood elevation; building permit for the 1963 rebuild.
cards.ask_next: When you rebuilt in 1963, what height did you aim for, and who told you it would be high enough?

quotes.text: And I tore the house down and raised it seven and a half feet from where the house was and built this present home.
quotes.speaker: Marie Williams (Grundy homeowner)

quotes.text: Now this house is supposed to be two feet higher than the house above me, but this ‘77 flood came four and a half feet into this house after raising it seven and a half feet.
quotes.speaker: Marie Williams (Grundy homeowner)

cards.title: Corps alerts county emergency managers before release changes
cards.place: Stonewall Jackson Dam, West Fork River, Lewis County, WV
cards.note: The Corps spokesman says large release changes come with a public notice plus a direct alert to county emergency managers, and the district has travel-time charts showing when a release reaches downstream points. Releases are set by the whole 16-reservoir system, not only local needs.
cards.verify: Stonewall Jackson Lake water control manual and Pittsburgh District notification procedures; Lewis County OEM contact records.
cards.ask_next: When the Corps changes releases at Stonewall Jackson, who calls you, how much notice do you get, and what do you pass on?

quotes.text: Usually in addition to a public notice, we'll alert county emergency managers so that they can be on the alert too for anything unusual.
quotes.speaker: John Reed (Corps of Engineers, Pittsburgh District public relations)

quotes.text: We have all sorts of charts and schedules that indicate when you start the release, how soon it'll reach such-and-such a point on the river so that you can get notices down as to when it's at.
quotes.speaker: John Reed (Corps of Engineers, Pittsburgh District public relations)

cards.title: Weston floods forced hospital patients over a mountaintop
cards.place: Weston, Lewis County, WV
cards.event: Late 1960s flood and recurring high water
cards.note: At a public meeting, hospital staff described taking patients by four-wheel drive over a mountaintop when water reached a certain level, and factory owners said workers could not get in. The hospital's access threshold is a specific, checkable trigger.
cards.verify: West Fork at Weston gauge stage at which hospital road access is lost; hospital emergency plan; transcript of Wise's 1983 public meeting.
cards.ask_next: At what river level does the road to the Weston hospital go under, and is there still a mountaintop route?

quotes.text: The ministry of the hospital told me about how when the water rises to a certain level, that you have to go take people and patients by four-wheel drive over a mountaintop to get them to the hospital.
quotes.speaker: Bob Wise (U.S. Representative, WV)

quotes.text: Owners of factories told me about how their employees couldn't get to work because of it and there was a lot of downtime.
quotes.speaker: Bob Wise (U.S. Representative, WV)

cards.title: Children's flood fears return with heavy rain and second disasters
cards.place: Hendricks and Parsons, Tucker County, WV
cards.note: A child development consultant told Tucker County caregivers that children who seem fine can relapse when heavy rain or a storm comes; local workers reported flooded families with small children who then had house fires. Recovery support for children needs to last past the first weeks and expect re-triggers.
cards.verify: Tucker County school counselor and mental health records from 1985-86; fire department incident logs for structure fires in flood-damaged homes.
cards.ask_next: After the flood, how long did schools and families see children react to rain or storms, and who was helping them?

quotes.text: So, my guess is that you often see children who seem to be doing all right until some heavy rains come or a storm.
quotes.speaker: Roberta Schoemberg (child development consultant)

quotes.text: We have had several families with small children, they were flooded. Now, their homes, they have had house fires.
quotes.speaker: Unidentified woman (participant, Hendricks children's workshop)

cards.title: Condemned houses were painted with numbers and stood for weeks
cards.place: Parsons, Tucker County, WV
cards.note: Houses judged uninhabitable were marked with painted red numbers for demolition but stayed standing a month or two, which was hard on owners; one renter's family was simply told their house was condemned. Marking and demolition timing, and how it is explained to occupants, matter.
cards.verify: Parsons and Tucker County demolition/condemnation lists and dates; FEMA substantial-damage determinations for the 1985 flood.
cards.ask_next: Who painted the demolition numbers, how were owners and renters told, and how long did marked houses stand?

quotes.text: The red marks, or anything left of it, the red marks meant that that was judged to be totally uninhabitable. But they stood for a month or two.
quotes.speaker: Unidentified man (participant, Hendricks children's workshop)

quotes.text: You can imagine what this meant to people whose home that was.
quotes.speaker: Unidentified man (participant, Hendricks children's workshop)

quotes.text: No, they just said that condemned it.
quotes.speaker: Bo Haddix (Parsons resident)

cards.title: Schools sent buses out with lists of where children should go
cards.place: Thomas grade school to Jenningston and Gladwin, Dry Fork, Tucker County, WV
cards.note: As the driver recalls, the school gave him phone numbers for children whose families had already left so the children could be taken elsewhere; he crossed the Jenningston bridge with water near its underside, while at Gladwin water was over the road by about 3:30 p.m., as recalled. School dismissal on a flooding afternoon put buses on low roads at the worst time.
cards.verify: Tucker County Schools dismissal and bus-route records for November 4, 1985; Dry Fork gauge record that afternoon.
cards.ask_next: On November 4, who decided when buses ran, and how did the schools know which children could not go home?

quotes.text: While I was loading up, the secretary come out and gave me telephone numbers of people that was already – didn't want their kids to come home because they had then left.
quotes.speaker: Tom Bonner (Gladwin resident, school bus driver)

quotes.text: When I got to the bridge, it was right up close to the bottom of the bridge.
quotes.speaker: Tom Bonner (Gladwin resident, school bus driver)

quotes.text: Well, about 3:30 [p.m.], my nephew, Joey, called and told me the water was running over the road.
quotes.speaker: Freddie Bonner (Gladwin resident)

cards.title: Fog grounded helicopters and debris made rope crossings impossible
cards.place: Dry Fork at Gladwin, Tucker County, WV
cards.note: For people stranded across the Dry Fork, neighbors called for a helicopter but none were allowed out in the fog and rain, and the narrator judged that a rope line could not survive the floating wood, hay and building parts. Low ceilings during the event removed air rescue.
cards.verify: Requests to WV National Guard or Coast Guard air units on November 4, 1985 and flight decisions; surface observations of ceiling and visibility at Elkins that evening.
cards.ask_next: That night, who could you call for air rescue, and who decided whether helicopters could fly?

quotes.text: They had called for a helicopter. They wouldn't let any helicopters out.
quotes.speaker: Tom Bonner (Gladwin resident, school bus driver)

quotes.text: Even if you’d a rope tied over there, you couldn't get there because it can kill you – broke the rope.
quotes.speaker: Tom Bonner (Gladwin resident, school bus driver)

quotes.text: If a helicopter – if it hadn't been so foggy and rainy, and the helicopters had come in, they'd have had plenty of time.
quotes.speaker: Tom Bonner (Gladwin resident, school bus driver)

cards.title: Parsons got no warning; St. George was overlooked entirely
cards.place: Virginia Street, Parsons, and St. George, Tucker County, WV
cards.note: A Parsons resident says no warning was given and credits the evening timing with keeping deaths down; a St. George resident says officials told her Hendricks had about a 20-minute warning but St. George was not thought of. Warnings, where they existed, were short and uneven between towns.
cards.verify: NWS Pittsburgh/Elkins warning products and times for Tucker County, November 4-5, 1985; county dispatch logs.
cards.ask_next: Did anyone get word to St. George or Parsons that night, and through whom?

quotes.text: There were no warnings.
quotes.speaker: Ona Hovatter (Virginia Street, Parsons resident)

quotes.text: If this would've come after midnight, Monday night, there'd been a lot of people drowning because they'd have been home in their beds.
quotes.speaker: Ona Hovatter (Virginia Street, Parsons resident)

quotes.text: I mean, they had had a 20-minute warning in Hendrix.
quotes.speaker: Joan Heckler (St. George resident)

cards.title: Parsons homes dry in 1954 took five feet in 1985
cards.place: 231 Virginia Street and Elkins Street, Parsons, WV
cards.note: In 1954 only the lower end of town (Elkins Street) flooded and this resident helped carry people out; his Virginia Street house stayed dry then but took five feet three inches in 1985, as recalled. Past-flood experience led him to discount the danger until his son made him leave.
cards.verify: Surveyed 1985 high-water marks on Virginia Street; 1954 Cheat/Shavers Fork crest at Parsons; window-sash watermark he describes.
cards.ask_next: Where exactly did the 1954 water stop in Parsons, and how does that line compare with 1985 street by street?

quotes.text: I had five foot and three inches of water in this living room right here, and mud.
quotes.speaker: Ona Hovatter (Virginia Street, Parsons resident)

quotes.text: I put on my hip boots and helped carry people out down on Elkins Street, but I didn't have a bit of water here.
quotes.speaker: Ona Hovatter (Virginia Street, Parsons resident)

cards.title: Sawmill logs and a broken mill-pond dike drove debris through Parsons
cards.place: Sawmill at the upper end of the bottom, Parsons, WV
cards.note: Residents say a sawmill at the upper end of town lost its log stock, a pond dike there broke, and logs ended up in the streets. Stockpiles and small impoundments upstream of town are debris and surge sources to inventory.
cards.verify: Sawmill location and pond permit (WV DNR dam/impoundment records); post-flood photos of log debris in Parsons streets.
cards.ask_next: Where was the sawmill pond, how big was it, and was it rebuilt after the dike broke?

quotes.text: See, we have a sawmill up in the upper end of the bottom here. They lost all their logs and everything.
quotes.speaker: Ona Hovatter (Virginia Street, Parsons resident)

quotes.text: See, the dike broke and that's why it left all such a force of water come down through here, from down through over there.
quotes.speaker: Ona Hovatter (Virginia Street, Parsons resident)

quotes.text: They had logs on this next street over here.
quotes.speaker: Helen Dotson (Limestone resident)

cards.title: A riverside house with no flood history lost its foundation
cards.place: Riverside lot down the alley, Hendricks, WV
cards.note: A house built near the river where water had not come in two generations flooded through the kitchen and down the basement stairs before the occupant knew, and the flood took the house, basement floor and the ground under it. Local memory of 'never flooded' was not a safe siting guide.
cards.verify: Tucker County floodplain maps and permits for Hendricks riverside lots before and after 1985; buyout or rebuild records for the lot.
cards.ask_next: Was that Hendricks lot ever shown as floodplain, and was anything rebuilt there?

quotes.text: Well, just like now, the water came in through the kitchen and down the stairs to the basement before my daughter even knew it was there.
quotes.speaker: Helen Dotson (Limestone resident)

quotes.text: See, the street went down to the river almost, and it just taken that whole corner of dirt and all.
quotes.speaker: Helen Dotson (Limestone resident)

quotes.text: Whenever they built there, no, it had never been there because, see, it had been in generations – a couple generations, and it never happened before.
quotes.speaker: Helen Dotson (Limestone resident)

cards.title: Donated relief went unclaimed; help worked best unasked
cards.place: Parsons and Davis, Tucker County, WV
cards.note: Clothing collected at schools went unclaimed and had to be moved out, which narrators put down to pride; volunteers found that offering help got refused, while simply starting work was accepted. Distribution that requires people to come and ask may miss those who need it.
cards.verify: Records of relief-goods collection and leftover disposal at Tucker County schools and the Elkins relief center; volunteer agency after-action notes.
cards.ask_next: How did people who needed supplies but would not ask for them get help after the flood?

quotes.text: But he said that there were just so much more than the people would come in and get.
quotes.speaker: Helen Dotson (Limestone resident)

quotes.text: When you go to help somebody, you have to be a little careful how you do it.
quotes.speaker: Helen Dotson (Limestone resident)

quotes.text: Don't act like you're helping them.
quotes.speaker: Ona Hovatter (Virginia Street, Parsons resident)

cards.title: Bystanders on the bank caught officers' rope at St. George
cards.place: St. George bridge approach, Cheat River, St. George, WV
cards.note: When a surge swept the sheriff's vehicle off the bridge approach, the officers climbed on top and threw a rope that residents on the bank caught and tied to a fence post, then pulled them in. The rescue depended on a spare rope and on people who happened to be watching.
cards.verify: Tucker County Sheriff and WV State Police incident reports for November 4, 1985; Cheat River at St. George/Parsons crest timing.
cards.ask_next: What rescue gear did responders carry that night, and how did they come to be on the St. George approach?

quotes.text: and they had this rope and they threw it at us.
quotes.speaker: Joan Heckler (St. George resident)

quotes.text: Then we tied it off on a fence post which is washed away by now, but we just pulled them.
quotes.speaker: Joan Heckler (St. George resident)

quotes.text: To see the water that high and to take that old bridge out, there was plenty of water.
quotes.speaker: Joan Heckler (St. George resident)

cards.title: Residents refused early evacuation, then needed boat rescue
cards.place: St. George, Tucker County, WV
cards.note: Neighbors who were urged to leave early said the water would not get that high and went upstairs; later a private boat paddled with two brooms took them out, and one resident would not leave without her dog. Pet and refusal issues delayed the rescue.
cards.verify: St. George rescue accounts in Tucker County fire department and sheriff logs; newspaper coverage of private boat rescues.
cards.ask_next: What would have convinced St. George residents to leave before dark, and what happened with pets?

quotes.text: They said, "No. The water is not going to get that high. We'll just go upstairs and we'll be fine."
quotes.speaker: Joan Heckler (St. George resident)

quotes.text: Just a boat and we had two brooms we used for row is what we have, paddles.
quotes.speaker: Darrell Heckler (St. George resident)

quotes.text: She didn’t want to go because the dog was there and she couldn’t find the dog.
quotes.speaker: Darrell Heckler (St. George resident)

cards.title: Drivers trusted bystanders and drove into rising water
cards.place: Seneca toward Petersburg, Pendleton County, WV
cards.note: A would-be rescuer asked a bystander whether he could cross water on the road, was told yes, reached a riverside trailer, and then had his truck stall within about 25 feet of the road as water came in fast. Overnight, people on shore saw his flashlight in a tree but could not reach him until morning.
