cards.verify: Pendleton County rescue logs for the Seneca area, November 4-5, 1985; South Branch/North Fork gauge timing.
cards.ask_next: When people on shore spot someone stranded at night, who do they call, and what can actually reach them?

quotes.text: I asked this man, I said, "Do you think I can make it across?"
quotes.speaker: Roger Lee Morral, Sr. (Seneca-area resident)

quotes.text: The water just came in so fast, just drowning my truck out.
quotes.speaker: Roger Lee Morral, Sr. (Seneca-area resident)

quotes.text: But anyway, they happened to see my light there, and they walked down along the creek to about where they thought I was at.
quotes.speaker: Roger Lee Morral, Sr. (Seneca-area resident)

cards.title: Outside officials and media did not grasp Parsons' damage
cards.place: Parsons, Tucker County, WV (calls from Pittsburgh)
cards.note: A relative calling from Pittsburgh was told by state police in Elkins that Parsons was fine, and Pittsburgh stations that Tucker County residents watch on cable carried little. Situational awareness outside the county lagged badly in the first days.
cards.verify: WV State Police Elkins detachment logs and public statements, November 5-6, 1985; Pittsburgh TV news archives for those days.
cards.ask_next: In the first two days, what did the state and the outside world know about Parsons, and how did they find out?

quotes.text: So, I quickly got on the phone and called the state police in Elkins, who assured me that there was nothing wrong in Parsons.
quotes.speaker: Mary Litman (Tucker County native living in Pittsburgh)

quotes.text: Because the folks in this part of West Virginia receive all of their information from Pittsburgh via cable.
quotes.speaker: Mary Litman (Tucker County native living in Pittsburgh)

cards.title: Jail prisoners were released by boat as water rose
cards.place: Parsons, Tucker County, WV
cards.note: A resident who helped that night says it got too deep to move prisoners on foot, so officers were let down to the jail in a boat on a rope and the prisoners were released to be picked up later. Detention facilities in the floodplain need their own evacuation plan.
cards.verify: Tucker County jail and sheriff records for November 4, 1985; jail location relative to the 1985 high-water line.
cards.ask_next: Where was the jail in 1985, when were prisoners moved, and where is it now relative to the floodplain?

quotes.text: Then they went down and they got a boat because it was too deep then to let the prisoners go.
quotes.speaker: Bo Haddix (Parsons resident)

quotes.text: So, we had a rope hooked to a boat and let the cops go down.
quotes.speaker: Bo Haddix (Parsons resident)

quotes.text: They opened it up and let them out.
quotes.speaker: Bo Haddix (Parsons resident)

cards.title: Stonewall land was bought dam-outward, explained poorly at first
cards.place: Stonewall Jackson Dam take area (West Fork, Skin Creek, Brownsville, Roanoke), Lewis County, WV
cards.note: The Corps bought land from the dam outward on the construction schedule, taking willing sellers early, and admits an early real estate meeting failed to explain the process; Rep. Wise asked for interim haying and grazing on acquired land not yet needed. Sequence, explanation and interim use shape how a large acquisition is received.
cards.verify: Corps Huntington District real estate acquisition schedule and outgrant/lease records for Stonewall Jackson Lake, 1977-1988.
cards.ask_next: How were families told when their parcel would be bought, and could former owners keep farming land until it was needed?

quotes.text: As I mentioned earlier, you start with the dam, and you work on out through the project acquiring what you need for specific project purposes, construction time that it's going to be filled with water and that sort of thing.
quotes.speaker: John Reed (Corps of Engineers, Pittsburgh District public relations)

quotes.text: We just didn't do a very good job of explaining the real estate process.
quotes.speaker: John Reed (Corps of Engineers, Pittsburgh District public relations)

quotes.text: So, I've spoken to the Corps of Engineers about the chance of an interim agricultural policy in which you permit haying to go on.
quotes.speaker: Bob Wise (U.S. Representative, WV)

cards.title: Grundy got a police door-knock hours before the 1977 crest
cards.place: Cow Town area and downtown Grundy, VA
cards.note: As recalled, police knocked about 4:30-5:00 a.m., water began coming heavy about 10:30-11:00 a.m., and the main high water was about 1:00-1:30 p.m. At a house near the river, the water went from a wet carpet to waist high within minutes.
cards.verify: Levisa Fork and Slate Creek gauge hydrographs for April 4, 1977; Grundy police and civil defense logs; Weather Service flood statements issued that morning
cards.ask_next: When the police came to your door that morning, what did they tell you to do, and how did they know the flood was coming?

quotes.text: Well, when I heard about it, the police came, and knocked on my back door and told me there was going to be a flood.
quotes.speaker: Harold Trivett (Grundy merchant, Family Shop)

quotes.text: Oh, about, I would say ten-thirty, eleven o'clock that way it started coming heavy.
quotes.speaker: Harold Trivett (Grundy merchant, Family Shop)

quotes.text: And, you know, it was just that quick. And then in a matter of minutes it was waist high.
quotes.speaker: Dorothy Trivett (Grundy resident, Cow Town area)

cards.title: Slate Creek bridge overtopped and town split into separate ends
cards.place: Slate Creek bridge, about a mile above Grundy, VA
cards.note: Water was almost a foot deep over a Slate Creek bridge when a council member drove home. The next morning he had to walk around the mountain to reach downtown. Another resident said no one could get from the lower end of Grundy to the upper end, and phones, power, water and sewer were all out.
cards.verify: VDOT bridge inventory and deck elevations for Slate Creek crossings; road closure records for Route 460 and Slate Creek road, April 1977
cards.ask_next: Which bridges or road sections cut Grundy into pieces first in 1977, and has anything been raised since?

quotes.text: And at the time that I went across the bridge the water was already about almost a foot deep going over the bridge.
quotes.speaker: Roger Powers (Grundy Town Council; Jackson Hardware family)

quotes.text: I couldn’t even go across the bridge to get downtown.
quotes.speaker: Roger Powers (Grundy Town Council; Jackson Hardware family)

quotes.text: When the water got up there was no way to come from the lower end of Grundy to the upper end of Grundy.
quotes.speaker: Chuck Crabtree (Grundy resident, business owner)

cards.title: Saturated hillside house slid within feet of neighbor
cards.place: Long Bottom, Slate Creek, near Grundy, VA
cards.note: A house built up the side of the mountain slid off after the rain, stopping about four or five feet from the narrator's house. His family left for two weeks even though floodwater never entered their home, so slides displaced people outside the flood zone.
cards.verify: Buchanan County building and damage records for Long Bottom; post-flood slide mapping or USGS landslide inventory for April 1977
cards.ask_next: Were homes built on cut slopes above Slate Creek ever inspected after 1977, and does the county limit building on those slopes now?

quotes.text: He had built it up the side of a mountain, and all the water and everything just loosened everything, and the house just slid off the mountain.
quotes.speaker: Roger Powers (Grundy Town Council; Jackson Hardware family)

quotes.text: It came within about four or five feet of coming down on top of my house.
quotes.speaker: Roger Powers (Grundy Town Council; Jackson Hardware family)

quotes.text: We did–actually I forgot to say we did have to move out of our house for two weeks because it wasn’t that the water got in it, but there was a mud slide on the home next door to me.
quotes.speaker: Roger Powers (Grundy Town Council; Jackson Hardware family)

cards.title: Slides kept coming off Brushy Run slopes after the flood
cards.place: Brushy Run near Wingo, Pendleton County, WV
cards.note: People walking out after the flood saw many fresh slides and chose routes above them, not below. The ground felt spongy for about a mile, and large slides in pasture had stopped partway down toward the run.
cards.verify: Post-1985 landslide inventories for Pendleton County (WVGES/USGS); aerial photos of Brushy Run from November 1985
cards.ask_next: After the flood, how did people decide which hillsides were safe to walk or rebuild under, and did anyone map the slides?

quotes.text: We saw so many floods, I mean, not floods, slides come down off the hill.
quotes.speaker: Helen Sites (Brushy Run resident)

quotes.text: All the way, the ground just felt like walking on a sponge.
quotes.speaker: Helen Sites (Brushy Run resident)

quotes.text: There was one slide after another in the pasture, great big ones.
quotes.speaker: Helen Sites (Brushy Run resident)

cards.title: Four Grundy buildings flood-proofed basements after 1977
cards.place: Trivett store (Family Shop), downtown Grundy, VA
cards.note: In 1977 a closed glass front door held water about a foot and a half higher outside than inside, but about two feet still got into the main floor. Afterward the owner sealed the basement windows and door, sloped the floor to a sump, and installed two electric pumps with a gasoline backup. He named only four flood-proofed buildings, and none had been tested by a flood.
cards.verify: Grundy building permits after 1977 for Jackson Hardware, Ben Franklin, Cumberland Bank and the Trivett building; Corps flood-proofing assessments for downtown Grundy
cards.ask_next: Has anyone checked whether the post-1977 flood-proofing on Main Street would hold at 1977 depths, and who maintains the pumps?

quotes.text: The water was a foot and a half higher outside than it was inside, but we still got about two feet of water in the main floor down there.
quotes.speaker: Harold Trivett (Grundy merchant, Family Shop)

quotes.text: We got two electric pumps, one gasoline pump as a backup.
quotes.speaker: Harold Trivett (Grundy merchant, Family Shop)

quotes.text: And that's not saying now that all of us that flood proofed are not vulnerable.
quotes.speaker: Harold Trivett (Grundy merchant, Family Shop)

cards.title: Route 460 right-of-way purchases covered Grundy's cost share
cards.place: Levisa Fork bend and old depot site, Grundy, VA
cards.note: As described, VDOT's land purchases for the four-lane Route 460 were credited as Grundy's local share of the Corps project. The raised highway would act as the levee, and businesses would move across the river to fill on the old depot site. The narrator said the town ran on a budget of about $1 million a year and could not have paid a $25-30 million share.
cards.verify: Corps Huntington District project cooperation agreement for Grundy; VDOT Route 460 acquisition records; the congressional authorization covering Grundy, Williamson and Matewan
cards.ask_next: How was the VDOT land credit written into the Corps agreement, and could another small town use the same arrangement?

quotes.text: when VDOT buys and has to do property acquisitions for the road, the federal government and the Corps of Engineers have agreed to let that acquisition be Grundy’s portion of the project.
quotes.speaker: Chuck Crabtree (Grundy resident, business owner)

quotes.text: It helps VDOT by having a place to put the four lane, and the four lane’s actually the levee.
quotes.speaker: Chuck Crabtree (Grundy resident, business owner)

quotes.text: VDOT always seemed reluctant to commit that kind of money in a lump sum.
quotes.speaker: Patrick Johnson (Grundy paralegal, later attorney)

cards.title: Cow Town houses sat below the road that flooded
cards.place: Cow Town area along Route 460, Grundy, VA
cards.note: Water ran two and a half to three feet deep on the road, as recalled, and houses below road grade flooded first. One owner warned that if the road project raises neighboring homes and hers cannot be raised, it will end up down in a hole.
cards.verify: Route 460 and Cow Town road profile versus first-floor elevations; the Corps/VDOT elevation and acquisition list for Cow Town
cards.ask_next: For homes that can't be raised when their neighbors are, what happens to drainage and access, and how is that handled in the plan?

quotes.text: Well, anyway, the water was running out on the road, two and a half, three feet deep in the road.
quotes.speaker: Harold Trivett (Grundy merchant, Family Shop)

quotes.text: Like on the other side of the road the houses were lower than the road. And they were the first ones hit.
quotes.speaker: Tim Potter (Grundy resident, age 11 in 1977)

quotes.text: But if they move everybody else up and we can it move ours up, we're going to be down in a hole, which won't be very good.
quotes.speaker: Dorothy Trivett (Grundy resident, Cow Town area)

cards.title: Neighbors rigged a rope line to hold a rowboat
cards.place: Trivett home on Route 460, Cow Town area, Grundy, VA
cards.note: The current was too swift for a rowboat. Neighbors across the street cast a line with a fishing rod, pulled a rope across, and tied it from the front door to a light pole. Two men held the boat along the rope to get the family out, though a short adult struggled to climb into it.
cards.verify: Grundy fire and rescue records for April 4, 1977; any other accounts of rope-guided boat rescues on Route 460
cards.ask_next: Who did the boat rescues on your street in 1977, and what gear did they have or wish they'd had?

quotes.text: And people across the street, they used a fishing rod, and they cast a line across with the rope and tied it to our front door and then to a light pole across the street. Because the water was too swift for the boat.
quotes.speaker: Dorothy Trivett (Grundy resident, Cow Town area)

quotes.text: And they held the boat with that rope.
quotes.speaker: Dorothy Trivett (Grundy resident, Cow Town area)

cards.title: Swift water and debris stopped a neighbor rope rescue
cards.place: Field below the Toth home, outside Parsons, WV
cards.note: Three neighbors in the only three life jackets tied themselves together to reach a family of six cut off in a field. Within ten to twenty feet the water went from waist to neck, and a log knocked one man under. They turned back, and a boat was unusable in the current and debris. The family survived in the attic.
cards.verify: Tucker County 911 and fire department logs for November 4, 1985; power company crew records for the lineman involved
cards.ask_next: When neighbors attempted water rescues that night, where did their gear come from, and did anyone know they were out there?

quotes.text: Well, the three of them had tied themselves together, the three that decided to go in the water put life jackets on.
quotes.speaker: Ruth Ann Toth (flood volunteer, later crisis outreach worker)

quotes.text: They only went ten, fifteen, twenty feet, and it had come up to their necks.
quotes.speaker: Ruth Ann Toth (flood volunteer, later crisis outreach worker)

quotes.text: The water was just so swift and there was so much debris coming out, they couldn't use the boat, even.
quotes.speaker: Ruth Ann Toth (flood volunteer, later crisis outreach worker)

cards.title: Stranded family's gunshot signals were mistaken for transformer blasts
cards.place: Field below the Toth home, outside Parsons, WV
cards.note: A family with no phone fired shots in sets of three every 15-20 minutes. Neighbors about 500 yards away thought they were transformers blowing, and no one recognized the signal until about 9:00 p.m. Isolated households need a distress signal people will recognize.
cards.verify: Neighbor and responder accounts; Tucker County dispatch logs for reports of gunfire or transformer explosions that evening
cards.ask_next: How would a household without a phone call for help in your area today, and do neighbors know what signal to listen for?

quotes.text: It was him firing a signal, trying to let people know that they were down there, because they don't have a phone or anything.
quotes.speaker: Ruth Ann Toth (flood volunteer, later crisis outreach worker)

quotes.text: the shots were going on right in front of their house all night, five hundred yards down over the hill.
quotes.speaker: Ruth Ann Toth (flood volunteer, later crisis outreach worker)

quotes.text: Because to me, it was transformers blowing up.
quotes.speaker: Ruth Ann Toth (flood volunteer, later crisis outreach worker)

cards.title: Lineworkers restored hospital, shelters, then outlying feeders first
cards.place: Parsons, WV, and lines toward Holly Meadows, St. George and Lead Mine
cards.note: With the bridge out, crews reached their trucks by detouring over the mountain. Power went first to the hospital, rescue squads and shelters such as the grade school and church. Next came lines serving many homes away from the river, because downtown would take weeks. The narrator's home had power back by Wednesday.
cards.verify: Monongahela Power restoration logs for Tucker County, November 1985; outage maps by circuit
cards.ask_next: Which buildings were on the utility's priority list in 1985, and is the shelter list shared with them before a flood?

quotes.text: I guess they got the hospital on first and the rescue squads, stuff like that, tried to get them power first, worked on that.
quotes.speaker: Ruth Ann Toth (flood volunteer, later crisis outreach worker)

quotes.text: It would take weeks to do downtown.
quotes.speaker: Ruth Ann Toth (flood volunteer, later crisis outreach worker)

quotes.text: They tried to pick up areas that weren't so highly affected with the water that were like us, back up way from the river and down St. George way, and along the highway and whatnot to fix stuff like that back up.
quotes.speaker: Ruth Ann Toth (flood volunteer, later crisis outreach worker)

cards.title: Hospitals and radio next door didn't know Parsons flooded
cards.place: Davis Memorial Hospital, Elkins, WV (receiving patients from Parsons)
cards.note: On Tuesday night a desk clerk at the Elkins hospital asked a patient's wife what flood she meant. Elkins and Clarksburg radio said nothing about a flood. A physician's husband driving home from Morgantown could only pick up WLS Chicago and spent 13 hours getting around blocked roads.
cards.verify: Elkins and Clarksburg station logs for November 4-5, 1985; EBS activation records; Davis Memorial Hospital admission logs
cards.ask_next: How did news of the Parsons flood first reach Elkins and the regional radio stations, and how long did it take?

quotes.text: Elkins Radio Station, Clarksburg, nobody said nothing about a flood.
quotes.speaker: Ruth Ann Toth (flood volunteer, later crisis outreach worker)

quotes.text: Elkins had no idea. It was Tuesday night, and they had very little word that – I guess maybe some people over there did, but the girl at the hospital had no idea it flooded over here at all.
quotes.speaker: Ruth Ann Toth (flood volunteer, later crisis outreach worker)

quotes.text: The only thing he could get was WLS out of Chicago.
quotes.speaker: Susan Schmitt (physician, St. George clinic)

cards.title: Shelter food lines learned to ask 'what can you cook in?'
cards.place: Parsons grade school soup kitchen and food distribution, Parsons, WV
cards.note: Volunteers found that people taking food had nothing to cook with, so they began asking and wished they had stocked no-cook food. A health officer had them keep cleaning supplies away from baby food and give out only sealed water, discarding donated well and spring water. On one day the site fed about 2,000 people.
cards.verify: Tucker County emergency services and Red Cross feeding counts, November 1985; county health department inspection notes for the grade school
cards.ask_next: What would you stock first in a flood food pantry now, and who checks food and water safety at volunteer sites?

quotes.text: I said, "What do you have to cook in?" We realized that we needed to start asking that.
quotes.speaker: Ruth Ann Toth (flood volunteer, later crisis outreach worker)

quotes.text: So, we had to take all the water we had that people brought in – from other areas, even – that was well water or spring water, and then just give out the bottled water from the mines and the Pepsi and anything – as long as it was sealed, we were all right.
quotes.speaker: Ruth Ann Toth (flood volunteer, later crisis outreach worker)

quotes.text: Then one day, they fed two thousand people.
quotes.speaker: Ruth Ann Toth (flood volunteer, later crisis outreach worker)

cards.title: Roadside farmhouse sheltered about nineteen stranded travelers overnight
cards.place: Nestor farm near the round barn, road from Parsons toward Elkins, WV
cards.note: With the road toward Elkins blocked near the round barn, about nineteen people spent the night at one farmhouse. Some stayed two nights, and a few slept in their cars. Guests called home on the house phone before it failed, so their families knew where they were.
cards.verify: WV DOH closure records for the Parsons-Elkins route (US 219) on November 4-5, 1985; location of the round barn relative to the flooded section
cards.ask_next: Where do travelers end up when the Parsons-Elkins road closes, and are those homes or churches known to the county as informal shelters?

quotes.text: Well, they could go to that house down there just around that turn, and they couldn't get through back toward Elkins, that round barn.
quotes.speaker: Edith Nestor (farm resident on road toward Elkins)

quotes.text: I think there were about nineteen stayed all night.
quotes.speaker: Edith Nestor (farm resident on road toward Elkins)

quotes.text: Everybody, I think, got to call home to tell them where they were.
quotes.speaker: Edith Nestor (farm resident on road toward Elkins)

cards.title: St. George housed everyone within two nights with outside help
cards.place: St. George, Tucker County, WV
cards.note: The small community organized itself. Everyone displaced had a place to stay by the second or third night, mostly doubled up in homes. A sanitation engineer helped, water came from Grafton and down the mountain, Grafton's fire department brought portable toilets, and the utility dug garbage pits. The narrator said larger Parsons had more infighting.
cards.verify: Tucker County EOC records; Grafton fire department mutual-aid logs; VEPCO assistance records, November 1985
cards.ask_next: Who coordinated water, sanitation and garbage in St. George that first week, and is that arrangement written down anywhere?

quotes.text: By the second or third night, there was no one in this area who didn't have a home.
quotes.speaker: Susan Schmitt (physician, St. George clinic)

quotes.text: We had fresh water brought down the mountain. Water was brought in from Grafton.
quotes.speaker: Susan Schmitt (physician, St. George clinic)

quotes.text: VEPCO helped with heavy equipment to dig pits for the garbage.
quotes.speaker: Susan Schmitt (physician, St. George clinic)

cards.title: Creek rose eight inches in fifteen minutes before bridge loss
cards.place: Bull Run near St. George, Tucker County, WV
cards.note: A babysitter reported the creek up eight inches in fifteen minutes and drove a child to safety. About half an hour later her bridge was gone and she was cut off for three days. Others had dismissed it as just rain.
cards.verify: Cheat River / Shavers Fork gauge rise rates near St. George on November 4, 1985; county records of private bridges lost on Bull Run
cards.ask_next: How many families on Bull Run depend on one private bridge, and how were they reached after it went out?

quotes.text: The river has come up eight inches in the last fifteen minutes and I think my bridge is going to wash off.
quotes.speaker: Susan Schmitt (physician, St. George clinic)

quotes.text: But she brought my daughter here, dropped her off, went back home again, and half hour later, her bridge was gone.
quotes.speaker: Susan Schmitt (physician, St. George clinic)

quotes.text: She was cut off for three days.
quotes.speaker: Susan Schmitt (physician, St. George clinic)

cards.title: Parsons could have warned Preston County hours ahead
cards.place: Parsons, WV, and downstream Preston County, WV
cards.note: A Parsons emergency volunteer said that, looking back, Parsons could have given downstream Preston County about six hours of warning, as he estimated. He believed they would be better prepared to warn people next time.
cards.verify: Cheat River gauge crest timing at Parsons versus Rowlesburg, November 1985; Tucker-to-Preston County dispatch logs
cards.ask_next: Is there now a set call from Tucker County to Preston County when the river is rising at Parsons, and who makes it?

quotes.text: But looking back on it, hell, we could have warned them people in Preston County and given them six hours to take care of ourselves.
quotes.speaker: Forest Blume (Parsons emergency volunteer)

quotes.text: But I believe if it ever happened again, which I hope to God never happens in my lifetime, but I believe we would be a little better prepared to warn people and try to do the right thing.
quotes.speaker: Forest Blume (Parsons emergency volunteer)

cards.title: Firefighters trapped at Hendricks tracked the flood by stair steps
cards.place: Russell Hebb house, Hendricks, Tucker County, WV
cards.note: Two firefighters reached an elderly couple, and with others eight people ended up trapped in the house. A rope line from rescuers across the street was torn away by a floating building, so they rode out the night upstairs, judging rise and fall by the 15-step staircase. The next morning rescuers ran a guide rope with a boat. A crevice they crossed was deeper than a room, and the narrator believed a night attempt would have failed.
cards.verify: Parsons and Hendricks fire department run reports; Tucker County dispatch log (which also told a spouse at 9:30 p.m. that the house had washed away)
cards.ask_next: What rope, boat and lighting gear did the Hendricks and Parsons crews have that night, and what was added afterward?

quotes.text: But then another building came down and hit our rope and got all tangled up.
quotes.speaker: Hank Thompson (law officer and volunteer firefighter)

quotes.text: There were fifteen steps in the house and the water was on the thirteenth step when it started going down.
quotes.speaker: Hank Thompson (law officer and volunteer firefighter)

quotes.text: But when we went across there was a crevice deeper than this room here, If we would have tried to get out at night we never would have made it.
quotes.speaker: Hank Thompson (law officer and volunteer firefighter)

cards.title: Vacated homes were stripped by looters within hours
cards.place: Little Skin Creek, Stonewall Jackson Dam project area, Lewis County, WV
cards.note: As people left acquired homes, looters stripped empty houses overnight, taking wiring, meter boxes and water lines. The sheriff could pass a remaining resident only once a night. After the 1985 flood on Brushy Run, residents also found footprints inside damaged trailers. Buyout and evacuated areas need a security plan.
cards.verify: Lewis County sheriff incident reports, 1979-1981; Corps real estate files on property condition at acquisition
cards.ask_next: When people move out under a buyout here, who secures the empty houses until demolition, and how quickly are they taken down?

quotes.text: Just as soon as people started moving away.
quotes.speaker: Edith Bell Holden (displaced Little Skin Creek landowner)

quotes.text: We can only come by here once tonight.
quotes.speaker: Edith Bell Holden (displaced Little Skin Creek landowner)

quotes.text: I mean, you go back and all your electric wire was gone, your meter boxes, everything.
quotes.speaker: Edith Bell Holden (displaced Little Skin Creek landowner)

cards.title: Displaced owners had to move before final compensation was known
cards.place: Stonewall Jackson Dam project area, Lewis County, WV
cards.note: As described, condemned owners had to leave on the Corps' schedule even before condemnation trials set the final amount, which was often higher than the first offer. Fair market value paid nothing extra for free gas, minerals or timber. Several narrators said the payment did not cover replacing a farm.
cards.verify: Corps Pittsburgh/Huntington District acquisition files and federal court condemnation awards (N.D. W.Va., Elkins) compared with initial offers
cards.ask_next: In a buyout here, when do owners learn the final amount compared with their move-out date, and what counts toward the value?

quotes.text: So, you don't have any idea until that point how much money you have to get another place.
quotes.speaker: Francine Snyder (dam opponent, watershed association)

quotes.text: If you have free gas, you don't get compensated extra for a lifetime worth of free gas.
quotes.speaker: Francine Snyder (dam opponent, watershed association)

quotes.text: We had mineral rights and coal, timber. We didn't get anything for that.
quotes.speaker: Edith Bell Holden (displaced Little Skin Creek landowner)

cards.title: FEMA trailer on private lot required owner-built septic and utilities
cards.place: Private lot by Priscilla Teter's garage, Pendleton County, WV
cards.note: A survivor who didn't want to go to the group trailer park was told she had to put in her own septic, water and electric before FEMA would deliver a trailer to a private lot. A nearby unit had been tied into a relative's septic, which she said was not legal. She also said survivors had no ID for flood tax relief, unlike Preston County.
cards.verify: FEMA temporary housing site inspection records for Pendleton County; county health department septic permits, 1985-86
cards.ask_next: When FEMA trailers went onto private lots here, who checked the septic and floodplain location, and were permits issued?

quotes.text: I'd have to put my own septic and my own water lines and electric.
quotes.speaker: Helen Sites (Brushy Run resident)

quotes.text: They had put in the drain lines and put the septic into his son's septic, which is not legal.
quotes.speaker: Helen Sites (Brushy Run resident)

quotes.text: In Preston County, they have IDs.
quotes.speaker: Helen Sites (Brushy Run resident)

cards.title: Brushy Run rose and fell, then surged after dark
cards.place: Brushy Run near Wingo, Pendleton County, WV
cards.note: As recalled, the water rose and fell all afternoon, a hillside stream was too high to cross by 2:00 p.m., and water came under a trailer at 3:30. A gush hit the house at about 4:30. Around 10:15-10:30 p.m. a roaring surge took part of the schoolhouse and several houses, including one hit by a floating trailer.
cards.verify: South Branch / North Fork gauge records for November 4, 1985; damage survey of Brushy Run schoolhouse and homes
cards.ask_next: Was there a second, later surge on your creek that night, and do people there know to stay out after the first crest passes?

quotes.text: Then it would go down, up and down all afternoon.
quotes.speaker: Helen Sites (Brushy Run resident)

quotes.text: When I looked out, I could see nothing but a big gush of water coming right at the house.
quotes.speaker: Helen Sites (Brushy Run resident)

quotes.text: It was around, I'd say, quarter after 10 or 10:30 p.m. We heard this awful noise.
quotes.speaker: Helen Sites (Brushy Run resident)

cards.title: Grundy neighborhood shared one well by hose during outage
cards.place: Cow Town area, Grundy, VA
cards.note: Town water was off for a while, and some homes went without power for at least three weeks, as recalled. Once power returned, one family's pumped private well supplied cleanup water to the whole street through hoses joined end to end. Drinking water was bottled.
cards.verify: Appalachian Power restoration records for Grundy, April 1977; Grundy water system outage records
cards.ask_next: How long were Grundy's water and power out in 1977 by neighborhood, and what private water sources did people rely on?

quotes.text: It took, I'd say at least three weeks before we got any power back for our homes where I live at.
quotes.speaker: Tim Potter (Grundy resident, age 11 in 1977)

quotes.text: The water hose ended up going from one end of the neighborhood to the other end.
quotes.speaker: Dorothy Trivett (Grundy resident, Cow Town area)

cards.title: Repeat flooding weeks later drove older residents away from St. George
cards.place: St. George and Pulp Mill Bottom, Tucker County, WV
cards.note: Water came up again at Thanksgiving and once more in February, flooding some homes that had just been cleaned out. The local doctor said many older residents left with family, so mostly younger households remained. People were reconsidering rebuilding in low areas such as Pulp Mill Bottom.
cards.verify: Cheat River gauge at Parsons for late November 1985 and February 1986; Tucker County rebuilding permits and buyout records for St. George and Pulp Mill Bottom
cards.ask_next: How many St. George households rebuilt in place after 1985, and did the second and third floods change who came back?

quotes.text: A lot of people took water again just last week when the river came up.
quotes.speaker: Susan Schmitt (physician, St. George clinic)

quotes.text: St. George is almost gone because it was largely elderly people whose families came and got them.
quotes.speaker: Susan Schmitt (physician, St. George clinic)

quotes.text: I sure wouldn't buy a house in the Pulp Mill Bottom, even if it was cheap.
quotes.speaker: Susan Schmitt (physician, St. George clinic)

cards.title: Parsons chief reported flood stage with no flood watch issued
cards.place: Parsons fire hall and Hendricks, Tucker County, WV
cards.note: A junior firefighter heard the Parsons chief call Elkins to report flood stage, and Elkins said no flood watch was out. The transcript does not say which agency in Elkins took the call.
cards.verify: NWS watch/warning issuance times for Tucker County on Nov 4, 1985; Parsons VFD and county dispatch logs; whoever answered the call in Elkins
cards.ask_next: Who did the chief call in Elkins that evening, what time was it, and when did a watch or warning finally reach you?

quotes.text: He called Elkins and told him it was a flood stage.
quotes.speaker: Michael Parsons (junior firefighter, Parsons VFD)

quotes.text: They told him that they didn't understand why we were at flood stage because we didn't even have a flood watch out, that we weren't even supposed to be flooding.
quotes.speaker: Michael Parsons (junior firefighter, Parsons VFD)

cards.title: Boats, ropes and a loader all failed to reach Hendricks
cards.place: Lower street near Blackwater-Dry Fork confluence, Hendricks, WV
cards.note: Small boats with 10-horsepower motors were holed and fouled in wire, a rope line across the street was torn away by a floating rooftop, and a front-end loader got stuck in a scour hole. Rescuers who went in became trapped themselves until daylight.
cards.verify: Parsons VFD after-action notes; equipment loss records; photos of the Hendricks street scour
cards.ask_next: What boats, motors and equipment did the department have that night, and what would you want staged before the next one?

quotes.text: We got down there and knocked a hole in the bottom of the boat. We got the motor tangled up in wire and everything else.
quotes.speaker: Michael Parsons (junior firefighter, Parsons VFD)

quotes.text: About that time, a rooftop came down the middle of the street and took the rope, jerked the post off the porch, took whatever they had tied to, took everything, and threw it down this river.
quotes.speaker: Michael Parsons (junior firefighter, Parsons VFD)

quotes.text: Then the next thing I know, they got hung up in a big hole, and they couldn't get into us.
quotes.speaker: Hank Thompson (Parsons firefighter)

cards.title: Dispatch did not know who was trapped in which house
cards.place: Hendricks, WV
cards.note: Eight people in one house and two firefighters across the street were treated as one party; families were told there was no hope. Phones worked on and off, and people kept contact all night by flashlight with a firefighter parked on the railroad tracks.
cards.verify: Tucker County dispatch log for Nov 4-5, 1985; phone company outage records
cards.ask_next: How did dispatch track who was where that night, and what would a written accountability board have changed?

quotes.text: But they had no idea that Jim and I and six other guys was in the house right directly across the street from them.
quotes.speaker: Hank Thompson (Parsons firefighter)

quotes.text: With the communications problem, they didn't know we were there.
quotes.speaker: Hank Thompson (Parsons firefighter)

quotes.text: I'd take my light about every half hour or so. I'd signal him.
quotes.speaker: Hank Thompson (Parsons firefighter)

cards.title: Hendricks water reached thirteenth stair, 1.5 feet below roofline
cards.place: Two houses on the lower street, Hendricks, WV
cards.note: Trapped groups measured the flood by counting stair steps; one two-story house filled to within about 1.5 feet of the top story, as recalled. The road between the houses was later said to be scoured 18-20 feet deep.
cards.verify: USGS post-flood high-water mark survey at Hendricks; photos of the two houses; road repair records
cards.ask_next: Which houses were these, and is there a mark or photo showing where the water stopped on the stairs?

quotes.text: I know the water was on the thirteenth step.
quotes.speaker: Hank Thompson (Parsons firefighter)

quotes.text: It got within about 1.5 feet of the top story of the house. It was a two-story house.
quotes.speaker: Michael Parsons (junior firefighter, Parsons VFD)

quotes.text: It was supposed to go up between 18 and 20 feet deep in the road between the two houses, the house we were in and the house they were in, washed all that out, just like a canal.
quotes.speaker: Michael Parsons (junior firefighter, Parsons VFD)

cards.title: Water rose about a foot every few minutes after dark
cards.place: Hendricks and Elk Lick bottom, Tucker County, WV
cards.note: Narrators recall the water going from about 2 feet on a first floor to nearly overhead in the time it took to check a phone, and a dry barnyard flooded within 15 minutes around 6:00-6:30 p.m. All rates are as recalled.
cards.verify: Gauge records on Dry Fork and Blackwater near Hendricks (if any survived); USGS indirect peak estimates
cards.ask_next: What times do you remember for when the water first crossed the road and when it was over the porch?

quotes.text: By the time we got back outside, it was clear up, almost over your head right in the house. That's how fast it rose.
quotes.speaker: Michael Parsons (junior firefighter, Parsons VFD)

quotes.text: It wasn't over fifteen minutes until the water went to pouring through there, and there wasn't any coming through whenever I left the barn.
quotes.speaker: Norman Long

cards.title: Residents stayed put expecting only minor water
cards.place: Hendricks; St. George; Pennsylvania Avenue, Parsons, WV
cards.note: Door-to-door warnings were ignored or refused because people judged by past floods; some acted as if not home. Several who stayed expected a little clean water on the floor, not four feet of debris-laden current.
cards.verify: Fire department evacuation records; Red Cross shelter rosters; rescue call logs for St. George and Parsons
cards.ask_next: When someone refused to leave that night, what did you say or do, and what would have changed their mind?

quotes.text: They'd turn off their lights and act like they weren't home.
quotes.speaker: Michael Parsons (junior firefighter, Parsons VFD)

quotes.text: Well, about 5:00, the boys came over and wanted us to leave with them. He said, no, it wasn't going to be that bad.
quotes.speaker: Thelma Lipscomb (St. George)

quotes.text: But we weren't prepared for the four feet of water with trees and everything else churning and destroying our furniture.
quotes.speaker: Arlene Brock (Pennsylvania Ave., Parsons)

cards.title: Firemen gave a four-minute order: medicine, pocketbook, nightclothes
cards.place: Kathleen Hall home, Parsons, WV
cards.note: A 73-year-old resident who had never left her home in a flood was given four minutes and a short list of what to grab, then physically carried down the stairs when she moved too slowly.
cards.verify: Parsons VFD evacuation roster; shelter intake records
cards.ask_next: What list did firefighters give people at the door, and who decided on it?

quotes.text: If you have medicine, get your medicine, and get your pocketbook. Don't bother about anything else because you don't have time.
quotes.speaker: Kathleen Hall (Parsons resident)

quotes.text: I said, "I've never left my home. I've never had to leave my home."
quotes.speaker: Kathleen Hall (Parsons resident)

cards.title: Resident read river rise from fence posts in her field
cards.place: Sampson home on the riverbank, St. George, WV
cards.note: One resident used a row of fence posts in the field as her guide that the river was all right, but the water still reached the road before her basement took any.
cards.verify: Field photos of the Sampson fence line; Cheat River gauge records for the afternoon of Nov 4
cards.ask_next: What local marker did you use to judge the river, and at what point did it stop being reliable?

quotes.text: That was my guideline of how I could tell that the river was all right.
quotes.speaker: Victoria (Icy) Shahan Sampson (St. George)

quotes.text: I guess it had risen so fast that it hadn't had time to seep in there.
quotes.speaker: Victoria (Icy) Shahan Sampson (St. George)

cards.title: Pennsylvania Avenue flooded from the slough, not the river
cards.place: Pennsylvania Avenue near the Black Fork, Parsons, WV
cards.note: Residents watching the river across the road were surprised when water arrived knee-high across the lawn from the slough side, after taking out the nursery bottom and railroad tracks. Watching the main channel was not enough here.
cards.verify: FIRM and post-flood inundation maps for Parsons; railroad damage reports; aerial photos of the slough
cards.ask_next: Where did the water first come onto Pennsylvania Avenue, and does the slough still carry overflow today?

quotes.text: Then I looked out the window and the water were up knee high, just raging through the lawn from across the slough, not the river where it normally would've come up.
quotes.speaker: Arlene Brock (Pennsylvania Ave., Parsons)

quotes.text: It took the nursery bottom before it even got to us.
quotes.speaker: Arlene Brock (Pennsylvania Ave., Parsons)

quotes.text: Washed the railroad tracks away too, you know.
quotes.speaker: Charles Brock (retired DNR wildlife manager)

cards.title: Opened doors to let floodwater pass through the house
cards.place: Brock home, Pennsylvania Avenue, Parsons, WV
cards.note: Trapped residents propped the front French doors open so water could flow out, having heard not to let pressure build. They said a closed bathroom held water about a foot deeper; this is their observation, not a tested claim.
cards.verify: Interior mud lines in the Brock house; structural damage inspection notes
cards.ask_next: Did the houses where doors were left open stay on their foundations more often than closed-up ones on your street?

quotes.text: Someone said not to let pressure build up in your home.
quotes.speaker: Arlene Brock (Pennsylvania Ave., Parsons)

quotes.text: Because the bathroom had got at least a foot deeper where we didn't have the door open.
quotes.speaker: Charles Brock (retired DNR wildlife manager)

cards.title: Water fell 18 inches in half an hour after 2:30 a.m.
cards.place: Pennsylvania Avenue, Parsons; St. George; Hendricks, WV
cards.note: Narrators in three towns recall a fast recession in the early morning: Parsons dropped 6 inches then 18 more within half an hour from about 2:30 a.m.; St. George began falling about 3:00 a.m. Times and amounts are as recalled.
cards.verify: USGS Cheat River and Black Fork hydrographs for Nov 5, 1985
cards.ask_next: When the water started falling, how long before people could safely walk out, and did anyone go back in too early?

quotes.text: So, then the waters began to recede about 2:30 a.m.
quotes.speaker: Arlene Brock (Pennsylvania Ave., Parsons)

quotes.text: Then within a half an hour, it was down eighteen more inches.
quotes.speaker: Arlene Brock (Pennsylvania Ave., Parsons)

cards.title: St. George water ran 16 feet above 1957 yard level
cards.place: Lipscomb home, St. George, WV
cards.note: The narrator says the 1888 and 1957 floods only reached his yard, while 1985 put 16 feet of water outside and 4 feet on his second floor, as recalled. His house is about a quarter mile from the channel.
cards.verify: USGS high-water mark survey at St. George; any 1957 flood photos or newspaper accounts of St. George
cards.ask_next: Where exactly did the 1957 water stop in your yard, and is there a photo or mark of it?

quotes.text: In 1957, they had another flood, and it got up in the yard. This thing was 16-foot above all of that.
quotes.speaker: Vittie Lipscomb (St. George)

quotes.text: I had 4-foot of water in my upstairs, 16-foot of water right out here.
quotes.speaker: Vittie Lipscomb (St. George)

cards.title: Elk Lick house 30-40 feet above river still flooded
cards.place: Long farm near Elk Lick, across the river from Hendricks, WV
cards.note: The 1954 flood covered the bottoms but stayed below the pine trees in front of the house; the narrators estimate the house sits 30-40 feet above river level and about 300 feet away, yet 1985 water came through it. Elevations are their estimates.
cards.verify: Survey elevation of the Long house relative to the Dry Fork channel; 1954 flood records for Hendricks
cards.ask_next: Can we survey the house floor and the 1954 line so we know how much higher 1985 really was?

quotes.text: But even in [19]54, it didn't come above the pine trees that stood in front of our house.
quotes.speaker: Cleta Long

quotes.text: We were probably 30 feet above the river level. Yes. At least 30, maybe 40 feet above the river level.
quotes.speaker: Cleta Long

cards.title: Elk Lick families chose to be flooded in, not out
cards.place: Elk Lick road and bridge, near Hendricks, WV
cards.note: The road at Elk Lick went under three or four times a year and washed out the bridge, so the household stocked up and went home whenever the river rose. That habit, built on past floods, kept them at home when the 1985 water exceeded anything they had seen.
cards.verify: County road closure and bridge repair records for Elk Lick
cards.ask_next: How many other households along roads that flood often follow the same stock-up-and-stay habit?

quotes.text: Because the water came over the road down at Elk Lick three, four times a year and would wash out the bridge.
quotes.speaker: Cleta Long

quotes.text: We would rather be caught in than caught out because at least if we were in, we knew the water wasn't going to come in our house.
quotes.speaker: Cleta Long

cards.title: Small runs became impassable torrents during self-evacuation
cards.place: Reservoir Hollow and Rebel Run, near Hendricks, WV
cards.note: Fleeing on foot, a couple found normally tiny runs 12-15 feet wide and fast enough to knock an adult down; they could see a lit house but could not cross and spent the night under a fodder shock. Evacuation routes on foot cross tributaries that rise too.
cards.verify: Culvert sizes and post-flood damage at Reservoir Hollow and Rebel Run
cards.ask_next: Which small runs cut people off from high ground that night, and are there safe crossing points now?

quotes.text: When we got to Reservoir Hollow, which is normally a little stream that goes through a small culvert, it was really wide.
quotes.speaker: Cleta Long

quotes.text: But it's usually, oh, 2, 3 foot wide at the most. That night it was about 12 or 15 feet wide.
quotes.speaker: Cleta Long

cards.title: Trees beside houses caught debris and saved them
cards.place: Long farm near Elk Lick; Shahan home, St. George, WV
cards.note: Big pines the Longs had planned to cut down caught debris and broke the current, and their house was the only building left. In St. George a house that floated off its foundation lodged between trees instead of washing away.
cards.verify: Post-flood photos of surviving structures and adjacent trees in Hendricks and St. George
cards.ask_next: Which houses that survived had big trees or other buildings on their upstream side?

quotes.text: So, we were going to have them cut down. They were the only thing that saved the house.
quotes.speaker: Cleta Long

quotes.text: But those trees caught all that debris and broke the water from the house.
quotes.speaker: Cleta Long

quotes.text: If it had not caught in those trees, it would have washed completely away.
quotes.speaker: Victoria (Icy) Shahan Sampson (St. George)

cards.title: Dozer logging roads make Elk Lick run off faster
cards.place: Elk Lick and Fernow Experimental Forest, near Parsons, WV
cards.note: A man who built logging roads for the Forest Service for 32 years says dozer roads now carry water off and Elk Lick rises and drops faster than when logging was done with horses. His wife heard the Fernow lab clocked the river near 40 mph, which is hearsay.
cards.verify: Fernow Experimental Forest streamflow and road-density records; any velocity measurements made by the timber and watershed lab in Nov 1985
cards.ask_next: Did the Fernow lab measure flows or velocities that night, and have stream responses changed since the road network grew?

quotes.text: These roads are what's carrying the water off.
quotes.speaker: Norman Long (retired Forest Service woods worker)

quotes.text: Now it looks raised and it goes clean and dry, then the water just runs off as fast as it comes.
quotes.speaker: Norman Long (retired Forest Service woods worker)

quotes.text: Someone said that they clocked the river at one point when they could get down to it going 40 miles an hour.
quotes.speaker: Cleta Long

cards.title: New channel through the bottom washed the rebuilt road again
cards.place: Long farm road, Elk Lick bottom near Hendricks, WV
cards.note: After the flood, sand filled the river at the head of the bottom and the water took a new straight course; a road rebuilt with culverts washed out after two days, on a much smaller rise.
cards.verify: Before/after aerial photos of the Dry Fork at Elk Lick; county road work orders
cards.ask_next: Since the flood, how small a rise now puts water across that bottom and road?

quotes.text: We'd only had a road for two days when it came up and washed it out again.
quotes.speaker: Cleta Long

quotes.text: It doesn't even have to raise all that much now to come down through.
quotes.speaker: Cleta Long

quotes.text: It just filled a mouth of Green Hole up there, the entrance where it goes out, and pushed it down through the bottom.
quotes.speaker: Norman Long (retired Forest Service woods worker)

cards.title: FEMA minimal-repair award cited a well the house lacked
cards.place: Long home near Elk Lick, Hendricks, WV
cards.note: The household received a $1,200 minimal repair letter earmarked for items like a pump and well they do not have; the inspector reached the house on a path they had just bulldozed and did not go inside.
cards.verify: FEMA inspection report for the property from the November 1985 West Virginia disaster
cards.ask_next: How were inspections done for houses with no road access, and how did people get errors corrected?

quotes.text: Then we got a letter from FEMA saying that we were eligible for $1,200 in minimal repair [laughter] so that we could get back in our house.
quotes.speaker: Cleta Long

quotes.text: We don't even have a pump or a well.
quotes.speaker: Cleta Long

quotes.text: I said, "Well, he certainly wasn't in the house because the house was locked up."
quotes.speaker: Cleta Long

cards.title: FEMA trailer placement on own lot took a governor's order
cards.place: Lipscomb lot, St. George, WV
cards.note: A couple with utilities intact on their own acre were offered only group trailer sites on Blackman Flats or Quality Hill, where they would have had to give up pets. They got a trailer on their lot only after confronting the governor; their wrecked house resting on a neighbor's well also blocked the neighbor's trailer.
cards.verify: FEMA temporary housing placement records for Tucker County; group site rules on pets
cards.ask_next: How were private-lot versus group-site trailer decisions made, and what happened to people with pets?

quotes.text: They'd let me have a trailer, but I'd have to go up to Blackman Flats or I'd have to go up on Quality Hill.
quotes.speaker: Vittie Lipscomb (St. George)

quotes.text: Well, we didn't want to go up to where they wanted to put these trailers because we'd had to give up our pets.
quotes.speaker: Thelma Lipscomb (St. George)

quotes.text: Well, the FEMA people said they wouldn't set him a trailer with my house on the well.
quotes.speaker: Vittie Lipscomb (St. George)

cards.title: Floodwater got inside sealed cans and into private wells
cards.place: St. George, WV; mouth of Looney's Creek near Grundy, VA
cards.note: Narrators found mud inside home-canned jars and commercial bottles that stayed sealed, freezers flipped and spilled, and in 1977 flooded wells had to be redrilled. Health bulletins told people not to use flooded canned goods.
cards.verify: WV and VA health department flood bulletins; well testing records after both floods
cards.ask_next: How many private wells were tested or redrilled after the flood, and who paid for it?

quotes.text: Yes, they had all kinds of bulletins out to don't use your canned stuff once it was flooded.
quotes.speaker: Vittie Lipscomb (St. George)

quotes.text: There would be mud inside that can on top of the fruit and vegetables.
quotes.speaker: Thelma Lipscomb (St. George)

quotes.text: As a matter of fact, my father had to redrill a well, because our well was contaminated.
quotes.speaker: Tim Potter (Town of Grundy personnel director)

cards.title: Flood insurance purchase deadline and paperwork stalled aid
cards.place: Parsons and St. George, Tucker County, WV
cards.note: One survivor was told a $5,000 payment depended on flood insurance she had to buy within a set number of days, then was told she had not bought it and had to hunt for proof. A farmer had only fire and lightning coverage and lost all barns and machinery.
cards.verify: NFIP policy counts in Tucker County before and after Nov 1985; IFG grant flood insurance requirement records
cards.ask_next: How many people were required to buy flood insurance as a condition of aid, and how many still carry it?

quotes.text: They said I hadn't taken it out. Only they only gave me so many days take it out and I took it out in January.
quotes.speaker: Kathleen Hall (Parsons resident)

quotes.text: I had fire insurance, lightning [laughter] and fire, but that's all. No flood, had the wrong kind that time?
quotes.speaker: John Anvill (St. George farmer)

cards.title: Older survivors lacked help for repairs months later
cards.place: Hendricks and Parsons, WV
cards.note: A volunteer helping a 76-year-old uncle rebuild said older people had no one to help or talk to; a hired helper took money and left. Mental health workers reported elderly survivors hit especially hard.
cards.verify: Crisis counseling program records; volunteer repair program rosters for Tucker County
cards.ask_next: Which older households were still without repairs in spring 1986, and who was checking on them?

quotes.text: But the old people like that, they don't have nobody to help them and don't have nobody to talk to them how they're feeling about it.
quotes.speaker: Danny Hebb (Hendricks resident)

quotes.text: He had my uncle to give him some money. Then he left and never come back.
quotes.speaker: Danny Hebb (Hendricks resident)

quotes.text: Well, I talked with Mental Health about that, and they said they had some of the elderly that were affected very much by it.
quotes.speaker: Arlene Brock (Pennsylvania Ave., Parsons)

cards.title: Ham radio was Grundy's only outside link overnight
cards.place: Grundy, Buchanan County, VA
cards.note: With power and phones gone, a local ham operator talked to Bluefield all night and that link brought National Guard supplies the next morning; helicopters were the only other way to get word in or out.
cards.verify: ARRL or local ham club records for April 1977; National Guard mobilization logs
cards.ask_next: Who were the ham operators in the county then, and is there a ham net in the plan today?

quotes.text: So that night he became our only communication link between Buchanan County and the outside world.
quotes.speaker: Ronald Cole (operations manager, WNRG radio, Grundy)

quotes.text: The helicopters were, outside of Gary's ham radio, were the only way that we could get word in or out to anybody.
quotes.speaker: Ronald Cole (operations manager, WNRG radio, Grundy)

cards.title: Grundy substation undermined about 4 p.m.; power out days
cards.place: Appalachian Power substation and Grundy, VA
cards.note: As recalled, water reached the substation about 4 p.m. and undermined the ground until transformers fell; one phone line to Bluefield was restored by the end of the next day and regular power took three or four days.
cards.verify: Appalachian Power outage and restoration records, April 1977; General Telephone restoration logs
cards.ask_next: Has that substation been moved or raised since 1977?

quotes.text: And just shortly after that the ground under them was undermined sufficiently so that the transformers began to fall over.
quotes.speaker: Ronald Cole (operations manager, WNRG radio, Grundy)

quotes.text: And by the end of that day they had a phone line, one phone line was open out of Buchanan County back to Bluefield.
quotes.speaker: Ronald Cole (operations manager, WNRG radio, Grundy)

cards.title: Coal company crews reopened undermined U.S. 460 before the state
cards.place: U.S. 460 about two miles west of Grundy, VA
cards.note: A section of U.S. 460 fell into the river; United Coal crews drilled and shot a cliff and dozed a bypass within days, faster than state crews could arrive. Private heavy equipment was the fastest access restoration.
cards.verify: VDOT damage and repair records for U.S. 460, April 1977; any mutual aid agreements with coal operators
cards.ask_next: Is there a standing agreement with private heavy-equipment owners to reopen roads after a flood?

quotes.text: There was one point about two miles west of town where U.S. 460 had been undermined.
quotes.speaker: Ronald Cole (operations manager, WNRG radio, Grundy)

quotes.text: Well, the next day, or the next three or four days, United had their crew down there with the rock drills and so on, and they drilled and shot this huge cliff and overhang and pulled it out of the way, then used their dozers and made a road around that spot.
quotes.speaker: Ronald Cole (operations manager, WNRG radio, Grundy)

quotes.text: There's no way the State could have gotten these roads opened up as quick as they did.
quotes.speaker: Tim Potter (Town of Grundy personnel director)

cards.title: Grundy hospital moved patients upstairs; 80 sheltered in courthouse
cards.place: Buchanan Hospital and Buchanan County Courthouse, Grundy, VA
cards.note: With water in the basement and first floor, the hospital ran on generators and moved emergency patients to the third and fourth floors. About 80 people, as recalled, spent the night on the courthouse third floor.
cards.verify: Hospital incident records; county shelter records for April 1977
cards.ask_next: Is the courthouse still a designated shelter, and where would hospital patients go now?

quotes.text: So they had to move all their emergency patients to the third and fourth floor, trying to stay ahead of the water.
quotes.speaker: Ronald Cole (operations manager, WNRG radio, Grundy)

quotes.text: As I got closer I learned that as many as, I think, eighty people had taken refuge in the courthouse, in the Buchanan County Courthouse, and spent the night up there on the third floor sleeping on benches in the courtroom and finding shelter as best they could.
quotes.speaker: Ronald Cole (operations manager, WNRG radio, Grundy)

cards.title: Debris blocked Looney's Creek culvert; two feet in minutes
cards.place: Mouth of Looney's Creek, west of Grundy, VA
cards.note: With Looney's Creek already at road level and the river high, debris plugged the culvert under the road and water went from none to two feet over the road in 15-20 minutes, as recalled.
cards.verify: VDOT culvert inventory for Looney's Creek at U.S. 460; photos from April 1977
cards.ask_next: Has the Looney's Creek culvert been enlarged or replaced since 1977?

quotes.text: And the next thing you know, here comes a lot of debris down the road, and it blocked off that culvert.
quotes.speaker: Tim Potter (Town of Grundy personnel director)

quotes.text: Within fifteen, twenty minutes we went from no water, to six inches of water, to two foot of water coming over the road.
quotes.speaker: Tim Potter (Town of Grundy personnel director)

cards.title: Unanchored sales-lot mobile homes floated into buildings
cards.place: Mobile home park and sales lot, mouth of Looney's Creek, near Grundy, VA
cards.note: Trailers on display for sale were not permanently mounted, lifted off, and scraped between apartment buildings, threatening people trapped inside; a double-wide disappeared once it reached the main channel.
cards.verify: Buchanan County floodplain ordinance anchoring requirements; business license for the sales lot; 1977 photos
cards.ask_next: Are mobile home sales lots in the floodplain now required to anchor or move inventory when a warning is issued?

quotes.text: I guess they weren't really permanently mounted. They were just more or less there for display or for sale.
quotes.speaker: Tim Potter (Town of Grundy personnel director)

quotes.text: When they go through sideways they were scraping both sides of both buildings.
quotes.speaker: Tim Potter (Town of Grundy personnel director)

cards.title: Slate Creek backs up into Long Bottom at Levisa flood stage
cards.place: Slate Creek mouth and Long Bottom, Route 83, Grundy, VA
cards.note: Slate Creek drains well by itself but meets the Levisa at an abrupt angle; when the river is at flood stage the creek cannot get in and backs up, flooding Long Bottom. The narrator also says upstream Oakwood ran off first and Grundy flooded last.
cards.verify: Corps of Engineers Grundy flood study backwater profiles for Slate Creek; Levisa gauge at Grundy
cards.ask_next: When the Levisa is high, how far up Slate Creek does backwater reach, and which homes in Long Bottom flood first?

quotes.text: So that when that channel is at flood stage, the secondary channel can't gain access, so the water backs up.
quotes.speaker: Ronald Cole (operations manager, WNRG radio, Grundy)

quotes.text: And they did have flooding in the Long Bottom section, which is the first large community that you come to proceeding up Route 83 on Slate Creek.
quotes.speaker: Ronald Cole (operations manager, WNRG radio, Grundy)

quotes.text: So it was hitting Grundy kind of last, as far as the flood stage was concerned.
quotes.speaker: Ronald Cole (operations manager, WNRG radio, Grundy)

cards.title: Floodplain repair limits froze Grundy's old downtown buildings
cards.place: Main Street, Grundy, VA
cards.note: Both narrators describe a 50 percent improvement limit and a no-rebuild rule after destruction as keeping owners from repairing downtown buildings, so rents stayed high and storefronts emptied. This is how they understood the rules.
cards.verify: Grundy and Buchanan County floodplain ordinance text; substantial improvement determinations on Main Street
cards.ask_next: How many Main Street owners asked about repairs and were told the 50 percent rule applied?

quotes.text: Because you can only do fifty percent of what the property value's worth.
quotes.speaker: Tim Potter (Town of Grundy personnel director)

quotes.text: And plus the fact if you buy a lot that's designated in the floodplain with a structure on it and that structure is destroyed by fire or any other cause, you can't rebuild in a floodplain.
quotes.speaker: Ronald Cole (operations manager, WNRG radio, Grundy)

cards.title: Weston floods about yearly; schools and firehouse in floodplain
cards.place: Weston, Lewis County, WV
cards.note: A Weston businessman says records since 1929 show about one flood a year, and the downtown, main schools, churches and the fire department sit in the floodplain of three streams. Plant workers are sent home early to get through before roads flood.
cards.verify: West Fork River gauge at Weston (record since 1929); critical facility locations on the Weston FIRM
cards.ask_next: Has the fire station or any school been moved out of the floodplain since Stonewall Jackson Dam was finished?

quotes.text: Floods occur in Weston on the average of once a year, and have been as long as we know.
quotes.speaker: Bill Adler (Weston businessman)

quotes.text: The fire department is in the flood plain.
quotes.speaker: Bill Adler (Weston businessman)

quotes.text: All the employees have to go home when floods occur so they can get home before the water gets too high.
quotes.speaker: Bill Adler (Weston businessman)

cards.title: Small watershed dams needed 50 percent local share
cards.place: Upper West Fork watershed, Lewis County, WV
cards.note: Weston backers say they rejected the small-watershed alternative because the county would have paid half the cost and Soil Conservation told them planning alone would take eight years; the big dam was federally funded.
cards.verify: SCS (now NRCS) PL-566 cost-share rules and planning records for the upper West Fork, 1974-80
cards.ask_next: Was a small watershed plan ever costed for the upper West Fork, and what was the local share in dollars?

quotes.text: But worse than that, the local community would be required to pay fifty percent of the cost of a small watershed system.
quotes.speaker: Bill Adler (Weston businessman)

quotes.text: We were told that it would be eight years in the planning alone.
quotes.speaker: Bill Adler (Weston businessman)

cards.title: Pay landowners before construction; awards took years to arrive
cards.place: Stonewall Jackson Lake take area, Skin Creek and Roanoke, Lewis County, WV
cards.note: A displaced farmer says appraising and settling with everyone before work began would have let people relocate on their own terms; she had a move-out date but no check, and court awards took two or three years. A supporter estimates about 20 percent of owners went to commissioners.
cards.verify: Corps Huntington District acquisition files and condemnation case dates for Stonewall Jackson Lake
cards.ask_next: In a buyout, how long did it take from offer to payment, and what did people do in between?

quotes.text: my theory was that they should have come in here and appraised and settled with everyone before any of this was started.
quotes.speaker: Mary Aspinall (Skin Creek dairy farmer)

quotes.text: You go to court, and you are given a certain amount of money. It's two or three years before you get that.
quotes.speaker: Mary Aspinall (Skin Creek dairy farmer)

quotes.text: But some amount of the property was maybe twenty percent of the landowners elected that course.
quotes.speaker: Bill Adler (Weston businessman)

cards.title: Local office told a homeowner it was safe to build
cards.place: Village above Skin Creek, Stonewall Jackson Lake area, Lewis County, WV
cards.note: A young man asked the local Corps office before building a new home, was told to go ahead, and later had the house taken and moved. The narrator says unqualified staff should refer questions instead of answering.
cards.verify: Corps take-line maps by date; building permit and acquisition dates for the village houses
cards.ask_next: When people ask whether they can build, who gives the answer, and is it written down?

quotes.text: now, the one boy, before he built this new home, he went to them and asked them if he was safe to build the home.
quotes.speaker: Mary Aspinall (Skin Creek dairy farmer)

quotes.text: But instead of that, they believed that information that they got from the local core office.
quotes.speaker: Mary Aspinall (Skin Creek dairy farmer)

cards.title: Relocated roads would cause slips, Highway Department warned
cards.place: West Fork valley roads, Lewis County, WV
cards.note: A dam opponent recalls the State Highway Department opposing the project around 1950 because existing roads were already on the best routes and relocated roads would bring slips and more maintenance. Relocated roads around reservoirs are a slide watch list.
cards.verify: WV State Road Commission correspondence on the dam (c. 1950); WVDOH slide repair records on relocated Lewis County roads
cards.ask_next: Which relocated roads around the lake have had slides since they were built?

quotes.text: One reason they opposed it was because they'd already put the roads on the best routes.
quotes.speaker: Francine Snyder (dam opponent, Roanoke area)

quotes.text: That's why the roads were located there, and that the new road relocations would – there would be slips, and there would be all kinds of problems that would require so much more maintenance by the road department that they opposed the project back in 1950.
quotes.speaker: Francine Snyder (dam opponent, Roanoke area)

cards.title: Debris breaking windows or doors caused sudden interior flooding
cards.place: Homes and downtown businesses, Grundy, VA
cards.note: Residents tried to keep water out by blocking doors, and held it to a few inches until floating debris broke a window or door. Water then filled the space almost at once, and in one store it pulled merchandise out a back window.
cards.verify: Post-1977 damage assessments and insurance claims for Grundy structures; Corps nonstructural flood-proofing study for Grundy (window and door openings, debris loads).
cards.ask_next: When you design flood-proofing or dry flood-proofing for structures here, how do you account for floating debris breaking openings, and do you tell owners not to rely on sealing doors?

quotes.text: Like one second we had six inches of water, the next thing we had three and a half foot of water.
quotes.speaker: Tim Potter (Grundy town personnel director; age 10-11 in 1977)

quotes.text: When the window broke, that let the water come in.
quotes.speaker: Tim Potter (Grundy town personnel director; age 10-11 in 1977)

quotes.text: A big span of wood came through this front door. The pressure then burst out a window in the back, and it just siphoned merchandise out the window.
quotes.speaker: unidentified speaker (FS)

cards.title: Grundy flood plan shifted from walls to highway-as-levee and relocation
cards.place: Downtown Grundy and the depot site, Grundy, VA
cards.event: Corps study 1982-1997, after the April 1977 flood
cards.note: The Corps project manager says reservoirs, floodwalls, channels and diversion tunnels studied in 1982-86 gave too little protection or cost too much once 1986 cost-sharing applied. The plan then moved to nonstructural measures combined with VDOT's Route 460, whose four-lane would act as part of the protective wall.
cards.verify: Corps Huntington District Grundy feasibility and design reports; WRDA 1986 cost-share provisions; VDOT Route 460 Grundy design documents; the Corps-town project cooperation agreement.
cards.ask_next: Now that the highway serves as part of the levee, who is responsible for inspecting and maintaining that section, and how is residual risk explained to the businesses behind it?

quotes.text: What we found was that all these measures either did not provide the total protection required for the town of Grundy and were not affordable to either the federal government or to the non-federal sponsor.
quotes.speaker: Jim Twohig (project manager, Grundy Project, Corps of Engineers Huntington District)

quotes.text: The project cost ranged from 200 to $300 million, of which their share would have been anywhere from twenty-five to fifty percent, including a five percent cash requirement.
quotes.speaker: Jim Twohig (project manager, Grundy Project, Corps of Engineers Huntington District)

quotes.text: Basically the four lane actually itself is going to be acting as a part of the wall to protect part of the town from the river itself.
quotes.speaker: Tim Potter (Grundy town personnel director)

cards.title: Residents judge new floods by 1957 and 1977
cards.place: Grundy and the Looney's Creek area, Buchanan County, VA
cards.note: In 1977 families first prepared only for basement water, because the 1957 flood had reached basements there. A long-time resident packs a bag whenever mud reaches her carport and rejects the idea that a low water table protects the town.
cards.verify: Levisa Fork at Grundy peak stages for 1957 and 1977; NWS flood categories for the Grundy forecast point; high-water marks on downtown buildings.
cards.ask_next: What do longtime residents use as their own cue to pack up or move out, and could it be tied to a gauge stage in your warnings?

quotes.text: Because in the '57 flood they said that it did get in the basements there at the homes on that side.
quotes.speaker: Tim Potter (Grundy town personnel director)

quotes.text: Within the last ten years, it's been in the carport, mud. When it does that, I pack a suitcase, get me some shoes.
quotes.speaker: unidentified speaker (FS)

quotes.text: We've even had some people say, "Well, the water table is low." No. That makes no difference. It's our terrain.
quotes.speaker: unidentified speaker (FS)

cards.title: Cleared floodplains, not headwater timbering, seen as aggravating 1985
cards.place: Seneca Rocks area and North Fork valley, WV
cards.note: A Forest Service archeologist, calling it her own opinion, says rainfall caused the flood and cleared agricultural floodplains may have made it worse, not national forest timber cutting. She cautions against labeling it a 500- or 1000-year flood, though it destroyed sites that earlier floods had spared for 2,000 to 3,000 years.
cards.verify: USGS peak-flow frequency analyses for the North Fork South Branch Potomac (1985); Forest Service harvest records for affected headwaters; archeological site records at Seneca Rocks and stratigraphy in the visitor-center channel cut.
cards.ask_next: When you talk with landowners about the 1985 flood, do you use return periods, and would floodplain revegetation or buffers on North Fork farmland be eligible for mitigation funding?

quotes.text: I think that the absence of vegetation in the floodplains because they're agricultural lands may have aggravated the flood.
quotes.speaker: Janet Brashler (forest archeologist, USDA Forest Service)

quotes.text: The flood that we had here, I think is really – can't be attributed to land management practices anywhere outside of the floodplain.
quotes.speaker: Janet Brashler (forest archeologist, USDA Forest Service)

quotes.text: I think you have to be really cautious about saying this is a 500-year, or a 1000-year, or 2000-year flood because those are statistical figures.
quotes.speaker: Janet Brashler (forest archeologist, USDA Forest Service)

cards.title: Buildings built in Slate Creek blamed for backing water into town
cards.place: Mouth of Slate Creek at Levisa Fork, downtown Grundy, VA
cards.note: A lifelong resident says the theater, firehouse and other buildings were built in the creek during her lifetime and block Slate Creek's outflow; the mayor says the town has cleaned riverbanks to improve flow.
cards.verify: Historic Sanborn maps or aerials of Slate Creek; building permits for structures over the channel; Corps hydraulic model of the Slate Creek confluence.
cards.ask_next: Which structures now sit in or over the Slate Creek channel, and does your hydraulic model show them raising flood stages upstream?

quotes.text: The way it is it blocks the water coming from Slate Creek into Levisa River, which makes it backup into the homes and businesses.
quotes.speaker: Marie Williams

quotes.text: The firehouse and several buildings are just right in the creek. When I grew up they were not there.
quotes.speaker: Marie Williams

quotes.text: But the town has spent a lot of money cleaning up the riverbanks and different things to give the water a better flow.
quotes.speaker: John Fleenor (mayor of Grundy)

cards.title: Flood threat deterred downtown investment; relocation to flood-free depot site
cards.place: Depot site across the Levisa Fork from the courthouse, Grundy, VA
cards.note: The redevelopment planner ties downtown decline to repeated flooding and describes moving commerce to flood-free sites; a merchant says owners hesitate to repair old buildings because of the next flood.
cards.verify: Grundy redevelopment plan and depot-site grading elevations versus 1977 flood level; post-project business relocation records.
cards.ask_next: How many downtown businesses actually relocated to the depot site, and what happened to those that stayed in the old floodplain?

quotes.text: As long as Grundy is seen as being under a serious flood threat, I think it can be expected to be a deterrent to downtown investment.
quotes.speaker: David Hefley (Chief of Planning, Booker Associates)

quotes.text: Number one, there will be many large flood-free sites available for redevelopment.
quotes.speaker: David Hefley (Chief of Planning, Booker Associates)

quotes.text: Well, the cost. Not only the cost, but the 'when are we going to have the next big flood.'
quotes.speaker: Dorothy Trivett

cards.title: Stonewall Jackson Dam: land taken far exceeded flood pool; floodplain relocation rejected
cards.place: West Fork River and Weston, Lewis County, WV
cards.note: A dam opponent contrasts 21,000 acres acquired with a 3,450-acre flood pool and says the Corps declined relocating Weston's floodplain properties, citing psychological harm.
cards.verify: Corps Pittsburgh/Huntington District Stonewall Jackson Lake real estate design memorandum and environmental documents; Weston flood damage history.
cards.ask_next: Was nonstructural relocation of Weston's floodplain ever costed against the dam, and what flood damages has Weston had since the dam opened?

quotes.text: I mean, they're buying 21,000 acres, and at flood pool, the lake is only 3450 acres.
quotes.speaker: Francine Snyder (West Fork Watershed Association)

quotes.text: At one point, you know, we said to the core, "Why not relocate the houses and businesses in the flood plain? That makes the most sense.
quotes.speaker: Francine Snyder (West Fork Watershed Association)

quotes.text: In it, it says that one reason that they didn't relocate – wouldn't consider relocating the flood plain is because they've discovered that it's psychologically harmful to relocate people.
quotes.speaker: Francine Snyder (West Fork Watershed Association)

cards.title: Sudden surge swept sheriff's vehicle off new St. George bridge approach
cards.place: St. George bridge approach, Cheat River, St. George, WV
cards.note: The sheriff and a state trooper crossed the approach once, then on the return a sudden wave washed their vehicle off; they note the bridge was newly finished. (OCR-transcribed interview.)
